triage.summary:
The gap is closed, and has been for a long time. Your database's best upper bound, σ√(KT log K), is the UCB-type rate. Algorithms that remove the √log K factor already exist, so the minimax regret for K-armed stochastic bandits with σ-subgaussian noise and known σ is Θ(σ√(KT)). That matches the Ω(√(KT)) lower bound (Auer et al. 2002, Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi 2012) up to constants.

1. **MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck, COLT 2009).** It reaches O(√(KT)) minimax regret. Its exploration bonus uses log₊(T/(K·n)) in place of log t. Both the Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi survey (arXiv:1204.5721) and arXiv:2511.18750, as seen in search results, describe it as the first minimax-optimal stochastic bandit algorithm and say it removes the extra √log K factor of UCB. I did not fetch the original paper, so I am not sure whether to date it 2009 (COLT) or 2010.
2. **The Lattimore–Szepesvári book (Bandit Algorithms, 2020).** Its table of contents shows Chapter 9, "The Upper Confidence Bound Algorithm: Minimax Optimality", with a section 9.1 on MOSS. I believe the chapter proves an O(√(Kn)) bound for 1-subgaussian rewards, but I did not see the theorem text this session, so I have not verified it.
3. **ADA-UCB (Lattimore, JMLR 2018).** Seen on the JMLR page, this strategy is minimax optimal up to constants and also asymptotically optimal for Gaussian noise. The paper says the upper bounds extend to subgaussian noise with a known constant.
4. **KL-UCB++ (Ménard & Garivier, ALT 2017, arXiv:1702.07211).** Its title states it is both minimax and asymptotically optimal, but for exponential-family rewards rather than general subgaussian noise.

Rescaling by σ gives the σ√(KT) rate, since σ is known.

papers.title: Minimax Policies for Adversarial and Stochastic Bandits (MOSS) — Audibert & Bubeck
papers.claim: MOSS reaches O(√(KT)) minimax regret for stochastic K-armed bandits, removing UCB's √log K factor. Its exploration bonus uses log₊(T/(K n)). Survey (arXiv:1204.5721) and arXiv:2511.18750, as seen in search results, call it the first minimax-optimal algorithm. The original paper was not fetched; it is cited as 2009 in some sources and 2010 in others.

papers.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems (Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi)
papers.claim: Per the search-result summary, the survey states MOSS regret is at most of order min{√(nK), (K/Δ) ln(nΔ²/K)} up to a numerical constant, and calls MOSS and PolyINF the first proved minimax-optimal algorithms.

papers.title: Refining the Confidence Level for Optimistic Bandit Strategies (Lattimore, JMLR 19)
papers.claim: ADA-UCB is minimax optimal up to constants, asymptotically optimal and sub-UCB for unit-variance Gaussian noise. The paper says the upper bounds extend to subgaussian noise with a known subgaussian constant.

papers.title: A minimax and asymptotically optimal algorithm for stochastic bandits (KL-UCB++, Ménard & Garivier)
papers.claim: Minimax-optimal O(√(KT)) and asymptotically optimal for exponential-family rewards. Per the search-result summary, the paper notes MOSS is not asymptotically optimal.

papers.title: Bandit Algorithms (Lattimore & Szepesvári), Chapter 9 'The Upper Confidence Bound Algorithm: Minimax Optimality'
papers.claim: Table of contents (seen) shows Chapter 9 on minimax optimality of UCB, with section 9.1 'The MOSS Algorithm'. The O(√(kn)) bound for 1-subgaussian rewards is not verified: theorem text was not seen this session.

triage.summary: Setting: stochastic linear bandit, fixed infinite action set with bounded norm, worst case over action sets. Upper bound d·√T·log T (OFUL, Abbasi-Yadkori et al. 2011); lower bound Ω(d·√T) (unit ball: Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis 2010, Lattimore & Szepesvári 2020). No source found this session closes this gap or explicitly calls it open, hence 'blank'. Related results that don't settle it: (1) Li, Wang & Zhou (COLT 2019, arXiv 1904.00242) prove Ω(d·√(T·log T)) for infinite action sets, but their introduction says it holds only 'when the action space changes over time'. Their matching upper bound (VCL-SupLinUCB) is for finitely many actions per round. So it does not apply to a fixed action set. (2) 'Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms' (arXiv 2502.17175, 2025) gives E2TC, which matches the lower bound Ω(min(d·σ·√T + d·‖θ‖_A, ‖θ‖_A·T)) up to a universal constant. That closes the gap for ellipsoidal sets including the unit ball, but not for arbitrary shapes. PEGE (Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis 2010) already gets O((‖θ‖+1/‖θ‖)·d·√T) on the unit ball with no log factor. For arbitrary fixed infinite action sets I found no lower bound above d·√T. I did not confirm a d·√(T·log T) upper bound for fixed infinite sets in any source this session, so the gap is between √(log T) and log T depending on whether that bound holds. I could not retrieve the Lattimore–Szepesvári book's chapter notes to check whether they call the remaining factor open. Authors of arXiv 2502.17175 and 1905.01435 were not confirmed this session, so they are not listed.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits (Yingkai Li, Yining Wang, Yuan Zhou)
papers.claim: Lower bound Ω(√(d·T·log T·log n)) for finite action sets and Ω(d·√(T·log T)) for infinite action sets that change over time. VCL-SupLinUCB matches up to iterated-log factors for finite action sets.

papers.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms
papers.claim: For ellipsoidal action sets (including the unit ball): lower bound Ω(min(d·σ·√T + d·‖θ‖_A, ‖θ‖_A·T)), and the E2TC algorithm matches it up to a universal constant, removing log factors.

papers.title: Tight Regret Bounds for Infinite-armed Linear Contextual Bandits
papers.claim: O(d·√(T·log T)·poly(log log T)) upper bound with a varying-confidence-level SupLinUCB, for the infinite-armed contextual setting with time-varying arms.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linear Contextual Bandits with Arbitrary Adaptive Action Sets (Tianyuan Jin)
papers.claim: Bounds for K-armed adaptive menus, matching up to log factors. Does not address fixed infinite action sets.

triage.summary: For fixed arbitrary compact action sets, the upper bound can be tightened to about d√(T log T)·poly(log log T) (Li & Chen 2019/2021; their setting allows changing action sets, so it should cover a fixed set). That beats the d√T·log^1.5 T rate inherited from Dani et al. The matching lower bound Ω(d√(T log T)) (Li, Wang & Zhou 2019) needs the action set to change between rounds, so it does not apply here. For fixed sets the best lower bound found is Ω(d√T) (unit ball or hypercube). So a √log T gap remains. For ellipsoids, which include the unit ball, it is closed: arXiv 2502.17175 (2025) shows Θ(dσ√T + d‖θ‖) up to constants. Banerjee & Gopalan (2023) say the Lattimore–Szepesvári book flags characterizing minimax regret across a wide variety of action spaces as an open problem. That statement is general and does not name this exact √log T gap. No paper found closes the gap for general compact fixed sets. The banditalgs.com blog could not be fetched (expired certificate).

papers.title: Tight Regret Bounds for Infinite-armed Linear Contextual Bandits
papers.claim: Upper bound O(sqrt(d^2 T log T)) x poly(log log T) for (possibly changing) infinite action sets. It matches the Omega(d sqrt(T log T)) lower bound of Li et al. 2019 up to iterated-log factors.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits
papers.claim: Lower bound Omega(d sqrt(T log T)) for infinite action sets, but the construction uses time-varying action sets, so it does not apply to a fixed action set.

papers.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms
papers.claim: For ellipsoid action sets (including the unit ball), the E2TC algorithm matches the lower bound Omega(min(d sigma sqrt(T) + d||theta||_A, ||theta||_A T)) up to a universal constant, so the log gap is closed for ellipsoids. Authors not verified in this session.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Linear Bandits in a wide variety of Action Spaces
papers.claim: Banerjee & Gopalan: the abstract says characterizing the minimax regret of linear bandits across a wide variety of action spaces was flagged as open in the Lattimore-Szepesvari book. They prove an optimal-order lower bound for a broad class of convex action sets (only the abstract was read).

triage.summary: Your database's bounds are order sqrt(KT log(K/delta)) above and sqrt(KT log(1/delta)) below (Gerchinovitz & Lattimore 2016), a sqrt(log K) gap at fixed delta. A 2026 arXiv preprint (Bacchiocchi, Cesari, Colomboni, 2608.12231, v2 25 Aug 2026) proves the matching lower bound in its Theorem 2. For any algorithm, a deterministic adaptive adversary with losses in [0,1] forces P(R_T >= c*sqrt(dT(log C(d,m) + log(1/delta)))) >= delta. This holds for delta <= delta_0 (a universal constant whose value the paper does not give) and T above a threshold polynomial in d, m and log(1/delta). With m=1 this is Omega(sqrt(KT log(K/delta))). The authors say this closes the remaining log K gap left by Gerchinovitz & Lattimore. Their algorithm's upper bound, O(sqrt(KT log(K/delta))), matches EXP3-KW, so the bound is tight up to constants. Caveats: (1) the lower bound needs an adaptive (non-anticipating) adversary, and the paper does not settle the oblivious case, where the only known lower bound remains sqrt(KT log(1/delta)); (2) the result is for confidence-tuned algorithms (delta fixed in advance); (3) it is a single, very recent preprint, not peer reviewed as far as I can tell. Gerchinovitz & Lattimore themselves (full text read) do not mention the log K gap or call it open. I tried to check Audibert & Bubeck's JMLR 2010 and COLT 2009 PDFs for a high-probability bound without log K under oblivious adversaries, but neither PDF rendered, so that question is unchecked.

papers.title: An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial m-Set Bandits
papers.claim: Theorem 2: for any randomized policy there is a deterministic adaptive non-anticipating adversary (losses in [0,1]) with P(R_T >= c*sqrt(dT(log C(d,m) + log(1/delta)))) >= delta, for delta <= delta_0 and T large. With m=1 this gives Omega(sqrt(KT log(K/delta))), which the authors say closes the log K gap left by Gerchinovitz & Lattimore. Their matching upper bound is O(sqrt(KT log(K/delta))) against adaptive adversaries, the same as EXP3-KW.

papers.title: Refined Lower Bounds for Adversarial Bandits
papers.claim: Theorem 1 gives a high-probability lower bound of sqrt((K-1)T log(1/(4 delta))), even for loss sequences fixed in advance. Upper bounds for delta-tuned Exp3.P-type algorithms are of order sqrt(KT log(K/delta)). The paper does not discuss this log K gap or list it as open.

papers.title: Explore no more: Improved high-probability regret bounds for non-stochastic bandits
papers.claim: Exp3-IX high-probability upper bound (the database's best upper bound).

triage.summary: The gap is closed when |F| is fixed and only K and T are tracked. Use each f in F's greedy policy, plus a uniform expert, as the experts for Exp4 (N ≤ |F|+1). Exp4 (Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund, Schapire 2002) then gets expected regret O(sqrt(KT ln N)) = O(sqrt(KT log|F|)), even against adversarial sequences. That is O(sqrt(KT)) with no log T factor, which matches the Omega(sqrt(KT)) lower bound already on file. Exp4.P (Beygelzimer et al. 2011) gives the same rate with high probability. Caveat: if |F| were tracked, a sqrt(log K) gap could remain. A survey reports a lower bound of order sqrt(KT log N / log K) for the related bandits-with-expert-advice problem, attributed to Seldin & Lugosi 2016. I did not check that it carries over to the realizable stochastic-context setting.

papers.title: The Nonstochastic Multiarmed Bandit Problem (Exp4)
papers.claim: Exp4 has expected regret O(sqrt(TK ln N)) against N experts when the experts include a uniform expert, which holds for any loss sequence. With the induced policies of a finite F as experts, this gives O(sqrt(KT)) for fixed |F|.

papers.title: Contextual Bandit Algorithms with Supervised Learning Guarantees
papers.claim: Exp4.P achieves O(sqrt(KT ln(N/delta))) regret with probability 1-delta.

papers.title: Bypassing the Monster: A Faster and Simpler Optimal Algorithm for Contextual Bandits under Realizability
papers.claim: Gives a statistically optimal, oracle-efficient algorithm for realizable contextual bandits over a general function class F; exact finite-class rate not seen (only the abstract was read).

triage.summary: The polynomial gap in K and the log T gap are closed by existing results; a residual √(log K) factor remains open for i.i.d. contexts. Lower bound: Agarwal et al. (AISTATS 2012, arXiv:1202.1334), Theorem 5.1, gives Ω(√(KT ln N/ln K)) for any N, K with ln N/ln K ≤ T. The instance has i.i.d. contexts (uniform over ⌊ln N/ln K⌋ values) and Bernoulli rewards, and the bound holds even under realizability, so it applies to the agnostic policy-class setting. This replaces the database's min(√(KT), N+√T) and gives K exponent 1/2 rather than 0. Upper bound: results against adversaries also hold for i.i.d. data. EXP4 gives O(√(KT ln N)) with no log T (cited from standard knowledge, not fetched this session), and O(√(KT log(N/K))) (Kale 2014) is reported as known in Ito 2024 and Cesa-Bianchi et al. 2024. Remaining gap: √(KT log(N/K)) vs √(KT log N/log K). The matching Ω(√(KT log(N/K))) lower bounds (Ito NeurIPS 2024, restricted feedback; Cesa-Bianchi et al. 2024, restricted feedback; Chase–Ito–Mehalel COLT 2026, adaptive non-stochastic adversary) do not directly transfer to i.i.d. contexts. I found no paper that states this stochastic log K gap as open, and none that closes it.

papers.title: Contextual Bandit Learning with Predictable Rewards
papers.claim: Theorem 5.1: for any N,K with ln N/ln K <= T, there exist a class of size <= N and an i.i.d. distribution D(x,r) (realizable) on which every algorithm has expected regret Omega(sqrt(KT ln N / ln K)); contexts i.i.d. uniform on floor(ln N/ln K) values.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Contextual Linear Bandits and Multi-Armed Bandits with Expert Advice
papers.claim: Ito (NeurIPS 2024): previously known bounds for bandits with expert advice were O(sqrt(KT log(N/K))) upper and Omega(sqrt(KT log N/log K)) lower; proves Omega(sqrt(KT log(N/K))) when the player picks an expert before seeing advice.

papers.title: Improved Regret Bounds for Bandits with Expert Advice
papers.claim: Cesa-Bianchi, Eldowa, Esposito, Olkhovskaya: lower bound of order sqrt(KT ln(N/K)) under a restricted feedback model, matching the known upper bound; standard-feedback case left unsettled.

papers.title: A Tight Lower Bound for Non-stochastic Multi-armed Bandits with Expert Advice
papers.claim: Chase, Ito, Mehalel (COLT 2026): Theorem 6.1, for T >= K ln(N/K) there is an adaptive adversary with R_T = Omega(sqrt(TK log(N/K))), so minimax is Theta(sqrt(TK log(N/K))) in the non-stochastic setting; the construction is adaptive, not i.i.d., and the oblivious case is only conjectured.

triage.summary: The log gap is a database artifact: the classical minimax lower bound is Omega(sqrt(KT)) for K>=2, so Omega(sqrt(T)) for K=2. Sources: Auer et al. 2002 (lower bound stated in the abstract, proved via a stochastic Bernoulli construction); the Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi 2012 survey (Bernoulli construction, order sqrt(nK)); Lattimore-Szepesvari Ch. 15 (1/27·sqrt((K-1)T), seen as restated in Azize & Basu 2022, Theorem 2, for Gaussian rewards). This matches the O(sqrt(T)) upper bounds (MOSS, KL-UCB-switch, Foster et al.), so only constant factors differ. Caveat: no PDF could be text-extracted (all fetches returned compressed binary), so I did not see the exact theorem statements or constants of Auer et al. 2002 or the survey. The Bernoulli/[0,1] applicability rests on the abstract, a search snippet and tutorial slides, not on the verified theorem text.

papers.title: The Nonstochastic Multiarmed Bandit Problem (Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund, Schapire), SIAM J. Comput.
papers.claim: Abstract: a matching lower bound shows the O(T^{-1/2}) per-round regret rate cannot be improved, i.e. Omega(sqrt(KT)) cumulative regret for K>=2. Bubeck's tutorial slides tie the hard case to a stochastic instance with gap ~1/sqrt(T). I could not read the theorem text.

papers.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi)
papers.claim: Search snippet: minimax lower bound of order sqrt(nK) for Bernoulli arms, with one arm shifted by ~sqrt(K/n), proved via KL divergence and Pinsker. Exact theorem not seen.

papers.title: When Privacy Meets Partial Information: A Refined Analysis of Differentially Private Bandits (Azize, Basu)
papers.claim: Theorem 2 restates the standard (Lattimore-Szepesvari) minimax lower bound (1/27)·sqrt(T(K-1)) for K>1, T>=K-1. Stated for Gaussian rewards.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed up to iterated-log factors, and the paper that closes it is the one the database already takes its lower bound from: Li, Wang & Zhou (COLT 2019, arXiv:1904.00242).

**Setting.** Linear contextual bandits with adversarial, time-varying finite action sets of size n.

**Lower bound.** The paper proves Ω(√(dT log T log n)) for n ≤ 2^{d/2}, valid when T ≥ d(log₂ n)^{1+ε}. Taking n = 2^{d/2} recovers the database's Ω(d√(T log T)); that substitution is my own inference, the paper does not state it.

**Upper bound.** The same paper's Variable-Confidence-Level (VCL) SupLinUCB algorithm "matches the lower bound up to iterated logarithmic factors". That gives O(√(dT log T log n)·poly(log log T)), which saves two √log T factors over earlier SupLinUCB analyses. The database instead lists LinTS (Agrawal & Goyal 2013), which is much looser.

**What remains open.** Only a poly(log log T) gap. If the database insists on exact log tightness, "open_known (log log gap)" would be the stricter label.

**Caveats.**
- I read only the abstract and search summaries, not the paper's theorem statements. The explicit form √(dT log T log n)·poly(log log T) is inferred from the abstract's "matches the lower bound up to iterated logarithmic factors" and a talk abstract by Yuan Zhou.
- I didn't check whether the upper bound's analysis needs any extra assumption beyond this setting, e.g. knowing σ.

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.00242 ; https://proceedings.mlr.press/v99/li19b.html ; https://itcs.sufe.edu.cn/41/5b/c10453a213339/page.htm

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits
papers.claim: Lower bound Ω(√(dT log T log n)) for finite time-varying action sets (n ≤ 2^{d/2}). The VCL SupLinUCB algorithm matches this lower bound up to iterated-logarithmic factors, saving two √log T factors over previous analyses. For infinite action sets, a talk abstract gives O(√(d²T log T)·poly(log log T)) against a lower bound of Ω(√(d²T log T)).

triage.summary:
The gap is not closed, but it is narrower than the database shows. The best upper bound in the database is O(d^{3/2}√T), from Theorem 1 of Ailon, Hatano & Takimoto (arXiv:1312.1530). That same paper uses the database's loss normalization (|π·s_t| ≤ 1 for all π, a loss set dual to the permutahedron). It states that CombBand (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2009) already gets regret O(n√(T log n)) in this setting. The catch is that CombBand needs to approximate a matrix permanent at each step, so it is computationally inefficient. The authors present their own O(n^{3/2}√T) bound as 'slightly worse regret' in exchange for O(n³) time per step. So the information-theoretic upper bound should be Õ(d√T), not d^{3/2}√T. Their main open question is whether O(n√T) regret can be achieved in O(n³) time: that is a question about efficiency, not about the minimax rate. They also give an efficient O(n√T) algorithm, but only for the more restricted loss class ‖s_t‖₁ ≤ 1.

On the lower bound side, I found no lower bound specific to the permutahedron that beats the generic Ω(√(dT)). The general Ω(d√T) lower bound for bandit linear optimization (Dani et al.) is proved for other action sets, such as the hypercube, so it does not automatically carry over here. Cohen, Hazan & Koren (arXiv:1702.07539) leave the regret rate for full permutations open, but they use a different combinatorial (semi-bandit-style) normalization. That makes the remaining exponent gap in d (0.5 vs 1, ignoring log factors) neither shown to be resolved nor explicitly identified as open in this normalization.

papers.title: Bandit Online Optimization Over the Permutahedron (Ailon, Hatano, Takimoto)
papers.claim: With losses satisfying |π·s_t| ≤ 1: BanditRank has regret O(n^{3/2}√T) at O(n³) time per step, and the paper reports that CombBand (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2009) achieves O(n√(T log n)) using permanent approximations. Under ‖s_t‖₁ ≤ 1, OSMDRank has regret O(n√T). The open question posed is about efficiency (O(n√T) regret in O(n³) time). The paper proves no bandit lower bound.

papers.title: Tight Bounds for Bandit Combinatorial Optimization (Cohen, Hazan, Koren)
papers.claim: Shows Θ̃(k^{3/2}√(dT)) regret for bandit combinatorial optimization, and leaves open the full-permutation case (k = n), asking whether the rate is Θ(n²√T). This uses a different loss normalization.

triage.summary: No result found that closes or explicitly flags as open the d-gap (O(n√T) upper vs generic Ω(√(nT)) lower) for adversarial bandit linear optimization over the permutahedron. In this setting the learner plays permutahedron vertices (permutations of {1,…,n}, d = n). Ailon–Hatano–Takimoto (ALT 2014) give O(n^{3/2}√T) for losses in the dual polytope (efficient, O(n³) per step) and O(n√T) for losses in the hypercube, but only for a more restricted set of loss vectors; the latter is presumably the database's Theorem 4. CombBand gets O(n√(T log n)) but needs a permanent each step. Searches turned up no permutahedron-specific lower bound. Cohen–Hazan–Koren (2017) and Ito et al. (2019) prove Θ(√(k³dT)) lower bounds for 0/1 combinatorial bandits including 'bandit ranking'. Ito et al. say their ranking result answers an open problem raised by Cohen et al.; per a search summary (unverified) that problem concerned full permutations, possibly asking whether the rate is Θ(n²√T). These results use the 0/1 permutation-matrix (assignment) representation with d = n², k = n and losses in [0,1]^d, not the permutahedron with d = n, so they don't carry over. PDF fetches returned unreadable compressed data, so I couldn't check Theorem 4's loss assumptions (e.g. whether it uses the ℓ1 ball) or whether the Ailon et al. paper discusses lower bounds or open problems.

papers.title: Bandit Online Optimization Over the Permutahedron
papers.claim: Regret O(n^{3/2}√T) with O(n^3) time per step for losses in the dual polytope; O(n√T) for hypercube losses, but only for a more restricted set of loss vectors. CombBand gets O(n√(T log n)) but needs a permanent computation each step.

papers.title: Tight Bounds for Bandit Combinatorial Optimization
papers.claim: Regret rate ~k^{3/2}√(dT) for 0/1 bandit combinatorial optimization, with lower bounds for instances including bandit shortest path and online ranking (0/1 representation, not the permutahedron).

papers.title: Improved Regret Bounds for Bandit Combinatorial Optimization
papers.claim: Lower bound Ω(√(dk³T)) (removes a √log T factor from Cohen et al.); applies to bandit ranking and, per the authors, answers an open problem raised by Cohen et al. 0/1 action vectors, not the permutahedron.

triage.summary: No published result closes the gap and none calls it open, so the verdict is blank. The recorded bounds also look unreliable. The upper bound O(√(dT log³T)) is Ailon, Karnin & Joachims (2014), Corollary 3.2, which I read in full text: Doubler with CONFIDENCEBALL2 on a compact convex set. It is probably a slip: Dani et al.'s CONFIDENCEBALL2 bound is about d√T times polylog factors (a secondary source also gives O(d√T)). With Theorem 3.1 of the same paper (constant overhead for base algorithms with polynomial regret), the correct reading is about d√(T log³T). My own unpublished argument suggests the lower bound should be d√T, not √(dT). With a linear link, a standard bandit learner can simulate a duel (x, y) by playing x and y and drawing a coin with probability (1 + r_x − r_y)/2. Standard linear-bandit lower bounds on convex sets (Dani et al. 2008; also cited as d√T in the DP-Dueling paper, Remark 4) therefore carry over up to constants. The matching √(dT) results (Saha 2021; Bengs, Saha & Hüllermeier 2022) are for finite sets of K arms with a log K factor, so they don't apply to convex bodies; Saha's arXiv v2 also carries a 'wrong result… major revision required' comment. Doubler plus an O(d√T log T) base algorithm such as OFUL should give O(d√T log T). Against Ω(d√T) that leaves only a log T gap, and I found no paper closing it for dueling feedback on a convex body. These bounds are my combination of existing theorems; no paper states them for this setting. The arXiv PDFs came back unreadable through my tools, so I relied on a text copy of the ICML version and on abstracts.

papers.title: Reducing Dueling Bandits to Cardinal Bandits
papers.claim: Theorem 3.1: Doubler adds a log T factor for polylog-regret base algorithms and only a constant factor for polynomial-regret ones. Corollary 3.2: with CONFIDENCEBALL2 on a compact convex set, regret O(√(dT log³T)), probably a misstatement of Dani et al.'s bound of about d√T.

papers.title: Stochastic Linear Optimization Under Bandit Feedback (Dani, Hayes, Kakade, COLT 2008)
papers.claim: Abstract: optimal regret is Θ*(√T) in general, and polylog rates are ruled out except in special cases such as polytopes. CONFIDENCEBALL2 handles infinite decision sets with O(d√T)-type regret (per a secondary summary).

papers.title: Optimal Algorithms for Stochastic Contextual Preference Bandits (Saha, NeurIPS 2021)
papers.claim: Finite context sets of K arms: Õ(√(dT log K)) upper bound and Ω(√(dT)) lower bound. The arXiv v2 comment says 'Wrong result with incremental contribution, major revision required'.

papers.title: Stochastic Contextual Dueling Bandits under Linear Stochastic Transitivity Models
papers.claim: CoLSTIM gets Õ(√(dT)) regret over finite arm sets, with a matching weak-regret lower bound.

papers.title: DP-Dueling: Learning from Preference Feedback without Compromising User Privacy
papers.claim: Non-private part of the regret is about d√T/κ. Remark 4 says this is optimal up to log factors, citing a d√T lower bound from Dani et al., Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis, and Abbasi-Yadkori et al.

triage.summary: Closed for undirected strongly observable graphs; still open for directed ones. Upper bound: Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari and Cesa-Bianchi (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2305.15383) prove O(sqrt(alpha*T*(1+ln(K/alpha)))) with q-Tsallis FTRL. This beats the database's sqrt(alpha*T)*log(KT) and has no log T factor. Their own lower bound is Omega(sqrt(alpha*T*ln K/ln alpha)), which shows a log factor in K is necessary. Chen, He and Zhang (arXiv:2307.07264) prove Theta(sqrt(T*sum_k log(m_k+1))) for disjoint-clique (grouped-arm) feedback. The conclusion of Eldowa et al. says this implies their algorithm is worst-case optimal up to constants for every (K, alpha); I read that on the ar5iv page and did not open the Chen et al. theorem itself. So the worst-case rate is Theta(sqrt(alpha*T*(1+log(K/alpha)))), not sqrt(alpha*T). For directed strongly observable graphs, Eldowa et al. report a best known bound of about sqrt(alpha*T*(log K)^3) and call the extension considerably harder; my searches found no later paper closing it. The arXiv PDF did not extract, so these statements come from the ar5iv HTML and abstracts.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Online Learning with Feedback Graphs
papers.claim: Upper bound O(sqrt(alpha T (1+ln(K/alpha)))) for undirected strongly observable graphs using q-Tsallis FTRL. Lower bound Omega(sqrt(alpha T ln K / ln alpha)) for alpha >= 2. Conclusion says follow-up work on disjoint cliques implies worst-case optimality up to constants for each (K, alpha). Says the directed case is considerably harder, with best known about sqrt(alpha T (log K)^3).

papers.title: On Interpolating Experts and Multi-Armed Bandits
papers.claim: Minimax regret Theta(sqrt(T sum_k log(m_k+1))) when arms are partitioned into groups that reveal each other's losses (disjoint-clique feedback graphs). Gives the matching lower bound Omega(sqrt(alpha T log(K/alpha))) for worst-case graphs with given K and alpha.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed, and the result is in the journal version of the same work your database cites. Audibert, Bubeck & Lugosi, "Regret in Online Combinatorial Optimization" (MOR 2014; arXiv:1204.4710), studies adversarial semi-bandits over an arbitrary set S ⊂ {0,1}^d of actions with ||v||_1 = m, with each loss coordinate in [0,1] (bounded loss per coordinate). Its Theorem 4, run on the ar5iv HTML version, uses OSMD/INF with the polynomial potential ψ(x) = (−x)^{−q}. This gives R_n ≤ q·sqrt(2/(q−1)·mdn), so 2·sqrt(2mdn) at q = 2, with no log factor. That bound assumes the horizon n is known, since the learning rate depends on it.

The paper notes that the negative-entropy OSMD bound sqrt(2mdn·log(d/m)) — essentially the cited upper bound, assuming E is the cited version's name for the action size m — has "an extraneous logarithmic factor compared to the lower bound." Its results table gives matching semi-bandit lower and upper bounds of order sqrt(mdn). The minimax regret is therefore Θ(sqrt(mdT)), and the sqrt(log) gap in d (and m) is closed.

I did not confirm the exact lower-bound constant: the journal paper reaches sqrt(mdn) by reduction to the d-armed bandit lower bound and gives no explicit constant. A search snippet for the COLT 2011 version (arXiv:1105.4871) says its upper and lower bounds are tight up to a constant factor outside the bandit game, so the cited paper may already have the log-free bound. I couldn't check this because I didn't open that paper.

papers.title: Regret in Online Combinatorial Optimization
papers.claim: Theorem 4: for semi-bandit feedback with losses in [0,1]^d and arbitrary S ⊂ {0,1}^d with ||v||_1 = m, OSMD/INF with potential (−x)^{−q} gives R_n ≤ q·sqrt(2/(q−1)·mdn), i.e. 2·sqrt(2mdn) at q = 2. Matching lower bound of order sqrt(mdn), so semi-bandit minimax regret is Θ(sqrt(mdn)). The negative-entropy bound sqrt(2mdn·log(d/m)) is called suboptimal by a log factor.

papers.title: Minimax Policies for Combinatorial Prediction Games
papers.claim: COLT 2011 companion paper (the cited audibert2011minimax). A search snippet says improving the semi-bandit upper bounds is a main result and that, apart from the bandit game, the upper and lower bounds are tight up to a constant factor.

triage.summary: Known bounds: the upper bound O(sqrt(KT log(K/δ))) comes from Exp3.P and Exp3-IX (Neu 2015). The lower bound Ω(sqrt(KT log(1/δ))) is Gerchinovitz & Lattimore 2016, which per Bacchiocchi et al. holds even for losses fixed in advance. The remaining gap is sqrt(log K). Bacchiocchi, Cesari & Colomboni (arXiv:2608.12231, 2026) prove a matching Θ(sqrt(dT log(K/δ))) high-probability bound for m-set bandits. For m=1 this shows log K is unavoidable for K-armed bandits, but only against ADAPTIVE non-anticipating adversaries: the lower bound uses a deterministic adaptive adversary. The paper says: "Our corollary closes this gap when the adversary is adaptive and non-anticipating." The parts of its HTML I read (main text and part of the appendices; the rest was cut off) say nothing about oblivious adversaries. I found no paper that closes the gap for oblivious adversaries and none that explicitly calls it open. I could not check whether Audibert & Bubeck's INF (JMLR 2010) or Tsallis-INF gives a log-K-free high-probability bound for oblivious adversaries, because the PDFs came back as unreadable compressed streams. So the oblivious case is unresolved from what I could verify. Bacchiocchi et al. should be added to the database for the adaptive variant.

papers.title: An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial m-Set Bandits (Bacchiocchi, Cesari, Colomboni)
papers.claim: High-probability regret Θ(sqrt(dT log(K/δ))) against adaptive non-anticipating adversaries. For m=1 this closes the sqrt(log K) gap left by Gerchinovitz-Lattimore, but only for adaptive adversaries; the lower bound uses a deterministic adaptive adversary.

papers.title: Refined Lower Bounds for Adversarial Bandits (Gerchinovitz, Lattimore)
papers.claim: No strategy can get high-probability regret smaller than order sqrt(KT log(1/δ)) (Theorem 1). Per Bacchiocchi et al., this holds even for loss sequences fixed in advance (oblivious). The paper also notes that tuning without knowing δ moves log(1/δ) outside the square root.

papers.title: Explore no more: Improved high-probability regret bounds for non-stochastic bandits (Neu)
papers.claim: Exp3-IX achieves high-probability regret O(sqrt(KT log K) + sqrt(KT/log K) log(1/δ)), and O(sqrt(KT log(K/δ))) when tuned for δ.

triage.summary: Closed by a 2026 preprint, Bacchiocchi, Cesari & Colomboni (arXiv:2608.12231). Its Theorem 2 / Corollary 1, with m=1 and d=K, shows that for every policy there is a deterministic adaptive non-anticipating adversary (losses in [0,1]) such that, with probability at least δ, R_T ≥ c·√(KT(log K + log(1/δ))). This holds for δ ≤ δ₀, a universal constant the paper does not give explicitly, and for T above a threshold polynomial in K and log(1/δ). It matches the Exp3.P upper bound O(√(KT log(K/δ))) up to constants, so the √(log K) gap is closed against adaptive adversaries. The Gerchinovitz–Lattimore lower bound √(KT log(1/δ)) is for loss sequences fixed in advance (oblivious). The same paper's Theorem 1 gives a matching high-probability upper bound against adaptive adversaries, with constant around 160. Caveats: this is an arXiv preprint (v2) with no peer review seen; I read only the first 100k of about 168k characters of the HTML; and the δ range and T threshold are not explicit. The oblivious case may still have the gap, but it is outside this setting.

papers.title: An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial m-Set Bandits
papers.claim: For δ ≤ δ₀ and T large, every policy faces an adaptive adversary with P(R_T ≥ c√(dT(log C(d,m)) + log(1/δ)))) ≥ δ; for m=1 this is Ω(√(KT log(K/δ))), matching their high-probability upper bound C√(KT(log K + log(1/δ))) (and Exp3.P's bound).

papers.title: Refined Lower Bounds for Adversarial Bandits
papers.claim: High-probability lower bound Ω(√(KT log(1/δ))) for oblivious (fixed in advance) loss sequences.

papers.title: Explore no more: Improved high-probability regret bounds for non-stochastic bandits
papers.claim: Exp3-IX upper bound of order √(KT log(K/δ)) with high probability.

triage.summary: Both bounds come from Babaioff, Dughmi, Kleinberg and Slivkins, "Dynamic Pricing with Limited Supply" (arXiv 1108.4142, EC'12). The paper calls the budget k and the number of buyers n (B and T here). Theorem 1.2 gives an O((k log n)^{2/3}) upper bound and says the result 'is the best possible up to a factor of O(log n)'. Theorem 6.1(a) gives an Omega(k^{2/3}) lower bound with no log factor. The abstract calls the lower bound 'matching'. In the part of the paper I could read, the authors acknowledge the log gap but don't pose it as an open question. The tool only read about the first 100k of 131k characters of the ar5iv version, so a closing section may address it. Three searches found no later paper that removes the log factor or proves a lower bound with one. I didn't do a full forward-citation search of the bandits-with-knapsacks literature. Verdict: neither closed nor explicitly known to be open.

papers.title: Dynamic Pricing with Limited Supply
papers.claim: Detail-free posted-price mechanism with regret O((k log n)^{2/3}) (Thm 1.2), 'best possible up to a factor of O(log n)'; lower bound: no detail-free strategy achieves o(k^{2/3}) regret (Thm 6.1(a)).

triage.summary:
The gap is closed only for the Euclidean ball (p = 2). For a general ℓp ball I found neither a log-free d√T upper bound nor any source saying the question is open, so the verdict is "blank."

For p = 2: Zhang, Hadiji & Combes (arXiv 2502.17175, 2025) study ellipsoidal action sets, which include the ℓ2 ball. They assume sub-Gaussian noise and known σ, and need no bound on ‖θ‖. Their algorithm (E2TC) gets R_T(θ) = O(min(σd√T + d‖θ‖_A, T‖θ‖_A)) with universal constants and a matching lower bound (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.1). For ‖θ‖ ≤ 1 the worst-case regret is therefore Θ(d√T) with no log T. This removes the log^1.5 T gap left by the Dani et al. (2008) upper bound.

The lower bound already matches the database. Ω(d√T) for the unit ball is due to Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis (2010) and Lattimore & Szepesvári (2020); I saw these only as restated in other papers, not in the originals. Banerjee et al. (2301.03597) extend it to ℓp balls for p in (1, ∞), under a condition on the dimension.

For p ≠ 2, the ellipsoid paper covers ellipsoids only and lists other structured action sets as future work. Every other result I found is either adversarial (Bubeck, Cohen & Li 2018), for heavy-tailed noise (2506.04775), or carries polylog factors.

papers.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms
papers.claim: For ellipsoid action sets (including the ℓ2 ball), with sub-Gaussian noise, known σ and no bound on ‖θ‖, E2TC achieves R_T = O(min(σd√T + d‖θ‖_A, T‖θ‖_A)) with universal constants and a matching lower bound. This gives log-free minimax regret Θ(d√T) when ‖θ‖ ≤ 1.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Linear Bandits in a wide variety of Action Spaces
papers.claim: Extends the Lattimore–Szepesvári Ω(d√T) lower bound to ℓp balls for p in (1, ∞), under a condition on the dimension.

papers.title: Sparsity, variance and curvature in multi-armed bandits
papers.claim: Adversarial linear bandits on the ℓp ball: about √(nT) regret for p in [1, 2] and a lower bound of about n√T for p > 2.

triage.summary:
The T-dependence gap is mostly an artifact of how the database states its upper bounds. Its entries are high-probability bounds with delta=1/T, which brings in log(NT). Bounds on expected regret avoid this. Kale (2014) gives O(sqrt(KT log(N/K))), which Chase, Ito & Mehalel cite as the matching upper bound. That bound is proved for non-stochastic expert advice, so it should also hold when contexts are i.i.d., which is a special case.

The K-dependence gap is the real one. The lower bound is sqrt(KT log N / log K), from Agarwal et al. 2012 and Seldin & Lugosi. The upper bound is sqrt(KT log(N/K)). Recent work closed this gap, but only outside the stochastic-context setting:
- Cesa-Bianchi, Eldowa, Esposito & Olkhovskaya (arXiv 2406.16802) prove Omega(sqrt(KT ln(N/K))), but only under a restricted feedback model.
- Ito (NeurIPS 2024) proves the same lower bound for a different protocol, where the player commits to an expert before seeing the advice.
- Chase, Ito & Mehalel (arXiv 2511.00257, COLT 2026) settle the minimax rate for the standard non-stochastic problem at Theta(sqrt(TK log(N/K))). Their hard instance uses an adaptive adversary: advice for a batch of arms is redrawn only after the learner pulls an arm from that batch, so advice is not i.i.d. across rounds. The authors only conjecture that the bound also holds against an oblivious adversary.

None of these lower bounds covers stochastic i.i.d. contexts with i.i.d. rewards, which is the setting asked about. I found no paper that removes the 1/log K factor there. The authors' stated conjecture marks the oblivious case, and by extension the stochastic case, as open.

One caveat: the Ito NeurIPS 2024 PDF did not render, so I could not check its hard instance directly. What I report about it comes from the abstract and search snippets.

papers.title: A Tight Lower Bound for Non-stochastic Multi-armed Bandits with Expert Advice (Chase, Ito, Mehalel)
papers.claim: Theta(sqrt(TK log(N/K))) minimax expected regret for non-stochastic bandits with expert advice, matching Kale (2014) upper bound; lower bound uses an adaptive adversary; authors conjecture it also holds against an oblivious adversary.

papers.title: Improved Regret Bounds for Bandits with Expert Advice (Cesa-Bianchi, Eldowa, Esposito, Olkhovskaya)
papers.claim: Omega(sqrt(KT ln(N/K))) worst-case lower bound under a restricted feedback model, improving previous sqrt(KT lnN/lnK).

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Contextual Linear Bandits and Multi-Armed Bandits with Expert Advice (Ito, NeurIPS 2024)
papers.claim: Omega(sqrt(KT log(N/K))) lower bound for MwE in the setting where the player chooses an expert before observing advice.

triage.summary: The √(log K) gap is closed: the worst-case simple regret is Θ(√(K/T)) for T ≥ K. A known reduction gives the matching upper bound. Recommend arm i with probability T_i(n)/n, where T_i(n) is the number of times arm i was played. Then expected simple regret equals expected cumulative regret divided by n. I saw this reduction stated in a search snippet attributed to Bubeck, Munos & Stoltz (arXiv 0802.2655, later versions). MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck, COLT 2009) has cumulative regret O(√(KT)) with no log factor. Combining the two gives simple regret O(√(K/T)), which matches the Ω(√(K/T)) lower bound up to constants. An explicit statement of this result appears in Oki & Sakaue (arXiv 2405.12439), which I read in its HTML version. Their Prop. 4.1 and Appendix B (with M arms and T′ rounds) run MOSS and return an arm uniformly at random from those played. They bound the cumulative regret by 39√(MT′)+M, citing Lattimore–Szepesvári Thm 9.1, and get simple regret ≤ 40√(M/T′). They call this a known result. The Lattimore–Szepesvári result assumes 1-subgaussian noise, and rewards in [0,1] are 1/2-subgaussian, so it applies here. Limitations: I could not extract text from the PDFs of Bubeck et al., the Lattimore–Szepesvári book or Bubeck's thesis. My evidence for the reduction in 0802.2655 is a search snippet, not the paper text. The closing citation is the Oki–Sakaue appendix together with the MOSS paper, whose abstract I saw saying it removes the extra log factor.

papers.title: Minimax Policies for Adversarial and Stochastic Bandits (Audibert, Bubeck)
papers.claim: MOSS, a modification of UCB1, has distribution-free cumulative regret of order √(nK) in stochastic K-armed bandits, removing the extra log factor.

papers.title: Pure Exploration for Multi-Armed Bandit Problems / Pure exploration in finitely-armed and continuous-armed bandits (Bubeck, Munos, Stoltz)
papers.claim: If the forecaster recommends arm i with probability T_i(n)/n, then E r_n = E R_n / n, so cumulative-regret upper bounds become simple-regret upper bounds. With MOSS this gives O(√(K/n)). Seen in a search snippet; I could not read the PDF.

papers.title: No-Regret M♮-Concave Function Maximization: Stochastic Bandit Algorithms and Hardness of Adversarial Full-Information Setting (Oki, Sakaue)
papers.claim: Prop. 4.1 / App. B: a MOSS-based pure-exploration algorithm that returns a random arm has simple regret ≤ 40√(M/T′), with no log M factor. It uses the cumulative bound 39√(MT′)+M from Lattimore & Szepesvári Thm 9.1. The paper describes the O(T^{-1/2}) simple regret as known.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed, and it only exists because the database is missing a result. The classical minimax lower bound for K-armed adversarial bandits is of order √(KT), with no log factor. Applied to K = 2, it gives Ω(√T), which matches Exp3's O(√(T log 2)) = O(√T) upper bound up to constants. The database's best lower bound, √T/log T (Pacchiano et al. 2020), is therefore weaker than what is already known.

Sources:
- **Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund and Schapire (SIAM J. Computing 2002).** The abstract I found says their O(T^{-1/2}) per-round convergence rate is best possible, shown by a matching lower bound.
- **Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi survey (arXiv 1204.5721), Theorem 3.4 "Minimax lower bound".** It states inf over forecasters, sup over reward distributions, of regret ≥ (1/20)√(nK). The rewards are i.i.d. Bernoulli, which also makes them an oblivious adversarial sequence in [0,1]. The proof compares Bernoulli(1/2) arms against Bernoulli(1/2 + √(K/n)).

The construction works for any K ≥ 2, but I did not see the explicit "K ≥ 2" or "n ≥ K" side conditions in the text I retrieved. The PDF fetches returned unreadable binary. From the snippets alone, then, the K = 2 case is a reasonable reading of the result rather than something I saw stated outright. The (K−1)n form of the lower bound in Lattimore–Szepesvári, Section 15.2, would cover K = 2 directly, but I could not see the theorem text.

Gerchinovitz & Lattimore (2016) refine these adversarial lower bounds further. Either way, the worst-case regret for K = 2 is Θ(√T).

papers.title: The Nonstochastic Multiarmed Bandit Problem
papers.claim: By Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund and Schapire (SIAM J. Comput. 32(1):48-77). Exp3 achieves an O(T^{-1/2}) per-round convergence rate to the best arm, i.e. O(√(KT log K)) regret. A matching lower bound shows this rate is best possible, i.e. Ω(√(KT)) regret for oblivious adversaries.

papers.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems
papers.claim: Theorem 3.4 (Minimax lower bound): inf over forecasters, sup over reward distributions, of regret ≥ (1/20)√(nK). Rewards are i.i.d. Bernoulli, hence in [0,1] and a valid oblivious adversarial sequence. Taking K = 2 gives Ω(√n), matching the Exp3 upper bound up to constants.

papers.title: Refined Lower Bounds for Adversarial Bandits
papers.claim: By Gerchinovitz & Lattimore (NeurIPS 2016). Refines the minimax Ω(√(KT)) lower bounds for adversarial bandits into more detailed, data-dependent lower bounds.

triage.summary: Known bounds: the upper bound O(sqrt(KT log(K/δ))) comes from Exp3.P and Exp3-IX (Neu 2015). The lower bound Ω(sqrt(KT log(1/δ))) is Gerchinovitz & Lattimore 2016, which per Bacchiocchi et al. holds even for losses fixed in advance. The remaining gap is sqrt(log K). Bacchiocchi, Cesari & Colomboni (arXiv:2608.12231, 2026) prove a matching Θ(sqrt(dT log(K/δ))) high-probability bound for m-set bandits. For m=1 this shows log K is unavoidable for K-armed bandits, but only against ADAPTIVE non-anticipating adversaries: the lower bound uses a deterministic adaptive adversary. The paper says: "Our corollary closes this gap when the adversary is adaptive and non-anticipating." The parts of its HTML I read (main text and part of the appendices; the rest was cut off) say nothing about oblivious adversaries. I found no paper that closes the gap for oblivious adversaries and none that explicitly calls it open. I could not check whether Audibert & Bubeck's INF (JMLR 2010) or Tsallis-INF gives a log-K-free high-probability bound for oblivious adversaries, because the PDFs came back as unreadable compressed streams. So the oblivious case is unresolved from what I could verify. Bacchiocchi et al. should be added to the database for the adaptive variant.

papers.title: An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial m-Set Bandits (Bacchiocchi, Cesari, Colomboni)
papers.claim: High-probability regret Θ(sqrt(dT log(K/δ))) against adaptive non-anticipating adversaries. For m=1 this closes the sqrt(log K) gap left by Gerchinovitz-Lattimore, but only for adaptive adversaries; the lower bound uses a deterministic adaptive adversary.

papers.title: Refined Lower Bounds for Adversarial Bandits (Gerchinovitz, Lattimore)
papers.claim: No strategy can get high-probability regret smaller than order sqrt(KT log(1/δ)) (Theorem 1). Per Bacchiocchi et al., this holds even for loss sequences fixed in advance (oblivious). The paper also notes that tuning without knowing δ moves log(1/δ) outside the square root.

papers.title: Explore no more: Improved high-probability regret bounds for non-stochastic bandits (Neu)
papers.claim: Exp3-IX achieves high-probability regret O(sqrt(KT log K) + sqrt(KT/log K) log(1/δ)), and O(sqrt(KT log(K/δ))) when tuned for δ.

triage.summary:
I found no source that closes this gap or calls it a known open problem for this exact setting. The setting is a fixed finite action set of K points, oblivious adversary, losses in the polar of the action set, and expected regret.

The setting's upper bound is O(√(dT log K)) (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi and Kakade, 2012, Theorem 4). Its abstract presents this only as an upper bound. It calls the d√(T log T) bound for compact action sets "minimax optimal up to a logarithmic factor", but makes no such claim for the √(dT log K) bound.

The only K-dependent lower bound I confirmed for a fixed action set is for K = 2^d. Shamir (2015), in the dual normalization, proves an Ω((d−1)√T) lower bound for the hypercube [−1,1]^d (Theorem 6, which needs T ≥ d⁴/4). Because the losses are linear, this also applies to the corner set {−1,1}^d, where d√T is the same order as √(dT log K). It also cites a prior Ω(d√T) lower bound for the Boolean hypercube. Two caveats: Shamir allows sub-Gaussian loss noise rather than strictly bounded losses, and says this relaxation costs only a √log T factor in lower bounds. At K = d (the simplex), Shamir's Ω(√(dT)) lower bound matches EXP3, and no log K term appears.

So √log K is needed at the extreme K = 2^d (up to the noise-model caveat), but I found no lower bound for general K.

The most relevant candidate is Ito (NeurIPS 2024), "On the Minimax Regret for Contextual Linear Bandits and Multi-Armed Bandits with Expert Advice". Its abstract states an upper bound of O(√(dT log(K·min{1, S/d}))) with a matching lower bound, where S is the number of contexts. With S = 1 this would give Θ(√(dT log(K/d))) and close the gap. However, I could not read the full text: the PDF did not extract and OpenReview was blocked by a browser check. I therefore could not confirm that the lower bound covers S = 1, nor its loss normalization or adversary model. It may need S ≥ d.

Bacchiocchi, Cesari and Colomboni (arXiv 2608.12231) prove a matching lower bound of order √(dT log(K/δ)). But it is a high-probability bound against adaptive adversaries for m-set bandits, so it does not settle the expected-regret question. Li et al. (2019), Ω(√(dT log K log T)), is for stochastic contextual bandits whose action sets change over time; I saw it only cited secondhand and did not fetch it.

The verdict is "blank" because Ito (2024) could not be checked. If its lower bound covers S = 1 under bounded polar losses, the verdict should be "closed".

papers.title: Towards minimax policies for online linear optimization with bandit feedback (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi, Kakade)
papers.claim: Exponential weights with John's exploration gives an O(sqrt(dn log N)) upper bound for N actions. The abstract claims no lower bound for this bound; only the d√(n log n) bound for compact action sets is called minimax optimal up to a log factor.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Bandit Linear Optimization (Shamir)
papers.claim: In the dual (polar) normalization with sub-Gaussian loss noise, gives an Omega((d-1)sqrt(T)) lower bound for the hypercube [-1,1]^d (Theorem 6, T >= d^4/4). This applies to the {-1,1}^d corner set (K=2^d), where it equals sqrt(dT log K) up to constants. Cites a prior Omega(d sqrt T) Boolean-hypercube bound, and gives Omega(sqrt(dT)) for the simplex (K=d).

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Contextual Linear Bandits and Multi-Armed Bandits with Expert Advice (Shinji Ito)
papers.claim: Abstract: an algorithm with regret O(sqrt(dT log(K min{1,S/d}))) for contextual linear bandits, with a matching lower bound (S = number of contexts). Not verified whether the lower bound covers S=1 (a fixed action set).

papers.title: An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial m-Set Bandits (Bacchiocchi, Cesari, Colomboni)
papers.claim: A high-probability lower bound Omega(sqrt(dT log(K/delta))) against adaptive adversaries for m-set bandits, matching EXP3-KW. Not an expected-regret lower bound for general fixed finite action sets.

triage.summary: For bandit linear optimization on the cube [-1,1]^d with losses in the l1 ball (|a^T z| <= 1), Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade (2012), Theorem 5, give R_n <= 2d sqrt(3 n log 2). The same paper states that d sqrt(n) is the minimax rate for the cube, citing Dani, Hayes & Kakade (2008): "this regret is minimax optimal" (Sec. 4) and "action sets (such as the hypercube) where the minimax rate is of order d sqrt(n)" (Intro). The Dani-Hayes-Kakade abstract claims the price of bandit information is at least sqrt(n), which against sqrt(nT) full-information regret means Omega(n sqrt T) bandit regret. I could not read their PDF, so their exact theorem, decision set and constant are unverified; that the construction is the bounded-loss cube comes from the 2012 paper's citation. Shamir (2015), Theorem 6, gives c(d-1)sqrt(T) on [-1,1]^d for T >= d^4/4 with stochastic losses whose mean lies in the l1 ball and whose tails are sub-Gaussian, not bounded by 1. So the d-exponent gap (1 vs 0.5) closes at Theta(d sqrt T); the database is missing the Omega(d sqrt T) lower bound.

papers.title: Towards Minimax Policies for Online Linear Optimization with Bandit Feedback (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi, Kakade)
papers.claim: Theorem 5: for A = {||x||_inf <= 1} and Z = {||z||_1 <= 1}, OSMD gives R_n <= 2d sqrt(3 n log 2). The paper says this is minimax optimal by Dani et al. 2008 ('there exists action sets (such as the hypercube) where the minimax rate is of order d sqrt(n)').

papers.title: The Price of Bandit Information for Online Optimization (Dani, Hayes, Kakade)
papers.claim: NeurIPS 2007 (vol. 20, printed 2008). Abstract: the gap between bandit and full-information regret is at least sqrt(n), i.e. an Omega(n sqrt T) bandit lower bound against O*(sqrt(nT)) full information. Cited by Bubeck et al. 2012 as the d sqrt(n) lower bound for the hypercube. PDF text not readable here, so the exact theorem and constant are unverified.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Bandit Linear Optimization (Shamir)
papers.claim: Theorem 6: on W = [-1,1]^d, regret >= c(d-1)sqrt(T) for T >= d^4/4, with stochastic losses whose mean is in the l1 ball and whose tails are sub-Gaussian (not almost-surely bounded). States it matches the O(d sqrt T) upper bound.

triage.summary: No log-free O(√(dT)) upper bound and no matching Ω(√(dT log T)) lower bound found for adversarial linear bandits on the unit ball with ℓ2-ball losses. The best upper bound is still 3√(dT log T) (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade 2012). Jacobsen, Baudry, Ito & Cesa-Bianchi (2026) call the minimax rate the 'folklore' Θ̃(√(dT)), with logs hidden. Their adversarial lower bound only has the weaker √(dT)·√(d/max(d, log T)) form (and covers direction regret). Their conjecture for the unconstrained problem, which they leave open, would suggest √(dT) for unit-ball comparators. Lévy et al. (COLT 2026) get O(d√(T log T)) on the ball, which doesn't improve things. No source explicitly calls the log gap open. Tool failures: the banditalgs.com post (expired certificate), archive.org (blocked) and the Lattimore–Szepesvári book PDF (unreadable binary) could not be checked.

papers.title: A Perturbation Approach to Unconstrained Linear Bandits (Jacobsen, Baudry, Ito, Cesa-Bianchi)
papers.claim: Calls the unit-ball minimax rate the folklore Θ̃(√(dT)). Theorem 5.2 gives a log-free stochastic lower bound √(dT)/64 ∧ T/(12d), but the adversarial lower bound is only C(√(dT) ∧ T/d)·√(d/(d∨log T)). Conjecture 5.3 on the unconstrained rate is left as an open problem.

papers.title: Self-Concordant Perturbations for Linear Bandits (Lévy, Valeau, Akhavan, Rebeschini)
papers.claim: FTPL gets O(d√(n ln n)) on the ℓ2 ball, matching SCRiBLe; no improvement on the ball.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Bandit Linear Optimization (Shamir)
papers.claim: Writes the unit-ball upper bound as O(√(dT)) and calls it brittle; shows Ω(d√T) for balls bounded away from the origin.

triage.summary:
The log K gap closes by combining standard published results. The database lower bound Ω(√(KT)) is also too weak: it is missing M_ctx.

**Upper bound.** Audibert & Bubeck (COLT 2009 / JMLR 2010) give INF / Poly-INF, which has pseudo-regret O(√(TK)) with no log factor. Zimmert & Seldin's Tsallis-INF gets the same rate anytime, without knowing the horizon. Running one such instance per context, in the same way as the "one Exp3 per context" argument from bubeck2012survey and Lattimore–Szepesvári §18.1, gives Σ_c O(√(K·T_c)) ≤ O(√(K·M·T)) by Cauchy–Schwarz. Because the base algorithm is anytime, the per-context counts T_c do not need to be known. This removes the √(log K) factor.

**Lower bound.** Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi (2012) state an Ω(√(nSK)) lower bound for S contexts, obtained by splitting the rounds evenly across contexts and applying the K-armed minimax lower bound in each. A search snippet says it needs a constant fraction of contexts to cover a constant fraction of the rounds, which a worst-case adversary can arrange.

**Result.** Both bounds are Θ(√(KMT)), so the minimax rate is settled up to constants.

**Caveats.**
- The search snippet attributes the stated √(nSK) lower bound to the Bubeck–Cesa-Bianchi monograph. Its main text did not load: the PDF was unreadable, and the ar5iv fetch returned text whose theorem numbering does not match the survey. So I have not checked the theorem number or exact constant myself.
- The √(KT) bound for INF and Tsallis-INF is a pseudo-regret guarantee. If "cumulative regret" here means expected regret against the best fixed per-context policy in hindsight under an adaptive adversary, that version can differ. Under the usual pseudo-regret convention the gap is closed.
- I found no single paper that states the combined Θ(√(KMT)) result. It is a direct folklore composition of the results above.

papers.title: Minimax Policies for Adversarial and Stochastic Bandits
papers.claim: Audibert & Bubeck, COLT 2009 (extended in JMLR 2010). The INF family removes the extraneous log factor and gets pseudo-regret O(√(nK)) for adversarial K-armed bandits. Run per context, this gives O(√(KMT)).

papers.title: Tsallis-INF: An Optimal Algorithm for Stochastic and Adversarial Bandits
papers.claim: Zimmert & Seldin, JMLR 2021. An anytime algorithm that needs no horizon knowledge and gets the optimal adversarial rate O(√(KT)) with no log factor. Running one copy per context gives O(√(KMT)) even when the per-context counts T_c are unknown.

papers.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems
papers.claim: Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi. According to a search-result snippet (I could not open the PDF), the monograph gives O(√(nSK ln K)) for Exp3 run per context and an Ω(√(nSK)) lower bound for S contexts. The snippet says the lower bound assumes a constant fraction of contexts covers a constant fraction of the rounds. This would give the missing M_ctx dependence in the lower bound.

papers.title: A Survey on Contextual Multi-armed Bandits
papers.claim: Gives the √(TCK ln K) upper bound for running one Exp3 per context with C contexts.

triage.summary: No paper found that closes the gap, and none found that explicitly calls it open. The gap is a √log T factor: the best confirmed upper bound is 3√(dT log T) (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade 2012) and the lower bound is √(dT)/20. Bubeck, Cohen & Li (2018) claim Õ(√(nT)) on ℓ_p balls for p in [1,2]; their Theorem 3 at p = 2 gives 64√(nT log T), which keeps the log factor and has a worse constant. Jacobsen, Baudry, Ito & Cesa-Bianchi (2026) cite only Õ(√(dT)) for the unit ball and call it minimax-optimal; their adversarial lower bound has an extra √(d/max(d, log T)) factor. Only the first half of that paper was read; the only open problem found there is a different one (Conjecture 5.3). From search results only: a 2025 self-concordant-perturbation paper (arXiv 2510.24187) gets O(d√(n ln n)) on the ℓ2 ball, and Zimmert & Lattimore (2022) get O(√(dT log(kT))) for k actions; both keep a log factor. Tool failures: text could not be extracted from the Lattimore–Szepesvári draft PDF (Section 28.4 and its notes are not verified), and the banditalgs.com unit-ball post did not load because of an expired certificate (a search snippet says it claims O(√(dn)), log factor unchecked). Either source may explicitly call the log factor open.

papers.title: Sparsity, variance and curvature in multi-armed bandits
papers.claim: Theorem 3 (ℓ_p ball, p in (1,2]): for p = 2, R_T ≤ 64·√(nT log T). The √log T factor remains.

papers.title: A Perturbation Approach to Unconstrained Linear Bandits
papers.claim: Cites only Õ(√(dT)) for the unit ball. Proves an adversarial lower bound C·min(√(dT), T/d)·√(d/max(d, log T)), with an extra factor relative to Ω(√(dT)). In the first half of the paper read, no explicit statement that the log gap is open.

papers.title: Towards Minimax Policies for Online Linear Optimization with Bandit Feedback
papers.claim: Mirror descent on the Euclidean ball achieves near-optimal regret up to a logarithmic factor (already in the database as the 3√(dT log T) upper bound).

triage.summary: No paper found that closes the gap for stochastic linear bandits on lp balls with p>2, and none that explicitly says the remaining log factor is open in this setting. Lower bound: d√T up to logs (Bubeck, Cohen, Li 2018, abstract). Search snippets also attribute a d√n lower bound for lp balls with 1<p<∞ to Banerjee & Gopalan (2023); the abstract I fetched mentions only a broad class of convex action sets. Upper bound: the database has Dani et al. 2008, about d√T·log^1.5 T. Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi, Kakade (COLT 2012) give d√(T log T) for any compact action set in the adversarial setting with bounded losses, which they call minimax optimal up to a log factor. If it transfers to Gaussian noise (with extra care, e.g. truncation), the gap would shrink to about √log T. Log-free minimax-optimal results exist only for ellipsoids, i.e. p=2 (Zhang, Hadiji, Combes 2025), not for p>2. The gap is therefore at least sqrt(log T), and its status is not explicitly stated in the literature I found.

papers.title: Sparsity, variance and curvature in multi-armed bandits
papers.claim: Lower bound of order d√T, up to log factors, for linear bandits on lp balls with p>2 (solving a Bubeck-Cesa-Bianchi-Kakade open problem); upper bound of order √(dT), up to log factors, for p in [1,2].

papers.title: Towards Minimax Policies for Online Linear Optimization with Bandit Feedback
papers.claim: Regret d√(n log n) for any compact action set (adversarial setting, bounded losses), described as minimax optimal up to a log factor; d√n for the hypercube.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Linear Bandits in a wide variety of Action Spaces
papers.claim: Abstract: an optimal regret lower bound for a wide class of convex action spaces. Search snippets (not the fetched abstract) say this includes lp balls with 1<p<∞ at order d√n.

papers.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms
papers.claim: Minimax-optimal regret of order dσ√T with no log factor for ellipsoid action sets (p=2 case only).

triage.summary:
For K-armed stochastic bandits with a fixed, known, strongly observable feedback graph, the literature already pins down the instance-dependent rate. It is c*(θ, G)·log T, where c* is the value of a linear program built from the graph and the instance (roughly, a minimum-cost exploration budget over the arms). Neither of your database's bounds reflects this. The upper bounds come from plain bandit algorithms that ignore the graph (UCB1, KL-UCB). The lower bound is just Ω(log T). So the polynomial gaps you see in Δ and K are an artefact of the incomplete database, not an open problem.

- **Lower bound.** Buccapatnam, Eryilmaz and Shroff proved an asymptotic Lai–Robbins-style lower bound that depends on the network structure. Their UCB-type and randomized policies match it up to a factor that does not depend on the network.
- **Matching upper bounds.** Wu, György and Szepesvári (NeurIPS 2015) proved problem-dependent lower bounds that do not need T → ∞. Their algorithms match those bounds up to a universal constant. A slide deck (ICML 2022) says their result is exactly asymptotically optimal in the {σ, ∞} case, which is the graph-feedback case. Marinov, Mohri and Zimmert (NeurIPS 2022) give an algorithm that is quasi-optimal both in finite time and asymptotically. They also show that no algorithm can reach the asymptotic constant c* in finite time on some instances.
- **Still open (refinements, not the main gap).** Marinov et al. leave open which graphs allow the finite-time rate to match the asymptotic rate up to constants. They also leave open graphs that change over time and the case where the learner does not know the graph.

Caveat: these results are stated for Gaussian or sub-Gaussian-type rewards. I did not check whether anyone has proved an exactly matching asymptotic constant for general [0,1] rewards (a KL- or Kinf-based constant). The order c*(G, Δ)·log T is settled up to constant factors.

papers.title: Stochastic Online Learning with Feedback Graphs: Finite-Time and Asymptotic Optimality
papers.claim: Marinov, Mohri, Zimmert (NeurIPS 2022). For a fixed, known feedback graph, gives an algorithm that is quasi-optimal both in finite time and asymptotically relative to the LP-based constant c*. Shows that no algorithm can reach c* in finite time on some instances, and gives a family of graphs where it can be reached.

papers.title: Online Learning with Gaussian Payoffs and Side Observations
papers.claim: Wu, György, Szepesvári (NeurIPS 2015). Proves problem-dependent lower bounds that do not need T → ∞, and gives algorithms matching them up to a universal constant (and the minimax bounds up to log factors). A later slide deck says the result is asymptotically optimal in the {σ, ∞} (graph-feedback) case.

papers.title: Reward Maximization Under Uncertainty: Leveraging Side-Observations on Networks
papers.claim: Buccapatnam, Eryilmaz, Shroff. Asymptotic lower bound for uniformly good policies that depends on the network structure. UCB-type and randomized policies match it up to a factor independent of the network.

triage.summary: The gap is closed. The database's lower bound Ω(√(T(D+K))) is weaker than what Cesa-Bianchi, Gentile, Mansour and Minora (COLT 2016) actually prove: Zimmert and Seldin's introduction quotes it as Ω(max{√(KT), √(dT log K)}) for a uniform delay d ≤ T/log K. Zimmert and Seldin (AISTATS 2020, arXiv:1910.06054) give an upper bound of O(√(KT) + √(D_total log K)), which for a fixed delay is O(√(KT) + √(dT log K)). The abstract says this matches the lower bound within constants and needs no prior knowledge of T or D. So the minimax regret is Θ(√(KT) + √(dT log K)), and the extra √(log K) in the stated upper bound is removed. Caveats: the lower-bound form was taken from the arXiv HTML introduction of Zimmert and Seldin, not checked in the 2016 paper itself (the arXiv PDF could not be read), and the tightness claim covers d ≤ T/log K.

papers.title: An Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial Bandits with Arbitrary Delays
papers.claim: Achieves O(√(kn) + √(D log k)) regret, where D is the total delay (for a fixed delay d, D = dn, giving √(kn) + √(dn log k)); the abstract says this matches the lower bound within constants and needs no knowledge of n or D. The introduction quotes Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2016) as proving a lower bound of Ω(max{√(kn), √(dn log k)}) for d ≤ n/log k.

papers.title: Delay and cooperation in nonstochastic bandits
papers.claim: As quoted by Zimmert and Seldin: proves the lower bound Ω(max{√(KT), √(dT log K)}) for a uniform delay d ≤ T/log K.

papers.title: A Best-of-Both-Worlds Algorithm for Bandits with Delayed Feedback
papers.claim: Restates the fixed-delay adversarial guarantee O(√(TK) + √(dT log K)); per the search result, also proves a lower bound matching the refined skipping-based upper bound.

triage.summary: The gap comes from mixing feedback models under an unspecified-observability partial-monitoring label. In Cesa-Bianchi et al. (STOC 2024, arXiv:2307.09478), the O(sqrt(T ln T)) upper bound (Thm 4) is for transparent feedback in the stochastic i.i.d. setting. Thm 5 gives a matching Omega(sqrt T) lower bound for that setting, even with full feedback and smooth environments, so the rate there is Theta~(sqrt T). The Omega(T^{2/3}) lower bounds apply only to weaker feedback: Thm 3 covers semi-transparent feedback, where the paper's Thm 2 is a matching upper bound, and bandit feedback is also Theta~(T^{2/3}) for smooth environments. Within each feedback model the paper's characterization is tight up to log factors. The database entry should be split by transparency level. I could not find or check the inherited bound from xu2022towards Theorem 7 (one search turned up nothing). It cannot be a T^{2/3} lower bound for transparent feedback, since that would contradict the upper bound.

papers.title: The Role of Transparency in Repeated First-Price Auctions with Unknown Valuations
papers.claim: Stochastic i.i.d. case: transparent/full feedback is Theta~(sqrt T), with O(sqrt(T ln T)) upper bound (Thm 4) and Omega(sqrt T) lower bound (Thm 5). Semi-transparent feedback is Theta~(T^{2/3}) (Thms 2 and 3). Bandit feedback is linear in general and Theta~(T^{2/3}) when smooth.

triage.summary: The setting is repeated first-price auctions with unknown valuations under stochastic i.i.d. full feedback (Cesa-Bianchi et al., STOC 2024). Theorem 4 gives O(√(T ln T)): it is stated for transparent feedback and carries over to full feedback, with the log coming from the epoch wrapper. Theorem 5 gives a lower bound of √T/2048 under full feedback via the two-experts embedding. The paper describes its characterization as tight "up to logarithmic factors". Its conclusion names only the σ-dependence as an open problem and says nothing about removing the √log T factor. Searches found no later paper giving a log-free √T upper bound in this setting; for arXiv:2510.16869 only the abstract was seen. So the gap is neither closed nor explicitly called open.

papers.title: The Role of Transparency in Repeated First-Price Auctions with Unknown Valuations
papers.claim: Theorem 4 gives an O(√(T ln T)) upper bound for transparent feedback (stochastic i.i.d.), which also applies to full feedback. Theorem 5 gives a lower bound of √T/2048 under full feedback. Results are described as tight up to log factors. The conclusion names σ-dependence as the open problem and does not mention the log factor.

papers.title: Optimal No-regret Learning in Repeated First-price Auctions
papers.claim: Different setting: adversarial private values (known to the bidder). Reports C√T log³T, i.e. Õ(√T) with log factors; does not give a log-free bound.

triage.summary:
Li, Wang and Zhou (COLT 2019, arXiv 1904.00242) close the log gap up to poly(log log) factors. I read their setting on the ar5iv page. It is a finite-action linear contextual bandit with at most n=K actions per round. An oblivious adversary fixes θ and all the action sets in advance, with ‖θ‖₂ ≤ 1 and ‖x‖₂ ≤ 1. This matches the queried setting.

- **Upper bound (Theorem 1):** VCL-SupLinUCB gets regret O(√(dT log T log n)) · poly(log log(nT)). The noise only needs to be 1-sub-Gaussian, so the bound covers rewards in [0,1]. It removes two √log T factors from the SupLinUCB bound of Chu et al. 2011, and in T it beats the database upper bound of order √T·log^0.75 T.
- **Lower bound (Theorem 2):** Regret is Ω(√(dT log n · log(T/d))) whenever n ≤ 2^{d/2} and T ≥ d(log₂ n)^{1+ε}. So in T, d and log n the bounds match up to iterated-log factors.

**Caveat:** the lower bound is built with unit-variance Gaussian noise, not rewards bounded in [0,1]. Moving it to bounded rewards, for example Bernoulli rewards with means near 1/2, is the usual adaptation, but I did not see it stated in the paper. Under a strict reading of the bounded-noise setting, the √log T lower-bound factor is therefore not explicitly proved. The bounds also hold only up to poly(log log) factors.

**Related recent work:** Jin (2026, arXiv 2609.15170), "Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linear Contextual Bandits with Arbitrary Adaptive Action Sets", is the source of the database's K^{1/4} bound. It covers adaptive menus and pins down how regret depends on K. When K ≤ d and T ≥ d², it gives matching Θ̃(K^{1/4}√(dT)) bounds.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits (Li, Wang, Zhou)
papers.claim: Oblivious adversarial finite action sets of size n, ||x||,||θ||≤1, sub-Gaussian noise. Upper bound: regret O(√(dT log T log n))·poly(log log(nT)) via VCL-SupLinUCB. Lower bound (Gaussian noise): Ω(√(dT log n log(T/d))) for n ≤ 2^{d/2}, T ≥ d(log n)^{1+ε}. Together these close the gap up to iterated logs.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linear Contextual Bandits with Arbitrary Adaptive Action Sets (Tianyuan Jin)
papers.claim: For adaptive menus: Õ(K^{1/4}√(dT)) when K ≤ d, which matches the lower bound Ω(K^{1/4}√(dT)) when T ≥ d². For K ≥ d: Õ(√(dT)·min{√d,(d log K)^{1/4}}) with a nearly matching lower bound.

triage.summary: Not closed. For a fixed arbitrary compact action set, the best upper bound I found is O(d√(T log T)) from phased elimination with G-optimal design (arXiv:2211.05632, from a search snippet). That is tighter than the database's d√T·log^1.5 T, and also beats OFUL's d√T·log T (Abbasi-Yadkori et al. 2011). The best lower bound is still Ω(d√T) (Dani et al. 2008; Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis 2010), so a √(log T) gap remains. Li, Wang & Zhou (COLT 2019) prove Ω(d√(T log T)) for infinite action sets, but only when the action space changes over time (adversarial, contextual). It does not apply to a fixed action set. Li & Chen (2019) match that bound up to iterated logs, also only for time-varying sets. I found no paper that closes the √(log T) gap for fixed action sets and no explicit statement that it is open; I could not check the Chapter 24 Notes of the Lattimore–Szepesvári book. Hence "blank".

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits (Li, Wang, Zhou)
papers.claim: Lower bound Ω(√(dT log T log n)) for finite action sets. It implies Ω(d√(T log T)) for infinite actions, but only 'when the action space changes over time'. The paper also notes OFUL's O(d√T log T) upper bound.

papers.title: Tight Regret Bounds for Infinite-armed Linear Contextual Bandits (Li, Chen)
papers.claim: Upper bound O(√(d²T log T))·poly(log log T), matching Ω(√(d²T log T)) for changing infinite action sets (contextual), not fixed ones.

papers.title: Solving Stochastic Contextual Bandits with Linear ...
papers.claim: States (search snippet) that Phased Elimination gets a high-probability O(d√(T log T)) regret bound by exploiting a fixed action space.

papers.title: Corruption-Robust Linear Bandits: Minimax Optimality and Gap-Dependent Misspecification
papers.claim: Elimination with G-optimal design gets O(d√(T log(T/δ)) + Z log T) regret, where Z is the corruption level.

triage.summary: Upper bound sqrt(dT log K) is from Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade 2012 (Exp2 with John's exploration, losses with |<a,l>|<=1). Dani-Hayes-Kakade 2008 give a d*sqrt(T) lower bound for the hypercube; with K=2^d that equals sqrt(dT log K), so the upper bound is matched in expectation at K=2^d. For K>=2^d it is tight up to log T via the general compact-set bound. Bubeck et al. call the finite-set rate optimal, but their only lower-bound example is the hypercube. For d<K<2^d, Bacchiocchi-Cesari-Colomboni (2026, arXiv:2608.12231) prove a matching high-probability lower bound Omega(sqrt(dT log(K/delta))) for m-set action sets (K=C(d,m)) under the same normalisation. It is not stated for expected regret, and converting it needs extra control (not done in the paper, not verified here). The best expected-regret m-set lower bounds (Cohen-Hazan-Koren 2017; Ito et al. 2019, rescaled) give sqrt(kdT), about sqrt(log(d/k)) short of sqrt(dT log K). So the gap is closed at K=2^d and in high probability for m-sets. I found no explicit expected-regret lower bound sqrt(dT log K) for every (d,K), and no paper calling this open. The Dani et al. and Bubeck et al. PDFs did not parse; Bubeck et al.'s claims were checked via ar5iv. I could not reach the Lattimore-Szepesvari book's chapter notes.

papers.title: Towards Minimax Policies for Online Linear Optimization with Bandit Feedback
papers.claim: For any finite action set with N actions, Exp2 with John's exploration gets regret O(sqrt(dn log N)) when |<a,z>|<=1. The paper says some action sets (e.g. the hypercube) have minimax rate of order d sqrt(n), citing Dani et al. 2008, which matches sqrt(dn log N) at N=2^d.

papers.title: The Price of Bandit Information for Online Optimization (Dani, Hayes, Kakade)
papers.claim: Cited by Bubeck et al. 2012 for an Omega(d sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound on the hypercube (K=2^d). The PDF text did not parse, so the theorem was not read directly.

papers.title: An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial m-Set Bandits (Bacchiocchi, Cesari, Colomboni)
papers.claim: With action-level normalisation |<x,l>|<=1 and K=C(d,m): high-probability upper bound O(sqrt(dT log(K/delta))) and a matching high-probability lower bound Omega(sqrt(dT log(K/delta))) for small delta. No expected-regret lower bound is stated.

papers.title: Tight Bounds for Bandit Combinatorial Optimization (Cohen, Hazan, Koren)
papers.claim: Expected-regret lower bound Omega(sqrt(d k^3 T / log T)) for bandit combinatorial optimization with item losses in [0,1].

papers.title: Improved Regret Bounds for Bandit Combinatorial Optimization (Ito et al.)
papers.claim: Improves the lower bound to Omega(sqrt(d k^3 T)). Rescaled by 1/k to action-level normalisation this is sqrt(kdT), short of sqrt(dT log C(d,k)) by about sqrt(log(d/k)).

triage.summary: He, Zhou, Zhang & Gu (NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2205.06811) close the gap up to log factors. In linear contextual bandits whose decision sets change over time (bounded l2 norm) and whose rewards are corrupted with total budget C, their CW-OFUL algorithm has regret Õ(d√T + dC) when C is known (Theorem 4.2, horizon written as K in the paper). Regret is pseudo-regret against the true, uncorrupted rewards. Propositions 4.7 and 4.8 give a matching Ω(max{d√T, dC}) lower bound. This beats the database's best upper bound (Ding et al.'s T^{3/4} rate) and matches the d√(T log T) lower bound up to logs. The upper bound doesn't depend on K. I inferred, without reading jin2026, that the K^{1/4}√(dT) lower bound only applies where it stays below d√T. Only logarithmic gaps remain. Caveats: I read the v2 HTML only up to character 100,000 of about 121,000. I didn't explicitly verify that the analysis allows an adaptive adversary with the budget counted along each sample path, though that is the standard model in this line of work.

papers.title: Nearly Optimal Algorithms for Linear Contextual Bandits with Adversarial Corruptions
papers.claim: CW-OFUL achieves Õ(d√T + dC) regret with known corruption level C, in linear contextual bandits with time-varying (possibly infinite) decision sets; Props 4.7–4.8 give an Ω(max{d√T, dC}) lower bound, so the algorithm is nearly optimal up to log factors.

triage.summary:
I found no paper that closes this gap, and none that explicitly says it is open, so the verdict is "blank".

In this setting the adversary corrupts the observed contexts (arm features), not the rewards.
