Ding, Hsieh & Sharpnack's RobustBandit (arXiv 2106.02978, AISTATS 2022) still has the best upper bound I could find for this setting. Without knowing the budget C, its regret is Õ(√d(C+1)T^{3/4} + d^{3/2}C T^{1/4}). If C is known, it is Õ(d(C+1)√T). That known-C bound is better in T than the bound in our database, but it is multiplicative in C, and our setting key does not say the learner knows C.

"Strategic Linear Contextual Bandits" (arXiv 2406.00551) is described in search snippets as saying that only one prior paper has studied adversarial context corruption; I could not open the PDF to check this myself. That prior paper is presumably Ding et al., with an Õ(d·C̃·√T) bound where C̃ is the total context perturbation. The paper does not state the gap as an open problem.

I searched for 2024–2026 work, including 2603.15596 and 2609.37189. The relevant recent papers are about reward corruption, and that line of work is essentially resolved. He et al. (2205.06811) get Õ(d√T+dC) with matching lower bounds. Liu et al. (2410.07533) mention an open problem, but it is about the C∞ dependence when rewards are corrupted (best known Õ(d√T+dC∞) upper vs Ω(d√T+√d C∞) lower). It says nothing about corrupted contexts.

I found no lower bound that depends on C for context corruption, and no algorithm that reaches d√T plus an additive term in C under context attacks. The remaining gap, especially in T and C, looks unresolved, but I can't cite anyone who explicitly calls it open.

papers.title: Robust Stochastic Linear Contextual Bandits Under Adversarial Attacks
papers.claim: RobustBandit handles reward or context attacks. Unknown budget C: Õ(√d(C+1)T^{3/4} + d^{3/2} C T^{1/4}). Known C: Õ(d(C+1)√T) via LinUCB with an enlarged exploration parameter.

papers.title: Strategic Linear Contextual Bandits
papers.claim: Per search snippets (PDF text not extractable), it says adversarial context corruption has only been studied by one prior work, which gets Õ(d C̃ √T) regret with C̃ the total context perturbation.

papers.title: Corruption-Robust Linear Bandits: Minimax Optimality and Gap-Dependent Misspecification
papers.claim: With reward corruption and adaptive action sets, the best known bounds are Õ(d√T+dC∞) upper and Ω(d√T+√d C∞) lower; the tight C∞ dependence is stated as open. This is about rewards, not contexts.

papers.title: Nearly Optimal Algorithms for Linear Contextual Bandits with Adversarial Corruptions
papers.claim: Gets Õ(d√T+dC) under reward corruption, nearly matching the lower bounds; contexts are not corrupted.

triage.summary: Closed up to logarithmic factors. The gap comes from the database's lower bound being too weak. Agarwal et al. (AISTATS 2012, arXiv:1202.1334), Theorem 5.1: for every N, K with ln N/ln K ≤ T and every algorithm, there is a policy class with |F| ≤ N and a fixed distribution D(x, r) over contexts and rewards, drawn i.i.d., under which regret is Ω(√(KT ln N/ln K)). The instance even satisfies realizability. The proof averages over random instances; a lower bound shown this way still holds when the learner is told each instance's context distribution. This matches the upper bound √(KT log(N T/δ)) from Dudík et al. 2011 up to logs in K and T, so the minimax rate is Θ̃(√(KT)). The extra √log T in the upper bound comes from the high-probability analysis with δ = 1/T. Exp4-type algorithms give O(√(KT ln N)) expected regret with no log T. Kale (2014) is cited, though I only saw the citation, for O(√(KT ln(N/K))). Only a log-factor question remains: ln N/ln K versus ln(N/K) in the stochastic case. Chase, Ito and Mehalel (2025) prove the tight Θ(√(KT log(N/K))) only against an adaptive adversary and leave even the oblivious case as a conjecture. No paper I found states the stochastic log-factor question as open.

papers.title: Contextual Bandit Learning with Predictable Rewards
papers.claim: Theorem 5.1: for all N, K with ln N/ln K <= T, every algorithm suffers expected regret Omega(sqrt(KT ln N / ln K)) on some policy class with |F| <= N and some fixed distribution D(x, r), drawn i.i.d., even under realizability. The proof averages over random instances (F, D).

papers.title: A Tight Lower Bound for Non-stochastic Multi-armed Bandits with Expert Advice
papers.claim: Theorem 6.1: for N >= 2K and T >= K ln(N/K), regret is Omega(sqrt(TK log(N/K))) against an adaptive adversary. This matches Kale's (2014) upper bound, giving minimax Theta(sqrt(TK log(N/K))) in the adversarial setting. The oblivious-adversary case is only conjectured, so the result does not settle the stochastic case.

triage.summary:
The T-dependence gap is mostly an artifact of how the database states its upper bounds. Its entries are high-probability bounds with delta=1/T, which brings in log(NT). Bounds on expected regret avoid this. Kale (2014) gives O(sqrt(KT log(N/K))), which Chase, Ito & Mehalel cite as the matching upper bound. That bound is proved for non-stochastic expert advice, so it should also hold when contexts are i.i.d., which is a special case.

The K-dependence gap is the real one. The lower bound is sqrt(KT log N / log K), from Agarwal et al. 2012 and Seldin & Lugosi. The upper bound is sqrt(KT log(N/K)). Recent work closed this gap, but only outside the stochastic-context setting:
- Cesa-Bianchi, Eldowa, Esposito & Olkhovskaya (arXiv 2406.16802) prove Omega(sqrt(KT ln(N/K))), but only under a restricted feedback model.
- Ito (NeurIPS 2024) proves the same lower bound for a different protocol, where the player commits to an expert before seeing the advice.
- Chase, Ito & Mehalel (arXiv 2511.00257, COLT 2026) settle the minimax rate for the standard non-stochastic problem at Theta(sqrt(TK log(N/K))). Their hard instance uses an adaptive adversary: advice for a batch of arms is redrawn only after the learner pulls an arm from that batch, so advice is not i.i.d. across rounds. The authors only conjecture that the bound also holds against an oblivious adversary.

None of these lower bounds covers stochastic i.i.d. contexts with i.i.d. rewards, which is the setting asked about. I found no paper that removes the 1/log K factor there. The authors' stated conjecture marks the oblivious case, and by extension the stochastic case, as open.

One caveat: the Ito NeurIPS 2024 PDF did not render, so I could not check its hard instance directly. What I report about it comes from the abstract and search snippets.

papers.title: A Tight Lower Bound for Non-stochastic Multi-armed Bandits with Expert Advice (Chase, Ito, Mehalel)
papers.claim: Theta(sqrt(TK log(N/K))) minimax expected regret for non-stochastic bandits with expert advice, matching Kale (2014) upper bound; lower bound uses an adaptive adversary; authors conjecture it also holds against an oblivious adversary.

papers.title: Improved Regret Bounds for Bandits with Expert Advice (Cesa-Bianchi, Eldowa, Esposito, Olkhovskaya)
papers.claim: Omega(sqrt(KT ln(N/K))) worst-case lower bound under a restricted feedback model, improving previous sqrt(KT lnN/lnK).

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Contextual Linear Bandits and Multi-Armed Bandits with Expert Advice (Ito, NeurIPS 2024)
papers.claim: Omega(sqrt(KT log(N/K))) lower bound for MwE in the setting where the player chooses an expert before observing advice.

triage.summary: The polynomial gap in K mostly comes from the database using a weak lower bound. The bound Ω̃(min(√(KT), N+√T)) is from Erez et al. 2024, which studies bandit multiclass classification with sparse rewards; there Õ(|H|+√T) is achievable. With general Bernoulli rewards and N ≥ K, the policy class can contain the K constant policies. That reduces to a K-armed stochastic bandit with trivial contexts, so the standard Ω(√(KT)) applies (for N < K, roughly Ω(√(NT))). I'm relying on that standard reduction, not a paper fetched this session. Dudik et al.'s √(KT log N) is therefore tight up to log factors. The remaining question is the log factor. For non-stochastic bandits with expert advice, Chase, Ito and Mehalel (2025) prove Ω(√(TK log(N/K))), which matches Kale's (2014) upper bound. But their hard instance uses an adaptive adversary. In their Future Work they conjecture the bound also holds against an oblivious adversary, which leaves that case, and so the stochastic i.i.d.-context case, open. Ito (NeurIPS 2024) proves Ω(√(KT log(N/K))) only for a restricted protocol where the learner picks an expert before seeing that round's advice. Seldin and Lugosi (2016) give Ω(√(KT ln N/ln K)); I only saw this through citations and couldn't confirm it holds with stochastic contexts. No paper I found settles the exact log factor for i.i.d. contexts with a known context distribution. The verdict 'open' is a judgement: Chase et al. flag the oblivious case as open but don't mention stochastic contexts specifically.

papers.title: A Tight Lower Bound for Non-stochastic Multi-armed Bandits with Expert Advice
papers.claim: Proves Ω(√(TK log(N/K))) for N≥2K, matching Kale's (2014) upper bound, using an adaptive adversary. Future Work conjectures the bound also holds against an oblivious adversary, which is still open.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Contextual Linear Bandits and Multi-Armed Bandits with Expert Advice
papers.claim: Ito (NeurIPS 2024): proves Ω(√(KT log(N/K))) for the restricted setting where the learner picks an expert before seeing that round's advice.

papers.title: The Real Price of Bandit Information in Multiclass Classification
papers.claim: Shows minimax regret Θ̃(min{|H|+√T, √(KT log|H|)}) for bandit multiclass classification (sparse rewards). This is the source of the database's lower bound, which is weak for general Bernoulli rewards.

papers.title: Improved Regret Bounds for Bandits with Expert Advice
papers.claim: Proves Ω(√(KT ln(N/K))) for N>K under restricted expert advice, improving on Seldin–Lugosi's Ω(√(KT ln N/ln K)).

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Regret Bounds for Bandits with Fixed Expert Advice
papers.claim: Experts are fixed, known distributions over arms. Gives lower bounds for some expert classes showing the algorithms are nearly optimal in some cases; the page fetched didn't say whether the lower bounds use i.i.d. losses.

papers.title: The Sample Complexity of Multiclass and Sparse Contextual Bandits
papers.claim: Tight PAC sample complexity for stochastic-context contextual bandits with s-sparse rewards and a finite policy class. Gives no regret bounds and no result for general (non-sparse) rewards.

triage.summary: The gap is not closed, and it is known to be open. The authors of the source paper say so themselves. Under strong stochastic transitivity (SST) plus the stochastic triangle inequality (STI), PAC ranking was studied in Falahatgar, Orlitsky, Pichapati and Suresh, "Maximum Selection and Ranking under Noisy Comparisons" (ICML 2017, arXiv:1705.05366). The upper bound in our database, O(K log^3 K log(K/δ)/ε²), is the Merge-Rank result (Lemma 4 on the ar5iv version). The same paper has a sharper result. It uses a noisy binary-search framework (Theorem 12 and Corollary 13) to get O(K log K (log log K)^3/ε²) comparisons, but only for δ = 1/K, i.e. constant-to-polynomial confidence. Its lower bound is Ω(K log(K/δ)/ε²) (Theorem 15 on ar5iv; there is no "Theorem 16"). At δ = 1/K that lower bound is Ω(K log K/ε²). So the true gap at δ = 1/K is only (log log K)^3, not log^3 K, and our database should record this tighter upper bound. In their conclusion the authors explicitly call closing the (log log n)^3 gap an open question. For arbitrary δ, the paper's best stated bound is still the log^3 K log(K/δ) one. Searches for later work that removes the (log log K)^3 factor under SST+STI found nothing. Related work exists but is in other settings: Ren–Liu–Shroff (arXiv:1806.02970) gives tight PAC total-ranking bounds, but under the MNL/Plackett-Luce model; Ren et al. 2020 (arXiv:2007.03133) treats best-k selection, not full ranking. One caveat: the setting is tagged SST only, but these bounds need STI as well. Falahatgar et al., NeurIPS 2017 ("Maxing and Ranking with Few Assumptions"), show that under SST alone, PAC ranking needs quadratically many comparisons. If the tag really means SST without STI, the database's upper bound would not apply.

papers.title: Maximum Selection and Ranking under Noisy Comparisons
papers.claim: Under SST+STI: Merge-Rank uses O(n log^3 n log(n/δ)/ε²) comparisons. Binary-Search-Ranking uses O(n log n (log log n)^3/ε²) comparisons for δ=1/n. Lower bound is Ω(n log(n/δ)/ε²). The conclusion explicitly says closing the (log log n)^3 gap is open.

papers.title: Maxing and Ranking with Few Assumptions
papers.claim: Under SST alone (no STI), maxing needs linearly many comparisons but PAC ranking needs quadratically many. Under the Borda metric with no assumptions, ranking takes O(n log n) comparisons.

papers.title: PAC Ranking from Pairwise and Listwise Queries: Lower Bounds and Upper Bounds
papers.claim: Tight lower and upper bounds for PAC total ranking, but under the MNL (Plackett-Luce for pairs) model, not general SST+STI.

triage.summary:
Under the usual stochastic linear bandit model (reward ⟨a,θ⟩ plus independent noise, unit-ball actions, θ in the unit l2 ball), the minimax rate is Θ(d√T) with no log T factor. This means the database entry has two problems.

1. **The lower bound is too weak.** Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis (2010) and Lattimore & Szepesvári (Bandit Algorithms, Thm 24.2) prove Ω(d√T) on the unit ball. The second-hand search excerpts and the Zhang et al. paper both report this; I did not open those two sources myself. This is stronger than the √(dT) bounds recorded.

2. **The upper bound is probably wrongly inherited.** The 3√(dT log T) bound comes from the adversarial bandit linear optimisation results (Bubeck–Cesa-Bianchi–Kakade 2012; Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi 2012 survey). Those assume the observed loss is exactly ⟨a, z_t⟩. With additive noise the observation is not linear in a, so the reduction fails. If it held, it would contradict the Ω(d√T) lower bound.

**Matching bounds.** Zhang, Hadiji & Combes (arXiv:2502.17175, 2025), which I fetched, gives both sides on ellipsoids, which include the unit ball:
- **Lower bound (Thm 2.1):** regret ≥ min(σd√T/16, BT/4) for any parameter norm B.
- **Upper bound (Thm 3.1, E2TC algorithm):** regret ≤ 6dσ√T + lower-order terms, giving O(min(σd√T + d‖θ‖, T‖θ‖)) (Cor. 3.1).
- **Applied here:** with ‖θ‖ ≤ 1, bounded ±1 noise is 1-sub-Gaussian, so the upper bound is O(d√T). Their lower bound uses Gaussian noise. I expect the same construction to give Ω(d√T) for bounded noise (e.g. Rademacher/Bernoulli rewards), but I have not checked that.

**Caveat.** If the database instead means the iid-loss-vector model (observe ⟨a, z_t⟩ with z_t iid in the unit ball, a special case of the adversarial model), then the √(dT log T) vs √(dT) gap is a different question, and I found no source closing it in this session. The 'bounded_pm1' noise label points to the additive-noise model, so the verdict is closed at Θ(d√T). The database should fix both the upper bound (drop the adversarial inheritance) and the lower bound (raise it to d√T).

papers.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms (Raymond Zhang, Hedi Hadiji, Richard Combes)
papers.claim: Ellipsoid action sets (unit ball included), sub-Gaussian noise with variance proxy σ². Thm 2.1: any algorithm has regret ≥ min(σd√T/16, BT/4). Thm 3.1: E2TC has regret ≤ 6dσ√T + O(σ²d²/‖θ‖ · log) + 290d‖θ‖ + exponentially small term. The rate is minimax optimal up to universal constants with no log T factor, i.e. Θ(d√T) on the unit ball with ‖θ‖ ≤ 1.

papers.title: Linearly Parameterized Bandits (Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis), as cited in 2502.17175 and search excerpts
papers.claim: Ω(d√T) minimax lower bound when the action set is the unit ball. The PEGE algorithm achieves O((‖θ‖+1/‖θ‖)d√T). Known only through citations; not fetched directly.

triage.summary:
I'm calling this gap closed, with caveats. The gap is a missing log T factor: the database lower bound is min(K/Δ_min, Δ_min·T), while UCB-type upper bounds are O(Σ log T/Δ_i). Knowing Δ does not remove the log T factor.

Bubeck, Perchet and Rigollet (COLT 2013, arXiv:1302.1611) prove that bounded regret is impossible when the learner knows only Δ. I read their Theorem 6 in the arXiv HTML v2. It uses ν = δ_0 ⊗ N(−Δ,1) and ν′ = δ_0 ⊗ N(Δ,1). For any policy and any n ≥ 1, max(R_n(ν), R_n(ν′)) ≥ log(nΔ²/2)/(4Δ). This gives Ω(log(TΔ²)/Δ) when T ≳ 1/Δ², which matches the UCB upper bound in T and Δ.

Caveats:
1. **Gaussian rewards.** The theorem uses Gaussian rewards (and a Dirac arm), not rewards in [0,1]. A Bernoulli adaptation would follow from the same change-of-measure argument, but I did not see it stated for [0,1] rewards.
2. **Two arms only.** The theorem covers two arms. A K-armed version of order K·log(TΔ²/K)/Δ is the natural extension, but I did not find it stated during this session.
3. **Erratum.** The paper's Microsoft Research page says the proof of Theorem 8 is incorrect. That theorem is the "only μ* known" result, not the "only Δ known" result used here. Theorem 6 is unaffected.

The Lai–Robbins asymptotic lower bound for consistent policies also implies log T growth on Bernoulli instances with gaps ≥ Δ_min. I did not re-verify it this session, so it is not cited. In the database's per-variable terms: T is closed (log T is necessary), Δ is closed, and K is closed only up to the multi-arm extension.

Sources: [arXiv abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.1611), [arXiv HTML v2](https://arxiv.org/html/1302.1611v2), [PMLR page](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v30/Bubeck13.html), [Microsoft Research page with the Theorem 8 note](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/?p=354779).

papers.title: Bounded regret in stochastic multi-armed bandits (Bubeck, Perchet, Rigollet, COLT 2013)
papers.claim: Theorem 6 (only Δ known): with ν = δ_0⊗N(−Δ,1) and ν′ = δ_0⊗N(Δ,1), every policy has max(R_n(ν), R_n(ν′)) ≥ log(nΔ²/2)/(4Δ), so regret must grow logarithmically even when Δ is known. Theorem 5 (both μ* and Δ known) gives Ω(1/Δ), and the authors also give a policy with bounded regret when both are known. The erratum on the Microsoft Research page concerns Theorem 8 (only μ* known), not Theorem 6.

triage.summary:
The gap appears to be closed at Θ(√(KT)), with no logarithmic factors.

**Upper bound.** Saha & Gaillard (ICML 2022, arXiv:2202.06694) present Versatile-DB, a reduction from dueling bandits to multi-armed bandits that runs Tsallis-INF-style online mirror descent. Two sources state its adversarial guarantee as 4√(KT)+1 pseudo-regret against any sequence of preference matrices, the benchmark being the Condorcet winner. Those sources are a search-result summary of the paper and the 2026 follow-up arXiv:2603.18972, which restates the bound. I could not read the theorem myself because the PDFs were unreadable compressed text, so the constant and exact conditions should be checked against Theorem 3.

**Why it applies to this setting.** In the stochastic utility-based model the preference matrix is fixed over time, so it is a special case of "any sequence". The utility-best arm is the Condorcet winner. Under the linear link P(i≻j) = (1+u_i−u_j)/2, the dueling regret Saha & Gaillard use coincides, up to a constant, with Ailon et al.'s utility regret. In a stochastic environment, pseudo-regret equals expected regret. Together these give O(√(KT)), which removes the log^{1.5} T factor in the Corollary 3.2 bound from Ailon et al. (2014).

**Lower bound.** Gajane et al. (2015, Theorem 2) give Ω(√(KT)), so the bound is tight in both K and T.

**Caveats.** If the utility_link class allows non-linear links, the equivalence between the two regret notions holds only up to link-dependent constants. Separately, the same rate may follow from "Sparring" (Ailon et al.'s scheme of pitting two copies of a bandit algorithm against each other) using a minimax-optimal adversarial MAB algorithm such as Tsallis-INF instead of EXP3. I did not find a source that states this, so it is only a likely route.

papers.title: Versatile Dueling Bandits: Best-of-both World Analyses for Learning from Relative Preferences (Saha, Gaillard)
papers.claim: Theorem 3 as reported in sources (exact statement not read): Versatile-DB (MAB reduction with Tsallis-INF-type OMD) gets pseudo-regret ≤ 4√(KT)+1 against any sequence of preference matrices (Condorcet benchmark), and also gap-dependent O(Σ log T/Δ_i) in stochastic Condorcet instances. For a fixed utility-based preference matrix this gives O(√(KT)), matching the Ω(√(KT)) lower bound.

papers.title: Best-of-Both-Worlds Multi-Dueling Bandits: Unified Algorithms for Stochastic and Adversarial Preferences under Condorcet and Borda Objectives (Akash, Gajane, Singh)
papers.claim: Restates that Saha & Gaillard (2022) achieve O(√(KT)) (4√(KT)+1) adversarial pseudo-regret together with instance-optimal stochastic regret for dueling bandits.

triage.summary: The bounds come from Gao, Han, Ren & Zhou, "Batched Multi-armed Bandits Problem" (NeurIPS 2019). The upper bound is sqrt(K)·T^{1/(2-2^{1-M})}·logK·sqrt(log KT) and the adaptive lower bound is sqrt(K)·T^{1/(2-2^{1-M})}/M^2. The paper says it is optimal only "within logarithmic factors" and does not say whether those factors can be removed. Later work does not close the gap. Esfandiari et al. (AAAI 2021) improve only the instance-dependent bound (9T^{1/B}ln(2KTB)Σ1/Δ_j). Its tight Θ̃(sqrt(T(K+T/B))) result is for adversarial bandits with fixed batch sizes, up to log factors. Jin et al. (ICML 2021) is about asymptotic optimality, and Kalkanli & Ozgur (NeurIPS 2021) use O(log T) batches. Batched linear-bandit papers keep log factors. A search-result summary of a Stanford poster for the Gao et al. paper said removing the M^{-2} factor in the adaptive lower bound is open. I could not read that PDF, so this is unconfirmed, and it does not cover the log K / log T factors. No source I found shows the gap closed or explicitly calls the log-factor gap open. I did not systematically check papers citing Gao et al. from 2022 onward. The Esfandiari PDF was also unreadable, so I used its HTML version.

papers.title: Batched Multi-armed Bandits Problem
papers.claim: BaSE policy gets regret optimal within log factors. Matching lower bounds hold for static grids (Thm 2) and for adaptive grids with an extra M^{-2} loss (Thm 3).

papers.title: Regret Bounds for Batched Bandits
papers.claim: Instance-dependent bound 9T^{1/B}ln(2KTB)Σ1/Δ_j for batched stochastic MAB. No problem-independent bound for the stochastic case. Adversarial bandits with fixed batch sizes: Θ̃(sqrt(T(K+T/B))), up to log factors.

papers.title: Almost Optimal Anytime Algorithm for Batched Multi-Armed Bandits
papers.claim: Asymptotically optimal regret with O(log log T · ilog^α T) batches. About asymptotic optimality, not the minimax rate for fixed M.

papers.title: Batched Thompson Sampling
papers.claim: Kalkanli & Ozgur: minimax regret O(sqrt(T log T)) with O(log T) batches.

triage.summary: I found no paper that closes the gap and none that explicitly calls it open. Esfandiari et al. (AAAI 2021) improve the upper bound to O(T^{1/M} log(KTM) Σ_i 1/Δ_i), at most K T^{1/M} log(KT)/Δ_min. This removes Gao et al.'s extra log K factor and uses adaptive batch sizes, where Gao et al.'s are fixed in advance. The best lower bound is still Gao et al.'s Ω(K T^{1/M}/(Δ_min M^2)), so a log(KT) factor and an M^2 factor remain unmatched. Gao et al. attribute the M^2 loss to adaptive batch boundaries and say it is at most polylog in T. Esfandiari et al. make no tightness claim for 1<M<log T. Three searches found no later result removing the log T factor for K-armed bandits. Fetching the arXiv PDF of 1910.04959 failed (unreadable), so the bound is from a text copy of the AAAI paper.

papers.title: Regret Bounds for Batched Bandits
papers.claim: Batched arm elimination with adaptive batch sizes and M batches: regret <= 9 T^{1/M} log(KTM) sum_{i:Delta_i>0} 1/Delta_i. Removes the log K factor of Gao et al. and replaces K/Delta_min with sum 1/Delta_i. Gives no new lower bound for general M.

papers.title: Batched Multi-armed Bandits Problem
papers.claim: Problem-dependent lower bound of order K T^{1/M}/(Delta_min M^2). The M^2 loss comes from adaptive grids and is argued to be at most polylog in T. The upper bound has extra log factors.

papers.title: Batched Dueling Bandits
papers.claim: Related setting: lower bound of order K T^{1/B}/(B^2 eps_min). The upper bound seen still carries a log T factor.

triage.summary:
I found no published result that closes this gap. The only lower bound that would close it was retracted by its own authors, so the question is known to be open.

**The gap.** In the regime T→∞, the upper bound is of order log(1/Δ)/Δ and the lower bound is of order 1/Δ. They differ by a log(1/Δ) factor; the extra K-dependence matters little for K=2.

**The retracted claim.** Bubeck, Perchet & Rigollet (COLT 2013, arXiv:1302.1611) study the case where the learner knows μ* but not Δ. Their abstract says that "bounded regret of order 1/Δ is not possible if one only knows μ*". Their introduction says that logarithmic growth of the rescaled regret ΔR_n is unavoidable even when μ* is known. This is their Theorem 8, which would make the log(1/Δ)/Δ rate tight.

**The erratum.** The paper's Microsoft Research page carries this note, which I fetched and saw directly: "The proof of Theorem 8 is not correct. We do not know if the theorem holds true." The arXiv page (v2, Feb 2013) has no erratum. Garivier, Ménard & Stoltz (2019) cite the erratum and only point to later work showing bounded regret is achievable when μ* is known (Bubeck et al. 2013; Faure et al. 2015).

**What's left.** I found nothing that proves Theorem 8 or improves the upper bound to O(1/Δ) when Δ is unknown. So whether the log(1/Δ) factor is necessary for K=2 Gaussian arms with μ* and σ known is still unresolved. My searches can't rule out a recent paper that fixes it.

**Caveats.** I couldn't read the full Theorem 8 statement, so I'm relying on how the abstract, introduction and erratum describe it. I also couldn't read the appendices of arXiv:1602.07182, so I didn't check whether the database's Theorem A.3 and C.1 come from that paper.

papers.title: Bounded regret in stochastic multi-armed bandits (Bubeck, Perchet, Rigollet), COLT 2013
papers.claim: Studies the case where μ* is known (plus a lower bound on Δ) and gives a policy with bounded regret. Its abstract says bounded regret of order 1/Δ is impossible if only μ* is known, and its introduction says logarithmic growth of ΔR_n is unavoidable even when μ* is known (Theorem 8). The authors' erratum on the Microsoft Research page says: 'The proof of Theorem 8 is not correct. We do not know if the theorem holds true.'

papers.title: Explore First, Exploit Next: The True Shape of Regret in Bandit Problems (Garivier, Ménard, Stoltz), Math. of OR 2019
papers.claim: Gives non-asymptotic, distribution-dependent regret lower bounds. Says bounded regret is achievable when μ* is known (citing Bubeck et al. 2013 and Faure et al. 2015) and cites the BPR erratum on Theorem 8.

triage.summary: For K=2 the gap in T is closed: worst-case regret is Θ(√T). A setting where the corruption budget can be any C ≥ 0 includes C = 0, the ordinary uncorrupted stochastic bandit, where regret against the uncorrupted rewards is ordinary stochastic regret. So the classical minimax lower bound Ω(√(KT)) applies (Auer–Cesa-Bianchi–Freund–Schapire; Lattimore–Szepesvári Ch. 15). Its proof uses Bernoulli arms Ber(1/2) and Ber(1/2±Δ) with Δ≈1/√T, which have rewards in [0,1] and fit K=2. Knowing C gives the learner no advantage when C = 0. This lower bound matches Exp3's O(√(T log 2)) upper bound up to constants, and the database's √T/log T lower bound (pacchiano2020model) is weaker than this textbook bound. Caveats: the joint dependence on C (presumably of the form √T + C) was not searched. I also could not read the theorem statements themselves: fetching the Slivkins book PDF returned unreadable binary, and the search results showed only abstracts, tables of contents and summaries. Exact constants should be checked against the originals.

papers.title: The Nonstochastic Multiarmed Bandit Problem
papers.claim: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund, Schapire (FOCS 1995 / SIAM J. Comput. 2002): their algorithm's per-round payoff approaches the best arm's at rate O(T^-1/2), and a matching lower bound shows this rate is best possible.

papers.title: Bandit Algorithms (Lattimore & Szepesvári), Chapter 15: Minimax Lower Bounds
papers.claim: Minimax lower bound of order √(KT) for stochastic K-armed bandits. The search results confirmed the chapter and section location only, not the exact theorem statement.

papers.title: Bubeck, MLSS 2016 tutorial (Part 1)
papers.claim: Two-armed Bernoulli argument with arms Ber(1/2) and Ber(1/2+ξΔ): for the worst-case Δ≈1/√T the lower bound is of order √T.

triage.summary: The polynomial gap in d appears to be closed up to a √log T factor, in the worst case over convex bodies. Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade (COLT 2012) state in their abstract that d√(n log n) regret for any compact action set is minimax optimal up to a log factor. That implies an Ω(d√T) lower bound for some convex body, the hypercube. Dani, Hayes & Kakade (NeurIPS 2007) say in their abstract that bandit regret exceeds full-information regret (√(nT)) by at least a factor of √n, which implies Ω(n√T). Shamir (2014/2015, Theorem 6) proves c(d−1)√T on [−1,1]^d for T ≥ d⁴/4, but with sub-Gaussian rather than bounded losses. So the d-exponent should be 1, matching Hazan–Karnin's d√(T log T) upper bound. Only a √log T factor remains in T. Caveats: I could not read the 2007 PDF (it returned compressed bytes), so I have not checked the exact bounded-loss theorem statement. The lower bounds are for specific bodies such as the hypercube, so the gap closes under the worst case over convex bodies, not for every body. Lattimore–Szepesvári Chapter 24 was not accessed.

papers.title: Towards Minimax Policies for Online Linear Optimization with Bandit Feedback (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi, Kakade)
papers.claim: The abstract gives d√(n log n) regret for any compact action set and says this is minimax optimal up to a log factor without further assumptions. The paper also gets d√n regret on the hypercube with an efficient algorithm.

papers.title: The Price of Bandit Information for Online Optimization (Dani, Hayes, Kakade)
papers.claim: The abstract gives lower bounds showing bandit regret exceeds full-information regret (O*(√(nT))) by at least a factor of √n, which implies an Ω(n√T) bandit lower bound. The exact decision set and loss normalisation were not checked because the PDF was unreadable.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Bandit Linear Optimization (Shamir)
papers.claim: Theorem 6: on the hypercube [−1,1]^d, regret ≥ c(d−1)√T for T ≥ d⁴/4. The loss mean is in the dual-norm unit ball, but losses are only sub-Gaussian, not bounded.

triage.summary: No published result closes this gap, and no paper says it is open. The database's upper bound (huang2024quantum) is Huang, Wang & Xu, 'Quantum Entanglement Path Selection and Qubit Allocation via Adversarial Group Neural Bandits' (arXiv:2411.00316). Its EXPNeuralUCB algorithm has sublinear regret guarantees. I saw only the abstract and search snippets, not the T^{3/4}·sqrt(log T) theorem itself, and the abstract does not mention time-varying action sets. The lower bound sqrt(KT)/20 comes from the generic adversarial K-armed bandit results; I did not see those papers in this session. I found no adversarial neural/NTK bandit result with Õ(√T) regret and no lower bound specific to this setting. In the stochastic neural setting, T^{3/4} is the known cost of the standard reduction to online regression (quoted by Deb et al., ICLR 2024, who sharpen it). That paper also notes the NeuralUCB/NeuralTS assumptions allow Ω(T) worst-case regret, but this does not settle the adversarial group setting. The 2026 quantum-NTK bandit work I found (arXiv:2601.02870) is stochastic. The gap (T^{3/4} vs T^{1/2}, and the K dependence) appears open but not explicitly acknowledged.

papers.title: Quantum Entanglement Path Selection and Qubit Allocation via Adversarial Group Neural Bandits
papers.claim: Proposes EXPNeuralUCB for adversarial group neural bandits (path = group, qubit allocation = arm), with theoretical performance guarantees and sublinear regret. The abstract states no explicit rate; per the database this is the T^{3/4} sqrt(log T) upper bound.

papers.title: Refined Lower Bounds for Adversarial Bandits
papers.claim: Refined lower bounds for (non-neural) adversarial bandits; argues several recent upper bounds are close to tight.

triage.summary: The database's upper bound is linear Thompson sampling (Agrawal & Goyal) with d set to K, so the setting is effectively a finite-armed linear contextual bandit with adversarial contexts. The neural_ntk label appears inconsistent with that. In this setting the polynomial gap in K is closed by SupLinUCB (Chu, Li, Reyzin & Schapire, AISTATS 2011): its O(sqrt(Td ln^3(KT ln T/δ))) upper bound matches their Omega(sqrt(Td)) lower bound up to log factors. Li, Wang & Zhou (COLT 2019) tighten this further: minimax regret is Omega(sqrt(dT log T log n)), and VCL-SupLinUCB matches it up to iterated logs, closing the log gap in T as well. The proceedings page does not state whether contexts are adversarial; that is assumed from the SupLinUCB line of work. If the NTK/neural model is meant literally, I found no neural-specific minimax lower bound. Known neural upper bounds are d̃·sqrt(T) for NeuralUCB/NeuralTS, which a 2024 ICLR paper argues can be linear in the worst case, and sqrt(Γ_k(T)·T) for SupNeuralUCB (Kassraie & Krause 2022), so that reading would be less clear-cut.

papers.claim: Lower bound Omega(sqrt(dT log T log n)) for linear contextual bandits with n <= 2^{d/2} actions; VCL SupLinUCB matches up to iterated logarithmic factors.

papers.claim: Argues NeuralUCB/NeuralTS can incur Omega(T) worst-case regret under their original assumptions.

triage.summary:
The gap is already closed, and by the same paper the database cites for its lower bound: ito2021optimal. The upper bounds in the database carry over from bandit algorithms (Tsallis-INF; Masoudian & Seldin), so they scale as sqrt(KT) and K log T. Those are too loose for full-information feedback.

Shinji Ito, "On Optimal Robustness to Adversarial Corruption in Online Decision Problems" (NeurIPS 2021, arXiv 2109.10963), has a matching upper bound for the expert problem. Its Theorem 3 covers Hedge with the decreasing learning rate η_t = sqrt(8 log N / t). In the adversarial regime with a self-bounding constraint, it shows pseudo-regret ≤ 33 + 100 log N/Δ + 10 sqrt(C log N/Δ). Hedge also has the standard worst-case bound sqrt(2T log N) + log N/8. The paper combines the two into O(min{log N/Δ + sqrt(C log N/Δ), sqrt(T log N)}). Here N is the number of experts, i.e. K.

The paper's Theorem 5 lower bound has exactly the same form, and the paper says it is tight up to a constant factor. So the order is known in every variable:
- K: log K, not sqrt(K).
- T: sqrt(T log K) in the worst case.
- Δ and C: log K/Δ + sqrt(C log K/Δ).

The database's upper-bound entries should be replaced by Ito's Theorem 3 plus the standard Hedge bound. Note that the worst-case sqrt(T log N) term is not stated in Theorem 3 itself. It comes from combining Theorem 3 with Theorem 1 (the standard Hedge bound); I read this in the ar5iv full text. Also relevant is earlier work by Amir et al. (2020), which showed decreasing Hedge has a linear dependence on C; I saw this only in a search-result summary of Ito's related work, not the paper itself.

papers.title: On Optimal Robustness to Adversarial Corruption in Online Decision Problems (Shinji Ito, NeurIPS 2021)
papers.claim: Expert problem, adversarial regime with a self-bounding constraint. Theorem 3: decreasing-rate Hedge has pseudo-regret ≤ 33 + 100 log N/Δ + 10 sqrt(C log N/Δ). Combined with the standard Hedge bound sqrt(2T log N), this gives O(min{log N/Δ + sqrt(C log N/Δ), sqrt(T log N)}). Theorem 5 gives a matching lower bound, tight up to a constant factor.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed. The "poly_gap in K" label is an artifact: K is fixed at 2 here. With K=2 there is only one suboptimal arm, so the sum over suboptimal arms in the upper bound is a single term in Delta_i = Delta_min. Both the upper bounds already in the database (bian2022maillard, and abbasi2011oful with delta=1/T) are therefore O(sigma^2 log T / Delta). That matches the lower bounds log T/(2 Delta) and log T/Delta up to constants, giving Theta(log T / Delta) with tight dependence on T and Delta.

The constants are also settled, in the source the database already uses for its lower bounds. "On Explore-Then-Commit Strategies" (Garivier, Lattimore, Kaufmann, NeurIPS 2016, arXiv:1605.08988) studies exactly this setting: two-armed Gaussian bandits, with and without knowledge of the gap Delta. It proves asymptotic lower bounds and gives fully sequential (non-ETC) strategies that are asymptotically optimal as T grows, so the leading constant is matched. It also shows that explore-then-commit strategies lose a factor of about 2 asymptotically.

What I confirmed this session: the paper's title, authors and its claim of asymptotically optimal fully sequential strategies, regardless of whether the gap is known, all came from one search. I did not open the paper to check the exact constant for the known-Delta case. I'm relying on the lower bounds the database already cites (Theorems 3 and 6) for that.

The database already marks the Delta and T dependence as tight. triage.summary:
This gap is already closed by classical results. For the two-armed subgaussian bandit where the learner knows σ, the worst-case regret is Θ(σ√T).

**Lower bound.** Lattimore & Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*, Chapter 15 (Theorem 15.1 and Exercise 15.2) show that for unit-variance Gaussian bandits with means in [0,1], every policy suffers regret at least (1/27)·√((K−1)T) on some instance. With K=2 that is Ω(√T). Gaussian noise with variance σ² is σ-subgaussian, so rescaling gives Ω(σ√T) here, and this holds even when σ is known. I did not open the book itself: the statement and the 1/27 constant come from surveys that restate it (arXiv 2412.02251 Theorem 6, and arXiv 2608.17841).

**Upper bound.** MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck, COLT 2009) gets regret O(√(KT)) with no log factor. Rescaling its confidence width by the known σ gives O(σ√T) for K=2. The database entry from bian2022maillard Corollary 5, √(2T·log 2)·σ, is already of this order.

**Why the database shows a gap.** Its only lower bound is the weaker √T/log T from Pacchiano et al. 2020, a model-selection paper. The standard Ω(√T) minimax lower bound is missing. Adding it gives matching orders, Θ(σ√T), and only constant factors differ.

Avner, Mannor & Shamir (ICML 2012), footnote 1 of Section 3, say the standard Ω(√(KT)) bandit lower bound carries over to decoupled algorithms. Their reason is that the difficulty comes from distinguishing slightly different distributions from T observations, which decoupling does not change. This is a remark with justification, not a formal theorem. Their Theorem 6 gives a formal c√(kT) lower bound only for decoupled algorithms whose exploration distribution is fixed. On the upper side, Rouyer & Seldin (COLT 2020) prove O(√(KT)) for Decoupled-Tsallis-INF and call it minimax optimal; jin2023improved matches this rate. The database's √(T log K) lower bound is simply weaker than the known Ω(√(KT)) bound. Exponents: K^{1/2}, T^{1/2}.

One caveat: that paper's abstract does not state the Ω(T^{2/3}) bound for semi feedback with adversarial values. For adversarial values under GBB with one-bit or two-bit feedback, it gives Ω(T^{3/4}) instead; its Θ̃(T^{2/3}) result is for independent values. So the semi-feedback lower bound is presumably in the body of CJLZ25 or follows from it, but I did not check this in the full text. I only have Jin's abstract for the match.

A second caveat: I matched the database entry to this paper by the citation key and the T^{2/3} rate. The setting is labelled only loosely ("continuum_other, partial_monitoring"), so the curators should confirm that jin2026tight is arXiv:2601.16412.

triage.summary:
I'm treating the gap as closed up to log factors, but this depends on how I read the setting. The setting lists no feature dimension d, and the bounds in your database don't involve one.

The stored upper bound, (K log KT)^{1/4}·sqrt(KT log T), looks like Jin 2026's bound with d set equal to K. That paper is arXiv:2609.15170, which gives Õ(K^{1/4}·sqrt(dT)) for 2 ≤ K ≤ d. It solves a harder problem: the action menu may depend on the unknown parameter and on the history. Its matching lower bound Ω(K^{1/4}·sqrt(dT)) applies only to that adaptive-menu model.

Your setting has i.i.d. (stochastic) contexts, a finite set of K arms, and features with a known norm bound. That is the standard K-armed linear contextual bandit, and SupLinUCB (Chu, Li, Reyzin, Schapire, AISTATS 2011) already gives O(sqrt(T·d·ln³(KT ln T/δ))) regret there, even for arbitrary contexts. Li, Wang and Zhou (COLT 2019) remove two sqrt(log T) factors and prove a lower bound that nearly matches. With d ≤ K, including the d = K case your database seems to use, this upper bound is Õ(sqrt(KT)). That matches the Ω(sqrt(KT)) multi-armed-bandit lower bound already in your database (Auer et al. 2002; Bubeck–Cesa-Bianchi 2012) up to polylog factors.

So the K-exponent gap (3/4 vs 1/2) closes once you count SupLinUCB, which predates the stored upper bound. The only gap left is in the log factors on the T side, and as far as I found, no one has pinned those down exactly.

Caveat: if the setting is meant to have a free dimension d much larger than K, or a policy or function class that isn't linear, this reduction may not apply. In that case the stored entries are probably mis-specified rather than reflecting a genuine open problem.

This appears to be the source of the database's K^{3/4} sqrt(T) bound (with d = K). It is not tight for i.i.d. contexts.

triage.summary: For a fixed finite action set with K arms (K arbitrary, not tracked), the minimax regret is known to be Θ̃(√(dT·min{d, log K})). The upper bound O(√(dT log K)) comes from phased elimination with G-optimal design (Lattimore–Szepesvári book; Lattimore et al. 2020) and from SupLinRel/SupLinUCB (Auer 2002; Chu et al. 2011; Li et al. 2019). The lower bound Ω̃(√(dT·min{d, log K})) uses the 2^d hypercube corners scaled into the unit ball; Lau et al. (2026) call it well-known and cite Zhou (2019) and Tajdini et al. (2025). With K = 2^d this gives Ω(d√T), matching the d-dependence of the Dani et al. upper bound (≈ d√T·polylog T). Since K is unrestricted here, the worst case is Θ̃(d√T) and the polynomial gap in d is closed; only log-T factors remain. Li, Wang and Zhou (COLT 2019) also settle the log factors (Ω(√(dT·log T·log n)) for n ≤ 2^{d/2}, matched up to iterated logs), but I believe their result is for action sets that can change each round and did not check whether it covers a fixed action set. The database's Ω(√(dT)) lower bounds are only tight in the small-K regime. Caveat: I could not read the book PDF or Zhou's lecture-note PDF (both came back as binary), so the hypercube lower bound rests on secondary citations from search snippets and the fetched Lau et al. page.

triage.summary: Tentatively closed by Shinji Ito, 'On the Minimax Regret for Contextual Linear Bandits and Multi-Armed Bandits with Expert Advice' (NeurIPS 2024; no arXiv version found). Seen in abstract and snippets: (i) for linear bandits with K actions it proves an O(sqrt(dT log^+(K/d))) upper bound, which it calls slightly better than the earlier O(sqrt(dT log K)); (ii) for contextual linear bandits with S contexts it gives O(sqrt(dT log(K min{1,S/d}))) with a matching lower bound. Chu, Li, Reyzin & Schapire (AISTATS 2011) prove that SupLinUCB gets regret O(√(Td·ln³(KT ln T/δ))) with K arms and contexts that can change over time. Bernoulli(1/2) loss construction gives a lower bound of about √((T/2) ln K) for any algorithm (Cesa-Bianchi et al. 1997; Cesa-Bianchi & Lugosi 2006). I saw this attribution only in a search summary and did not open either source. Gravin–Peres–Sivan 2016 also show MW's regret is exactly √(T ln K/2) and give a (2/3)√(T ln K/2) lower bound for broad MW families. The database's √(KT) upper bounds are bandit bounds carried over to full information, so they are loose. The √(T log K) lower bound already matches the right order, and the gap is closed.

triage.summary: The gap seems to come from how the database recorded the upper bound, not from an open problem. Upper bound: in Bai, Jin, Wang & Xiong (arXiv 2102.11494, NeurIPS 2021), Theorem 5 is for *linear* bandit games and gives O~(d^2/ε^2). Setting d=K (one-hot features) gives the K^2/ε^2 bound in the database. The same paper also handles the finite-action bandit game directly. I read these statements on the ar5iv page. Theorem 2 gives O~(AB/ε^2) samples to reach a (gap_ε + ε)-approximate Stackelberg value. Theorem 3 is a matching lower bound: with about AB/ε^2 or fewer samples (times an absolute constant, with A, B ≥ 3), any algorithm has error g+ε with probability ≥ 1/3 on some instance. If K is the number of arms, meaning leader–follower action pairs (K = AB), the bound is Θ~(K/ε^2) and tight. That matches the Ω(K/ε^2) lower bound credited to li2023tight. Caveats: (1) The database setting is only labelled 'other_pure_exploration, K-armed, Bernoulli'. I assume it is the Stackelberg/bandit-game problem from bai2021sample, so the verdict depends on that reading and on K = AB. (2) The paper's model has noisy rewards, possibly sub-Gaussian/bounded. I didn't check that Theorem 3's hard instances are Bernoulli, though bounded-reward lower bounds of this kind usually are. (3) I could not find or confirm the li2023tight paper. (4) If K instead means each player's action count (A = B = K), the bound is Θ~(K^2/ε^2) by Theorems 2 and 3, which is also tight. Either way, the gap is closed by Theorems 2 and 3 of the same paper.

Theorem 3: matching lower bound, Ω(AB/ε^2) samples are needed (A, B ≥ 3). Theorem 5: linear bandit games, O~(d^2/ε^2), which is the source of the database's K^2/ε^2 bound with d=K.

triage.summary:
The gap is already closed in the literature: the minimax regret is Θ(d√T). The database's lower bound of order √(dT) is too weak, and its upper bound of order d√(T log T) has an extra log factor that isn't needed.

Upper bound: Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi and Kakade (COLT 2012, arXiv:1202.3079) study exactly this setting: the hypercube [-1,1]^d with losses in the L1 ball (cross-polytope), the polar of the hypercube. Their computationally efficient mirror-descent algorithm with the entropic regularizer has regret about 2d√(3n log 2) = O(d√n), with no log n factor. Here n is the horizon, i.e. T in your notation.

Lower bound: the same paper says the d√n regret "is minimax optimal" and attributes the matching Ω(d√n) lower bound to Dani, Hayes and Kakade (2008). It also says there are action sets "(such as the hypercube) where the minimax rate is of order" d√n. The Dani–Hayes–Kakade NeurIPS 2007 paper establishes that bandit feedback costs at least a √d factor more than full information, whose regret is of order √(dT); that is the source of the Ω(d√T) lower bound.

So for both T and d the order is Θ(d√T). I read the 2012 statements in the ar5iv HTML version of arXiv:1202.3079. For the 2007 paper I only saw the abstract and proceedings records; I did not check the exact theorem statement in its PDF.

triage.summary: The gap is closed up to constants by results missing from the database. Only abstracts and search snippets were checked, not full PDFs. Upper bound: Tsallis-INF (Zimmert & Seldin, JMLR 2021) gets regret O(sum_i log T/Delta_i + sqrt(C sum_i log T/Delta_i)) in a setting that includes stochastic bandits with adversarial corruption. This is linear in K, has a single log T, matches the Lai-Robbins log T/Delta rate at C=0, and is at most O(sum log T/Delta_i + C) by AM-GM. That removes the extra K and log T factors in the Lykouris et al. 2018 bound. Masoudian & Seldin (COLT 2021) refine the log factor and the C dependence. Lower bound: Ito (NeurIPS 2021) proves a bandit lower bound tight up to a log factor; a search summary gives it as Omega(N/Delta + sqrt(CN/Delta)), N = number of arms, but the exact expression was not seen. With Lai-Robbins this shows the sqrt(C...) shape is near-optimal. Caveats: (1) the KL-based Lai-Robbins bound matches log T/Delta only up to constants when arm means are bounded away from 0 and 1; (2) I believe, but did not confirm in the papers, that Zimmert-Seldin's setting allows adaptive adversaries and bounds regret against corrupted losses; (3) Ito's bandit lower bound leaves a log-factor gap in the C-dependent term only, not in the K, log T or Delta gaps listed for this setting.

papers.title: Tsallis-INF: An Optimal Algorithm for Stochastic and Adversarial Bandits (Zimmert, Seldin)

triage.summary: The gap is mostly a mismatch of parameters: the database's upper bounds are graph-agnostic √(KT) bandit bounds, while its lower bounds are √(αT), with α the graph's independence number. For strongly observable graphs, Alon et al. (COLT 2015) show minimax regret Θ̃(√(αT)), with an upper bound of about √(αT ln K). The database only has this paper's lower-bound theorem. Eldowa et al. (NeurIPS 2023) tighten this to an O(√(αT(1+ln(K/α)))) upper bound and an Ω(√(αT ln K / ln α)) lower bound for α>1. This matches √(KT) for bandits (α=K) and √(T ln K) for experts (α=1), and leaves only a ln α factor for intermediate α. If the worst case is taken over all graphs with K arms, α can equal K, so √(KT) is tight there as well. Up to log factors, the dependence on K and α is settled; only the exact log factor for intermediate α remains open.

triage.summary:
The √(log K) gap is closed for adaptive (non-anticipating) adversaries by a recent preprint. It may still be open for oblivious adversaries.

The preprint is Bacchiocchi, Cesari & Colomboni, "An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial m-Set Bandits" (arXiv:2608.12231, 2026). Its Corollary 1 (the m = 1 case of Theorem 2) states a lower bound that holds when K ≥ 2, δ ≤ δ₀ for a universal constant δ₀, and T is at least a threshold polynomial in K and log(1/δ). Under those conditions, every randomized policy faces a deterministic adaptive non-anticipating loss process in [0,1]^K under which, with probability at least δ, R_T ≥ c·√(KT(log K + log(1/δ))). This matches the known O(√(KT log(K/δ))) upper bounds (Exp3.P; Exp3-IX by Neu 2015) up to constants, and the authors say it closes the √(log K) gap left by Gerchinovitz & Lattimore. The paper also gives its own upper bound of 160·√(dT(log K + log(1/δ))).

Caveat: the setting is listed as "adversarial_unspecified". The Gerchinovitz & Lattimore lower bound in the database, Ω(√(KT log(1/δ))), holds even for loss sequences fixed in advance (oblivious). The new log K lower bound uses an adaptive adversary. In the parts of the paper I could read, I found no claim that the log K term is needed against oblivious adversaries, and no claim that it is known to be open. So if the intended setting is oblivious, the gap may still be open.

I only saw the paper's abstract and HTML page through fetch summaries, not the full proofs. The paper is a recent preprint and has not been independently checked.

The search summary also reports an earlier √(αT ln K) bound for undirected strongly observable graphs. So the polynomial dependence √(αT) is settled, and the remaining log(K/α) versus log_α K gap is a known open problem.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed, and it was closed before the paper your database uses for the upper bound. In this setting (oblivious adversary, semi-bandit feedback, losses in [0,1]^d, every action a binary vector with exactly m ones), the minimax regret is Θ(√(mdT)), with no log factor.

- **Upper bound:** Audibert, Bubeck & Lugosi, "Regret in Online Combinatorial Optimization" (arXiv 1204.4710; Math. of OR 2014; COLT 2011 precursor "Minimax Policies for Combinatorial Prediction Games", arXiv 1105.4871). Their Theorem 4 runs mirror descent with the INF potential ψ(x) = (−x)^(−q), q = 2, and gets R_n ≤ 2√(2mdn). I read this in the ar5iv HTML version of the paper.
- **Lower bound:** the same paper gives Ω(√(mdn)), built from the √(dn) bound for the standard d-armed bandit. Your database's Kveton et al. 2014 bound, min(Tm, √(Tdm))/20, already matches this order.
- **Your database's upper bound** (Neu 2015, FPL-TrIX, 13·m·√(Td(log(d/m)+1))) is loose in two ways. It has the extra log(d/m) factor, and it scales as m·√d rather than √(md), so it is off by an extra √m too. The same ABL paper's negative-entropy version (Theorem 3) gives √(2mdn·log(d/m)), which still carries the log.

Zimmert, Luo & Wei (ICML 2019, arXiv 1901.08779) also give a semi-bandit algorithm that works in both stochastic and adversarial settings. Their abstract says its leading constants are optimal in the previously studied worst-case sense, but I didn't check the exact form of their adversarial bound.

So in this regime the d-exponent is tight at 1/2 with no log gap, and the m-dependence is √m on both sides.

papers.title: Regret in Online Combinatorial Optimization
papers.claim: Semi-bandit, losses in [0,1]^d, ||a||_1=m: OSMD with INF potential psi(x)=(-x)^{-2} achieves R_n <= 2 sqrt(2 m d n) (Theorem 4); matching lower bound Omega(sqrt(mdn)); negentropy OSMD gives sqrt(2mdn log(d/m)) (Theorem 3).

papers.title: Minimax Policies for Combinatorial Prediction Games
papers.claim: COLT 2011 precursor of the paper above. Its abstract says that, except for the bandit game, the upper and lower bounds are tight up to a constant factor, which covers semi-bandit.

papers.claim: Semi-bandit algorithm that works in both stochastic and adversarial settings, with square-root regret in the adversarial case. The abstract says its leading constants are optimal in the previously studied worst-case sense; the exact adversarial bound was not checked.

triage.summary: The database bounds come from Neu & Valko, arXiv:2604.25269 (the NeurIPS 2014 paper, posted 2026). Its Corollary 1 bound, 2m√(2dT(log d+1)), is for the restricted-feedback setting with stochastic availability, not full information. Its Appendix D lower bound of order √(Td) is for the same setting. Its full-information bound (Theorem 1) depends on d only through log d. So the database entry appears mislabelled. For the setting as keyed (full information, oblivious adversarial availability, best-ordering/policy benchmark), Kleinberg, Niculescu-Mizil & Sharma (COLT 2008 / MLJ 2010) is reported to prove an Ω(√(T n log n)) lower bound that holds against an oblivious adversary, with a matching upper bound up to a constant. With m=1 this closes the √(log d) gap in d. Caveats: (1) I confirmed the exact Ω(√(Tn log n)) statement only through a search-result summary and the paper's abstract ('(almost) information-theoretically optimal'). The PDFs could not be fetched (certificate errors / binary content). (2) The dependence on m (the upper bound is linear in m, the lower bound has no m) is not resolved by anything I found. (3) In the literal Neu–Valko restricted-feedback, stochastic-availability setting, the log d gap is not discussed in the paper and seems unresolved. The authors only claim the √(dT) scaling is asymptotically tight.

papers.claim: Neu & Valko (NeurIPS 2014; arXiv 2026). Corollary 1 (restricted feedback): R_T ≤ 2m√(2dT(log d+1)). Theorem 1 (full information): R_T ≤ 2m√(2L*_T(log d+1)). Appendix D: an Ω(√(Td)) lower bound from d/2 pairs of sleeping experts with stochastic availability. No lower bound in m or in log d.

papers.claim: Kleinberg, Niculescu-Mizil, Sharma (COLT 2008; MLJ 2010). Benchmark is the best ordering of the actions. Reported (via search summary) to give an Ω(√(T n log n)) full-information lower bound under adversarial availability, holding even for an oblivious adversary, with an upper bound matching up to a constant. The abstract says the bounds are '(almost) information-theoretically optimal'.

papers.title: Hardness of Online Sleeping Combinatorial Optimization Problems
papers.claim: Kale, Lee, Pál (NeurIPS 2016). Computational hardness for sleeping combinatorial problems, including k-subsets. Also an unconditional exponential-in-d ranking-regret lower bound under stochastic losses and availabilities.

papers.title: Sleeping Experts and Bandits with Stochastic Action Availability and Adversarial Rewards
papers.claim: Kanade et al. (AISTATS 2009). Reported (via search summary) to give an O(√(T log n)) full-information bound under stochastic availability, which shows the √(Td) lower bound does not apply to full information with stochastic availability.

triage.summary:
The gap looks closed, up to constants and in the usual asymptotic sense. The database's best upper bound (pacchiano2020model) is loose, and its lower bound min(K/Δ_min, Δ_min·T) is missing the log T factor.

Upper bound: UCB (Auer, Cesa-Bianchi & Fischer 2002) gets regret O(Σ_i log T/Δ_i + Σ_i Δ_i) without knowing Δ_min. That is at most O(K log T/Δ_min). It is linear in K and in 1/Δ_min with a single log T, which removes the polynomial gaps in K (2/3 vs 1) and Δ (-1/3 vs 1) and the log² T. The paper I saw states this for UCB1 with rewards in [0,1]. The sub-Gaussian version is the standard textbook variant, but I did not confirm it from a source this session.

Lower bound: Garivier, Kaufmann & Lattimore (NeurIPS 2016) prove a Lai–Robbins-type bound for two-armed Gaussian bandits that holds even when the gap Δ is known (their Theorem 6): liminf R_T/log T ≥ 1/(2Δ). Their fully sequential Δ-UCB matches it, and its leading term is about log(TΔ²)/(2Δ). So knowing Δ only saves a constant factor and the regret is still logarithmic in T. Extending to K arms uses the same change-of-measure argument: K−1 arms each at gap Δ_min, and an alternative that raises one arm by 2Δ_min keeps the minimum gap at Δ_min. This gives Ω(K log T/Δ_min). That K-arm extension is my own inference; I did not see it stated in a paper. Together these give Θ(K log T/Δ_min) when all gaps equal Δ_min.

Caveats:
- The matching lower bound is asymptotic and for consistent strategies. A finite-T minimax bound over instances with gap Δ would have the form K/Δ·log(TΔ²/K).
- Bubeck, Perchet & Rigollet (COLT 2013) claim that knowing only Δ cannot give bounded regret (log growth is unavoidable). But the authors' Microsoft Research page says the proof of their Theorem 8, their main lower bound, is incorrect and that they do not know whether the theorem holds. So I don't rely on it.
- I could not extract text from the arXiv, PMLR or Microsoft PDFs, so I don't have the exact non-asymptotic statements.

papers.title: On Explore-Then-Commit Strategies
papers.claim: For two-armed Gaussian bandits, the results hold whether or not the gap Δ is known. The asymptotic lower bound for any (consistent) strategy is liminf R_T/log T ≥ 1/(2Δ) (Theorem 6, generalising Lai–Robbins). Δ-UCB, which uses the known gap, matches it with limsup R_T/log T ≤ 1/(2Δ). ETC strategies are suboptimal by a factor of 2.

papers.title: Finite-time Analysis of the Multiarmed Bandit Problem (Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer)
papers.claim: UCB1 has regret at most 8 Σ_{i:Δ_i>0} ln T/Δ_i + (1+π²/3) Σ_i Δ_i, which is O(K log T/Δ_min) without knowing Δ_min. This is stated for rewards in [0,1]; the sub-Gaussian variant is standard but was not confirmed this session.

papers.title: Bounded regret in stochastic multi-armed bandits (Bubeck, Perchet, Rigollet)

triage.summary:
The gap is closed by classical results. For stochastic K-armed bandits, worst-case regret is Θ(√(KT)), so with K=2 it is Θ(√T) with no log factor either way. The database bounds (Õ(√T) upper, Ω(√T/log T) lower) are loose versions of this.

Upper bound: MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck, 2009/2010) has distribution-free regret of order √(KT) with no log factor. The 2012 survey by Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi states this in Section 4.3 ("up to a numerical constant"). I saw that statement on the survey page. Other papers in the search results quote MOSS constants of 39√(KT)+ΣΔ and 49√(KT), but I didn't confirm those in the original paper. I didn't open the original MOSS paper.

Lower bound: the same survey (Theorem 7.9, minimax lower bound) gives inf sup R_n ≥ (1/20)√(nK). The supremum is over i.i.d. {0,1}-valued (Bernoulli) reward distributions, and the setup only needs K ≥ 2. Bernoulli rewards are (1/2)-subgaussian, so this applies to the subgaussian K=2 setting and gives Ω(√T). It sits in the chapter on adversarial bandits, but the rewards in the hard instance are stochastic i.i.d. Lattimore & Szepesvári's Bandit Algorithms covers the same result in Chapter 15, §15.2 "Minimax Lower Bounds" (I only saw the table of contents, not the theorem text).

So the minimax regret for K=2 is Θ(√T). Pinning down the exact constant is a separate, finer question that isn't settled.

papers.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi)
papers.claim: Theorem 7.9: minimax lower bound inf sup R_n >= (1/20) sqrt(nK) over i.i.d. {0,1}-valued reward distributions (stochastic, hence subgaussian), K>=2. Section 4.3: MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck 2010) attains regret <= const * min{sqrt(nK), (K/Δ) ln(nΔ²/K)}, i.e. O(sqrt(nK)) with no log factor.

triage.summary: For K=2, the database's upper bound (16 log(T/Δ)/Δ, from OFUL) and lower bound (log T/(2Δ)) differ only by constants. Both scale as log T / Δ, and the "poly_gap" flag on K is an artifact because K is fixed at 2. Garivier, Lattimore & Kaufmann (NeurIPS 2016) treat exactly the two-armed Gaussian case. They give fully sequential strategies with finite-time regret bounds that are asymptotically optimal, matching the Lai-Robbins constant, and minimax order-optimal; the database's log T/(2Δ) lower bound is their Theorem 6. Lattimore (JMLR 2018) gives a strategy for unit-variance Gaussian noise that is asymptotically optimal and minimax optimal up to constants, plus a finite-time lower bound that very nearly matches its upper bound. Only abstracts and summaries were seen, so the exact constants are not confirmed. Both papers assume Gaussian noise; the match carries over to subgaussian noise as worst-case bounds, since Gaussian instances are subgaussian and give the lower bound. The gap is closed.

triage.summary: The gap appears to be closed by the same paper your database already uses for the lower bound. Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis, "Linearly Parameterized Bandits" (arXiv:0812.3465; Math. of OR 2010), states in its abstract that when the arms are the unit sphere, the regret is Θ(r√T), where r is the dimension d. The upper bound comes from their phase-based explore/exploit policy (PEGE), which removes the log^{1.5} T factor in the bound inherited from Dani et al. 2008. So in T and d the minimax regret is Θ(d√T), with no log gap. I only read the abstract, not the theorem statements. Caveat: the paper's upper bound (Theorem 3.1) has constants that depend on its assumptions about the unknown parameter — bounds on its norm and a lower bound on its norm. Your entry says "parameter_set: unbounded", so the match is exact only up to those constants. The noise assumption (Gaussian / sub-Gaussian, known sigma) is compatible. Your database should add PEGE's O(d√T) upper bound for the sphere.

triage.summary:
I found no published result that closes the gap for an arbitrary fixed convex body. What I could verify:

**Upper bound.** The best upper bound in your database is about d·√T·log^1.5 T, taken from Dani et al. 2008. The literature does better: an order-d√(T log T) bound for any compact action set. This comes from Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade (COLT 2012) for adversarial losses bounded by 1, and the abstract says it is "minimax optimal up to a logarithmic factor". In the stochastic setting, discretising the body and running a finite-arm optimal-design method (phased elimination with a G-optimal design, from the Lattimore–Szepesvári book) gives the same rate. I did not check that page in this session.

**Lower bound.** The lower bound of order d√T is classical. Searches show it attributed to Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis for the unit ball and to Lattimore–Szepesvári more generally; I did not open those sources myself.

**What remains.** The real gap is a factor of √log T between d√T and d√(T log T), not log^1.5 T.

**Special cases that are closed:**
- Ellipsoids, including the unit ball: Zhang, Hadiji & Combes (arXiv 2502.17175, 2025) prove Θ(dσ√T) up to a universal constant, with no log factors.
- Hypercube: Bubeck et al. 2012 give an efficient algorithm with regret of order d√T. That result is adversarial, and I saw it only in a secondary summary, not in the paper.

**Arbitrary convex bodies.** Recent papers still state their general-action-set bounds with log factors. Examples are OLSOFUL (Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits, arXiv 1904.00242) and an FTPL paper, arXiv 2610.17818, whose bound I saw only in a search summary. I found no matching d√T upper bound or ω(d√T) lower bound for this case.

**Caveat on the verdict.** "open_known" here means the log gap is acknowledged and appears unresolved. I did not find an explicit statement calling it an open problem.

triage.summary:
I think the log gap is already closed: the optimal rate is Θ(d√T). There is one caveat about the noise model, set out below.

**Upper bound.** Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade (COLT 2012, arXiv 1202.3079) give an efficient Online Stochastic Mirror Descent algorithm on the hypercube with regret of order d√n. That has no log factor. They say it beats the best efficient bound by a √(d log n) factor and is minimax optimal on the hypercube. It is stated for bandit linear optimization with adversarial losses. Stochastic i.i.d. losses are a special case, so it bounds the expected pseudo-regret here too.

**Lower bound.** Shamir (COLT 2015, arXiv 1408.2368) is the source of the lower bound in your database. Theorem 6 gives Ω(d√T) on [-1,1]^d for T ≥ d⁴/4, using a stochastic construction with sub-Gaussian (Gaussian) losses. In Section 5, Shamir says this lower bound "matches the O(d√T) upper bound attained in [5]". Reference [5] is Bubeck–Cesa-Bianchi–Kakade 2012. He adds that this algorithm plays only on the corners of the hypercube. His introduction also gives the hypercube minimax regret as Θ(d√T).

Your database's upper bound (Dani et al. 2008, about d√T·log^1.5 T) is therefore loose. The d√T log factor is removed by the 2012 adversarial result.

**Caveat.** That result assumes bounded losses, roughly |⟨a,z⟩| ≤ 1. Carrying it to unbounded sub-Gaussian reward noise needs the usual estimator-variance argument. I did not check that step in the full proof. Shamir's framework, which allows sub-Gaussian losses, treats the two bounds as matching.

**Tool issues.** I could not extract text from the Lattimore–Szepesvári book PDF or the PMLR PDF of Shamir's paper. I read Shamir's paper from the ar5iv HTML version instead.

papers.title: Towards Minimax Policies for Online Linear Optimization with Bandit Feedback
papers.claim: Authors: Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi, Kakade (COLT 2012). An efficient OSMD algorithm achieves regret of order d√n on the hypercube, with no log factor. This improves on prior efficient algorithms by √(d log n) and is minimax optimal for the hypercube. Stated for adversarial bandit linear optimization with bounded losses.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Bandit Linear Optimization
papers.claim: Author: Shamir (COLT 2015). Theorem 6 gives an Ω(d√T) lower bound on [-1,1]^d (T ≥ d⁴/4) using sub-Gaussian stochastic losses. Section 5 says it matches the O(d√T) upper bound attained by Bubeck–Cesa-Bianchi–Kakade 2012, and the introduction states the hypercube minimax regret is Θ(d√T).

triage.summary: The source paper itself (tang2020bandit = Tang, Ho, Liu, 'Bandit Learning with Delayed Impact of Actions', arXiv 2002.10316, NeurIPS 2021) gives a main upper bound of Õ(KT^{2/3}) and a matching lower bound of Ω(KT^{2/3}), according to the arXiv abstract I fetched. The database's upper bound T^{K/(K+1)}log^{1/(K+1)}T comes from Lemma D.1, which looks like an intermediate step or baseline, not the paper's main result. So the gap is closed up to log factors in both K and T. Caveat: in the paper, the simplex setting comes from the delayed-impact model (the arm-pull history is a point on the simplex). I assume the database entry encodes that same model.

papers.title: Bandit Learning with Delayed Impact of Actions
papers.claim: The abstract says the algorithm achieves Õ(KT^{2/3}) regret and gives a matching Ω(KT^{2/3}) lower bound, with K the number of arms and T the horizon. Authors: Wei Tang, Chien-Ju Ho, Yang Liu (NeurIPS 2021; first on arXiv in 2020).

triage.summary:
The gap looks closed, but only if this setting is the one the upper bound came from. That depends on an inference, explained below.

**Upper bound source.** The O~(T^{2/3}) upper bound is credited to "jin2026tight". The best match I found is "Tight Regret Bounds for Fixed-Price Bilateral Trade" by Chen, Jin, Lu and Zhang (arXiv 2504.04349). Its abstract does not say it is stochastic, but it covers independent values, which amounts to stochastic i.i.d. draws. It sets a price on a continuum and gets one-bit or two-bit (partial-monitoring) feedback. For globally budget-balanced fixed-price mechanisms it reports a tight Θ~(T^{2/3}) regret bound. Matching the database key to this paper is my inference; I did not confirm the 2026 venue or theorem numbers.

**Matching lower bound.** The same setting already has an Ω(T^{2/3}) lower bound, which is far stronger than the log(T) lower bound in the database:
- Chen, Jin, Lu and Zhang claim tightness, so their own lower bound applies.
- Cesa-Bianchi, Cesari, Colomboni, Fusco and Leonardi, "A Regret Analysis of Bilateral Trade" (EC'21, arXiv 2102.08754), prove Θ~(T^{2/3}) for realistic (posted-price) feedback with independent valuations that have bounded densities. The journal version is "Bilateral Trade: A Regret Minimization Perspective" (Mathematics of Operations Research, 2024).

So the worst-case rate in T is Θ~(T^{2/3}). The database's log(T) lower bound is from Weed, Perchet and Rigollet, "Online learning in repeated auctions" (COLT 2016, arXiv 1511.05720). It is an instance-dependent bound for a different problem (bidding in repeated Vickrey auctions), so it is not the tight worst-case lower bound here.

**Caveats.**
- The T^{2/3} rate needs independent values with bounded densities. Without bounded densities, or with dependent values, the regret becomes linear (journal version of Cesa-Bianchi et al.). If this setting is meant as a broad catch-all "bounded" partial-monitoring class with no density assumption, no single upper bound covers it. In that case the database is combining incompatible sub-settings.
- Partial-monitoring theory in general (Bartók et al. 2014) gives Ω(T^{2/3}) for globally observable games. Di Gennaro, Eldowa and Cesa-Bianchi (arXiv 2510.19158) extend T^{2/3} rates, tight in some instances, to linear partial monitoring.
- I read abstracts and search snippets only, not the full theorem statements.

papers.title: Tight Regret Bounds for Fixed-Price Bilateral Trade
papers.claim: Independent values with one-bit or two-bit feedback: tight Θ~(T^{2/3}) regret for Global Budget Balance fixed-price mechanisms (upper and lower). Correlated or adversarial values: Ω(T^{3/4}).

papers.title: A Regret Analysis of Bilateral Trade
papers.claim: Realistic (posted-price) feedback with independent valuations that have bounded densities: Θ~(T^{2/3}) regret. Without bounded densities: linear regret. Full feedback: Θ(√T).

papers.title: Online learning in repeated auctions
papers.claim: Repeated Vickrey auctions where the value is observed only after winning: logarithmic regret against well-behaved (stochastic) adversaries, plus minimax lower bounds. This is the source of the database's log T lower bound.

papers.title: Partial Monitoring—Classification, Regret Bounds, and Algorithms
papers.claim: Finite partial-monitoring games have minimax regret of order 0, √T, T^{2/3}, or T. Globally observable games give Θ(T^{2/3}).

papers.claim: Linear partial monitoring: T^{1/2} regret in locally observable games and T^{2/3} in globally observable games, tight in some instances.

triage.summary: Effectively closed, with caveats: a very recent, unreviewed preprint (Zhang, arXiv:2610.26116, 19 Oct 2026, Theorem 4.1) settles the minimax dynamic regret for K-armed non-stationary bandits with known variance budget Q and variation budget B, up to one log(KT) factor: Θ̃(min{T, K + √(KQ) + (KQBT)^{1/3} + √(KT)·min{B, √B}}). The cubic term's K dependence is K^{1/3}, better than the K^{2/3} in Wei-Hong-Lu Theorem 3.1, and the matching lower bound makes it tight. Your database's lower bound has no K dependence. Caveat: the paper's Q = Σ_t max_a σ²_{t,a} and its B leaves out the initial vector, while Wei-Hong-Lu use a full-vector variance and a variation that includes the initial vector. The paper itself warns that this distinction matters when comparing dependence on the number of arms. Since Λ ≥ Q, the new upper bound improves Wei-Hong-Lu under their Λ. Whether the lower bound still carries a K factor under the full-vector Λ depends on how the hard instances spread variance over arms, which I did not verify (I read only part of the full text). arXiv:2403.10732 (2024) had earlier said the K, V, B dependence gap against the Wei-Hong-Lu lower bound remained.

papers.title: Variance-Aware Non-Stationary Bandits: All-Budget Regret Bounds and Adaptation Costs
papers.claim: Theorem 4.1: with Q bounding Σ_t max_a σ²_{t,a} and B bounding Σ_{t≥2}‖μ_t−μ_{t−1}‖_∞, both given to the learner, the minimax dynamic regret is min{T, A + √(AQ) + (AQBT)^{1/3} + √(AT)·min{B, √B}} up to one log factor, with matching lower bounds. It contrasts its A·Q cubic term with the A²·(full-vector variance) term of Wei-Hong-Lu Theorem 3.1.

papers.title: Tracking the Best Expert in Non-stationary Stochastic Environments

papers.title: Variance-Dependent Regret Bounds for Non-stationary Linear Bandits
