triage.summary:
I found no published result that closes this gap, and no source that says it is open. The verdict is therefore "blank".

The source of both bounds is Wei, Hong and Lu, "Tracking the Best Expert in Non-stationary Stochastic Environments" (NeurIPS 2016, arXiv 1712.00578). Its abstract says it gives "matching lower bounds" for the full-information case. It also says that when V and Λ are constant, regret still grows like T^{1/3}. That agrees with your database: the bounds match in T, and the only gap is a log K factor in front of the (Λ·T·V)^{1/3} term.

I could not check whether the lower-bound theorem has a log K term, or whether the paper treats that gap as open. The arXiv PDF came back as compressed binary that I couldn't read, and the abstract page gives no theorem statements.

Two related papers turned up in search, but neither settles this:
- Gokcesu et al., arXiv 2208.03708, "Optimal Tracking in Prediction with Expert Advice", claims minimax-optimal dynamic regret with experts. Its setting is adversarial losses, not this stochastic setting with a variance measure Λ.
- arXiv 2102.07666, "A closer look at temporal variability in dynamic online learning", also concerns experts but does not address this setting.

I saw no paper that proves a Ω((Λ·T·V·log K)^{1/3}) lower bound. I also saw none that removes the log K factor from the upper bound.

papers.title: Tracking the Best Expert in Non-stationary Stochastic Environments
papers.claim: Studies dynamic regret for experts and bandits with a variance measure Λ, drift V and number of changes Γ. Gives upper bounds and claims matching lower bounds. In the full-information case with V and Λ constant, regret still grows as T^{1/3}. The K-dependence of the lower bound was not visible in what I could read.

papers.title: Optimal Tracking in Prediction with Expert Advice
papers.claim: Claims minimax-optimal dynamic regret for prediction with expert advice under adversarial, possibly unbounded losses. Not specific to the stochastic, variance-dependent (Λ) setting.

triage.summary: This is not a real gap: the two bounds come from different feedback models. The upper bound, about sqrt(T log T), is Theorem 4 of Cesa-Bianchi et al. (STOC 2024), which covers i.i.d. first-price auctions with transparent feedback. The lower bound, Omega(T^{2/3}), comes from Xu & Wang (2022) for pricing with buy/no-buy feedback and unknown noise (and also matches Theorem 3 of Cesa-Bianchi et al. for semi-transparent feedback). The two can't apply to the same problem, since the upper bound grows more slowly than the lower bound. Each model is already tight up to log factors. With transparent feedback the rate is about sqrt(T): Theorem 4 gives the upper bound and Theorem 5 an Omega(sqrt T) lower bound that holds even with full feedback. With semi-transparent feedback the rate is about T^{2/3} (Theorems 2 and 3). The apparent gap comes from the setting key leaving partial-monitoring observability "unspecified", which mixes bounds from different feedback models into one cell. The rates above were read from the summary table in the arXiv HTML version (first part of the page only). A later Xu–Wang paper, 'Optimal Contextual Pricing under Agnostic Non-Lipschitz Demand' (NeurIPS 2026 poster), was seen only as a search-result summary claiming Õ(T^{2/3}) regret matching Kleinberg–Leighton. Whether it covers exactly the 2022 linear-noisy-valuation model was not checked, so it is not counted here as closing that problem.

papers.title: The Role of Transparency in Repeated First-Price Auctions with Unknown Valuations
papers.claim: Characterizes minimax regret, up to log factors, by transparency level. With transparent feedback in i.i.d. environments, Theorem 4 gives O(sqrt(T ln T)) and Theorem 5 gives a matching Omega(sqrt T) lower bound. With semi-transparent feedback, Theorems 2 and 3 give Θ̃(T^{2/3}). With bandit feedback, Theorem 1 gives Omega(T) in general, and the rate is Θ̃(T^{2/3}) in smooth environments.

papers.title: Towards Agnostic Feature-based Dynamic Pricing: Linear Policies vs Linear Valuation with Unknown Noise
papers.claim: Proves an Omega(T^{2/3}) lower bound and an O(T^{3/4}) upper bound for pricing with linear valuations and unknown noise. Also gives a minimax rate of about d^{1/3}T^{2/3} for the linear-policy problem. This is a different feedback model from the transparent auction setting behind the sqrt(T) upper bound.

triage.summary: Closed. The minimax worst-case regret is Θ(√(mdT)). Audibert, Bubeck & Lugosi (arXiv 1204.4710, MOR 2014) prove two semi-bandit bounds for arbitrary action sets 𝒜⊂{0,1}^d with ‖a‖₁=m. Theorem 3 (OSMD with negative entropy) gives √(2mdn log(d/m)); this is the bound the database currently holds. Theorem 4 (OSMD with the INF-type potential ψ(x)=(−x)^(−q)) gives q√(2/(q−1)·mdn), which is 2√(2mdn) at q=2 and has no log factor. Table 1 of that paper lists the semi-bandit minimax rate as √(mdn). The bound is for adversarial losses, so it also covers stochastic i.i.d. losses in [0,1]. It matches the Kveton et al. lower bound min(Tm,√(mdT))/20 up to constants; actions with ‖a‖₁≤m can be handled by padding with dummy coordinates (my own argument, not stated in the paper). Zimmert, Luo & Wei (ICML 2019) also give a log-free √(mdT) adversarial bound with a hybrid regulariser. That attribution comes from later papers; I could not read the 1901.08779 PDF, and its abstract only says O(√T).

papers.title: Regret in Online Combinatorial Optimization
papers.claim: Theorem 4: OSMD with potential ψ(x)=(−x)^(−q) gives semi-bandit regret ≤ q√(2/(q−1)·mdn), i.e. 2√(2mdn) at q=2, for arbitrary action sets with ‖a‖₁=m (adversarial, so it also covers stochastic). Matches the Ω(√(mdn)) lower bound; Theorem 3 is the negentropy bound √(2mdn log(d/m)).

papers.title: Beating Stochastic and Adversarial Semi-bandits Optimally and Simultaneously
papers.claim: FTRL with a hybrid regulariser gets O(log T) stochastic and O(√T) adversarial regret; later papers report its adversarial bound as O(√(mdT)) (O(√(kmT)) for k≤m/2 in the cardinality-constrained setting). Not read directly.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Regret for Efficient Stochastic Combinatorial Semi-Bandits
papers.claim: CMOSS gets O(log k·√(kmT)) for cardinality-constrained semi-bandits; describes Zimmert et al. 2019 as achieving O(√(kmT)) for k≤m/2 and Kveton et al. as giving the Ω(√(kmT)) lower bound.

triage.summary: The gap is closed up to log factors. Luo, Tong, Zhang & Zhang (ALT 2023, arXiv:2210.01376) explicitly allow an adaptive adversary that picks the loss l_t and graph G_t based on the learner's past actions, with G_t revealed only after the action for strongly observable graphs (the 'uninformed setting'). Their Theorem 3 gives, with probability at least 1-6δ, Reg ≤ Õ(√(Σ_t α_t log(1/δ)) + max_t α_t log(1/δ)). The tuning uses knowledge of α_t; the paper says a doubling trick removes this. For a fixed graph this is Õ(√(αT)+α), matching the existing Ω(√(αT)) lower bounds (Mannor-Shamir 2011, Alon et al. 2015). The K-exponent gap (upper 0.5 vs lower 0) is an artifact of writing the uppers in K and the lowers in α. Worst case over graphs, the K-armed bandit (α=K) is a strongly observable instance, so the lower bound is Ω(√(KT)), matching the √(KT) uppers. I could not read the full PDFs of Kocák et al. 2014 or Neu 2015; per Luo et al., Neu 2015's bound had poly(K) dependence and needed self-loops on every node.

papers.title: Improved High-Probability Regret for Adversarial Bandits with Time-Varying Feedback Graphs
papers.claim: Adaptive adversary choosing l_t and G_t based on past actions; strongly observable G_t revealed after the action (uninformed setting). Theorem 3: with probability ≥1-6δ, Reg ≤ Õ(√(Σ_t α_t log(1/δ)) + max_t α_t log(1/δ)), removing the poly(K) dependence of prior work.

papers.title: Efficient learning by implicit exploration in bandit problems with side observations
papers.claim: Exp3-IX reaches near-optimal regret without needing to know the observation system before choosing an action (Kocák, Neu, Valko, Munos; NIPS 2014).

papers.title: Explore no more: Improved high-probability regret bounds for non-stochastic bandits
papers.claim: High-probability regret bounds via implicit exploration (IX), including side observations (graph feedback); per Luo et al., this bound had poly(K) dependence and needed self-loops on every node.

triage.summary:
The gap exists only because the database's best upper bounds are plain bandit bounds (Tsallis-INF, about sqrt(KT)), which ignore the feedback graph. The literature already has upper bounds that scale with the independence number alpha. That matches the existing Omega(sqrt(alpha T)) lower bound up to log factors, so the K-dependence gap is closed.

- **Kocák, Neu, Valko & Munos (NeurIPS 2014), Exp3-IX:** handles an adversarially chosen sequence of directed observation systems and does not need to see the graph before acting. Its regret is near-optimal, about sqrt(alpha T) up to logs.
- **Alon et al. (SIAM J. Comput. 2017, arXiv 1409.8428):** Exp3-DOM / Exp3-SET bound regret in terms of graph properties (independence number or dominating set) for time-varying graphs.
- **Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari & Cesa-Bianchi (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2305.15383):** proves an upper bound of O(sqrt(alpha T (1 + ln(K/alpha)))) for strongly observable undirected graphs using q-Tsallis FTRL. It extends to time-varying graphs without needing to know their independence numbers in advance. They also prove a lower bound of Omega(sqrt(alpha T ln K / ln alpha)) for alpha > 1, which pins the minimax rate down to log factors.

So the polynomial K-gap (upper exponent 0.5 vs. lower 0) disappears once the upper bound is stated in terms of alpha ≤ K: both sides are sqrt(alpha T) up to logs. Only a small log-factor gap remains, in the regime 1 < alpha < K.

Caveats:
- I did not check whether these upper bounds are stated for adaptive adversaries or only for oblivious ones / pseudo-regret.
- The Eldowa et al. result is for undirected graphs. For directed strongly observable graphs, the bounds carry extra log factors.
- For Kocák et al. and Alon et al., the regret rates above come from abstracts and search summaries. I did not open either paper or check exact theorem statements.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Online Learning with Feedback Graphs
papers.claim: Upper bound O(sqrt(alpha T (1+ln(K/alpha)))) for strongly observable undirected feedback graphs via q-Tsallis FTRL, extending to time-varying graphs without prior knowledge of their independence numbers; lower bound Omega(sqrt(alpha T ln K / ln alpha)) for alpha>1.

papers.title: Efficient learning by implicit exploration in bandit problems with side observations
papers.claim: Exp3-IX has near-optimal (about sqrt(alpha T), up to logs) regret for adversarially chosen directed observation systems, without needing to know the observation system before acting.

papers.title: Nonstochastic Multi-Armed Bandits with Graph-Structured Feedback
papers.claim: Exp3-DOM (graph revealed before acting) and Exp3-SET (revealed after) have regret bounded by graph properties such as independence or dominating-set number, for time-varying feedback graphs.

triage.summary: Worst case over arbitrary strongly observable graphs (all self-loops) and the minimax rate is Θ(√(KT)), so the gap is closed. Upper bound: every arm has a self-loop, so a plain bandit algorithm works; Tsallis-INF gets 4√(KT)+1 (already in the database). Lower bound: the adversary can pick the self-loop-only graph, which has α = K and is the ordinary K-armed bandit, so Ω(√(αT)) from Alon et al. becomes Ω(√(KT)). This is also the classical Auer et al. 2002 bound; I found that paper's matching-lower-bound claim, but no snippet showed the exact √(KT) statement (a Bubeck MLSS 2016 slide credits it with √(Tn)). The K 'poly gap' only appears because the lower bound is written in α and the upper bounds in K; the K exponent should be tight at 0.5. Graph-dependent bounds are still not fully tight: Eldowa et al. (NeurIPS 2023) prove an upper bound of O(√(αT(1+ln(K/α)))) and a lower bound of Ω(√(αT ln K/ln α)), which match at α = 1 and α = K but differ in the log factor in between.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Online Learning with Feedback Graphs
papers.claim: Upper bound O(sqrt(alpha T (1+ln(K/alpha)))) via q-Tsallis FTRL; lower bound Omega(sqrt(alpha T ln K / ln alpha)) for alpha>1; matches the bandit (alpha=K) and experts (alpha=1) cases.

papers.title: The Nonstochastic Multiarmed Bandit Problem
papers.claim: Abstract states that a matching lower bound shows the O(T^(-1/2)) per-round rate is best possible. The Omega(sqrt(KT)) worst-case form is credited to this work by a Bubeck MLSS 2016 slide but was not shown verbatim in snippets. Applies here because an all-self-loop graph sequence is exactly the bandit problem.

triage.summary: The gap is mostly a mismatch of parameters: the database's upper bounds are graph-agnostic √(KT) bandit bounds, while its lower bounds are √(αT), with α the graph's independence number. For strongly observable graphs, Alon et al. (COLT 2015) show minimax regret Θ̃(√(αT)), with an upper bound of about √(αT ln K). The database only has this paper's lower-bound theorem. Eldowa et al. (NeurIPS 2023) tighten this to an O(√(αT(1+ln(K/α)))) upper bound and an Ω(√(αT ln K / ln α)) lower bound for α>1. This matches √(KT) for bandits (α=K) and √(T ln K) for experts (α=1), and leaves only a ln α factor for intermediate α. If the worst case is taken over all graphs with K arms, α can equal K, so √(KT) is tight there as well. Up to log factors, the dependence on K and α is settled; only the exact log factor for intermediate α remains open.

papers.title: Online Learning with Feedback Graphs: Beyond Bandits
papers.claim: For strongly observable feedback graphs, minimax regret is Theta_tilde(sqrt(alpha T)): upper bound O(sqrt(alpha T ln K)) (up to logs) matching the Omega(sqrt(alpha T)) lower bound.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Online Learning with Feedback Graphs
papers.claim: Upper bound O(sqrt(alpha T (1+ln(K/alpha)))) via q-Tsallis FTRL for strongly observable graphs, plus lower bound Omega(sqrt(alpha T ln K / ln alpha)) for alpha>1; tight for bandits and experts, within a ln(alpha) factor in between.

triage.summary: Up to log factors, the gap is already closed. It shows up only because the database's upper bounds are stated in terms of K (Tsallis-INF / Masoudian et al., which are plain bandit bounds), while its lower bounds are stated in terms of the independence number α. For strongly observable feedback graphs, published upper bounds scale as √(αT) up to logs. Alon, Cesa-Bianchi, Dekel & Koren (2015, which the database already cites for its lower bound) and Alon et al.'s SIAM J. Comput. 2017 paper give Õ(√(αT)), and per my recollection also Õ(√(Σ_t α_t)) for time-varying graphs; I did not check this against the text this session. Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari & Cesa-Bianchi (NeurIPS 2023) give O(√(αT(1+ln(K/α)))). The search snippet says their result extends to time-varying graphs without knowing the independence numbers in advance, which covers this database key (oblivious sequence of graphs, known in advance). The same paper proves a lower bound of Ω(√(αT ln K / ln α)) for every α > 1. This matches the upper bound for the T-dependence and for α-polynomial dependence, so in that sense the minimax rate is Θ̃(√(αT)). Only a sub-logarithmic factor of order ln(K/α) versus ln K/ln α in general remains. So in terms of α, the polynomial gap the database reports for K is not real: the regret depends polynomially on α rather than K, and K enters only through a log factor. I saw the claims from Eldowa et al. in a search-result abstract summary. I did not open the full theorem statements.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Online Learning with Feedback Graphs (Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari, Cesa-Bianchi), NeurIPS 2023
papers.claim: Upper bound O(sqrt(alpha T (1+ln(K/alpha)))) for strongly observable feedback graphs via q-Tsallis FTRL; the snippet says it extends to time-varying graphs without prior knowledge of their independence numbers. Lower bound Omega(sqrt(alpha T ln K / ln alpha)) for alpha > 1.

papers.title: Nonstochastic Multi-Armed Bandits with Graph-Structured Feedback (Alon, Cesa-Bianchi, Gentile, Mannor, Mansour, Shamir), SIAM J. Comput. 2017
papers.claim: The abstract says it gives tight regret bounds that depend on combinatorial properties (the independence number) of the feedback graph. Per my recollection, not confirmed in a snippet this session, this includes Õ(sqrt(alpha T)) for time-varying graphs.

triage.summary: I found no published result that closes the sqrt(log K) gap for oblivious adversaries, and the literature treats the gap as known. Upper bounds: Exp3.P and Exp3-IX give O(sqrt(KT log(K/δ))). Lower bound: Gerchinovitz & Lattimore (2016) give Ω(sqrt(KT log(1/δ))), which holds even for a loss sequence fixed in advance, i.e. an oblivious adversary. A recent preprint by Bacchiocchi, Cesari & Colomboni (arXiv 2608.12231, Aug 2026) proves a matching Θ(sqrt(KT log(K/δ))) bound at m=1. Its lower bound uses a deterministic adaptive non-anticipating adversary, and the paper says it closes the gap only in that model. It does not address oblivious adversaries in the portion I could read; the end of the appendix was cut off. The preprint has not been peer reviewed and I did not check its proofs. I could not parse the Gerchinovitz–Lattimore PDF itself, so the claim that they leave the gap open comes from a search snippet and the NeurIPS 2016 review. In the setting in question (oblivious adversary, K arms, high-probability regret), the sqrt(log K) gap therefore still appears open.

The authors say this closes the Gerchinovitz–Lattimore sqrt(log K) gap only when the adversary is adaptive; oblivious adversaries are not addressed in the portion read (the appendix was truncated).

papers.title: Refined Lower Bounds for Adversarial Bandits
papers.claim: Lower bound of Ω(sqrt(KT log(1/δ))) on high-probability regret, even for loss sequences fixed in advance; this leaves a sqrt(log K) gap to the δ-tuned upper bounds. The open-gap reading comes from a search snippet and the NeurIPS review, because the PDF could not be parsed.

papers.title: Explore no more: Improved high-probability regret bounds for non-stochastic bandits
papers.claim: Exp3-IX has high-probability regret O(sqrt(KT log K) + sqrt(KT/log K) log(1/δ)).

triage.summary:
The polynomial gap in d is closed, but only up to a √log T factor. The database's lower bounds of order √(dT) come from multi-armed-bandit results (Auer et al. 2002 and the 2012 Bubeck survey) and are not tight for linear bandits on convex bodies.

**Lower bound.** Shamir, "On the Complexity of Bandit Linear Optimization" (arXiv:1408.2368), proves an Ω(d√T) lower bound on the hypercube for T ≥ d⁴/4. The hypercube is itself a convex body. I saw this claim, quoted from the full text, in a search-result summary. The abstract I fetched only says that "the price of bandit information … can be as large as d". Shamir also notes that this matches an O(d√T) upper bound that plays only the corners of the hypercube. Dani, Hayes and Kakade (COLT 2008) had earlier given lower bounds of order d√T for stochastic linear bandits, and a stochastic lower bound also applies against an oblivious adversary. One caveat: I did not check that Shamir's loss class is exactly the polar of the action set with ±1-bounded noise.

**Upper bound.** For general convex bodies the best upper bound is O(d√(T log T)). That is Hazan & Karnin's volumetric spanners (the database's source), and Zimmert & Lattimore (COLT 2022) get the same rate against adaptive adversaries.

**What remains.** So the worst-case rate over convex bodies is d√T up to a √log T factor. In the database's terms: the d exponent is settled at 1, and the T dependence is pinned up to √log T.

**Is the √log T gap open?** I found no source that removes it for general convex bodies, and none that states explicitly that it is open. Banerjee & Gopalan (arXiv:2301.03597) say that characterizing minimax regret across action spaces had been open, and they give an "optimal" lower bound for a wide class of convex action sets. I only saw their abstract, so I could not check their exact rate, whether it is stochastic or adversarial, or what they say about log factors.

triage.summary:
The T-dependence gap is mostly an artifact of how the database states its upper bounds. Its entries are high-probability bounds with delta=1/T, which brings in log(NT). Bounds on expected regret avoid this. Kale (2014) gives O(sqrt(KT log(N/K))), which Chase, Ito & Mehalel cite as the matching upper bound. That bound is proved for non-stochastic expert advice, so it should also hold when contexts are i.i.d., which is a special case.

The K-dependence gap is the real one. The lower bound is sqrt(KT log N / log K), from Agarwal et al. 2012 and Seldin & Lugosi. The upper bound is sqrt(KT log(N/K)). Recent work closed this gap, but only outside the stochastic-context setting:
- Cesa-Bianchi, Eldowa, Esposito & Olkhovskaya (arXiv 2406.16802) prove Omega(sqrt(KT ln(N/K))), but only under a restricted feedback model.
- Ito (NeurIPS 2024) proves the same lower bound for a different protocol, where the player commits to an expert before seeing the advice.
- Chase, Ito & Mehalel (arXiv 2511.00257, COLT 2026) settle the minimax rate for the standard non-stochastic problem at Theta(sqrt(TK log(N/K))). Their hard instance uses an adaptive adversary: advice for a batch of arms is redrawn only after the learner pulls an arm from that batch, so advice is not i.i.d. across rounds. The authors only conjecture that the bound also holds against an oblivious adversary.

None of these lower bounds covers stochastic i.i.d. contexts with i.i.d. rewards, which is the setting asked about. I found no paper that removes the 1/log K factor there. The authors' stated conjecture marks the oblivious case, and by extension the stochastic case, as open.

One caveat: the Ito NeurIPS 2024 PDF did not render, so I could not check its hard instance directly. What I report about it comes from the abstract and search snippets.

triage.summary:
I think the gap is closed at Θ̃(T^{2/3}), but this rests on reading the database's setting as fixed-price bilateral trade (selling at a posted price, where only part of the outcome is observed). The setting key is vague, so that reading is my inference.

**Where the two bounds come from.** The upper bound in your database comes from jin2026tight. That is Yaonan Jin, "Tight Regret Bounds for Bilateral Trade under Semi Feedback" (arXiv:2601.16412, 2026). It gives an Õ(T^{2/3}) mechanism for budget-balanced fixed-price bilateral trade under semi feedback. Its abstract states this for *adversarial* values. Your stochastic i.i.d. cell probably inherited the bound because an adversarial upper bound also holds for i.i.d. values. The log(T) lower bound comes from Weed et al. 2015 on repeated auctions, which is a different problem. Its log T rate is a per-instance (margin-type) bound, so it is far from the true worst-case rate here.

**Lower bounds that close the gap.** Both papers below have stochastic, partial-feedback, continuum-of-prices lower bounds of order T^{2/3}:
- Cesa-Bianchi, Cesari, Colomboni, Fusco, Leonardi, "A Regret Analysis of Bilateral Trade" (arXiv:2102.08754). With realistic (posted-price) feedback and independent i.i.d. valuations with bounded densities, it reports Θ̃(T^{2/3}). The table of contents lists a section on the T^{2/3} lower bound under realistic feedback.
- Chen, Jin, Lu, Zhang, "Tight Regret Bounds for Fixed-Price Bilateral Trade" (arXiv:2504.04349, ICALP 2026). With independent values it reports a tight Θ̃(T^{2/3}) bound for budget-balanced mechanisms under one-bit and two-bit feedback. Jin 2026 cites this paper as the source of its matching Ω(T^{2/3}) lower bound.

Both lower bounds come from a subclass of i.i.d. problems, so they also apply to the broader stochastic class. That gives a worst-case lower bound of Ω(T^{2/3}), which matches the inherited Õ(T^{2/3}) upper bound up to log factors.

**Caveats.**
- I have not checked that Jin's semi-feedback model and the feedback model in the lower-bound papers are exactly the same. CJLZ25's one-/two-bit feedback is probably the same or a closely related model.
- If the setting is read as completely general stochastic partial monitoring over a continuum with only bounded rewards, the bounds no longer match. Cesa-Bianchi et al. show that without bounded densities, regret under realistic feedback is Θ(T). In that reading, T^{2/3} would not be an upper bound for the whole class.

Either way, the log T lower bound in your database is not the right worst-case comparison. I read the abstracts and search summaries, not the full PDFs, so I have not checked the proofs.

Up to logarithmic factors, the gap is closed. It mostly comes from the bounds being stated in different terms. The upper bounds in the database depend on K, while the lower bound depends on the independence number α of the graph. That is why K looks poly-gapped (exponent 0.5 vs 0).

Their extension to time-varying graphs gives O(√(ᾱT)·ln(KT)), where ᾱ is the average of the per-round α_t. Since Exp3.G uses the graph only after the action is chosen, revealing it after the action is fine. This matches the Ω(√(αT)) lower bound up to log factors.
- **Adaptive adversary:** Alon et al. assume a loss sequence fixed in advance. For the adaptive case, Luo, Tong, Zhang & Zhang (ALT 2023, arXiv 2210.01376) give a high-probability bound of about Õ(√(Σ_t α_t) + max_t α_t) for time-varying strongly observable graphs, with no poly(K) dependence. High-probability bounds of this kind usually carry over to adaptive adversaries, but I did not check this paper's adversary assumptions.
- **Log factors (undirected graphs):** Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari & Cesa-Bianchi (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2305.15383) give an upper bound of O(√(αT(1+ln(K/α)))) using q-Tsallis FTRL. They also prove a lower bound of Ω(√(αT·ln K/ln α)) for α>1, which shows some log factor is needed whenever α<K. I did not confirm that this bound covers directed or time-varying graphs.

Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi (2012, arXiv 1204.5721), Theorem 3.4 in Section 3.3, gives a lower bound of (1/20)·√(nK) for any forecaster. It is built from i.i.d. Bernoulli rewards: one arm has mean 1/2 and another has mean 1/2+√(K/n), with n the horizon (T here). Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund & Schapire (SIAM J. So the lower bound carries over to the adaptive K=2 setting, for both pseudo-regret and expected regret.

One caveat: if "regret" against an adaptive adversary meant policy regret, the rates would differ (e.g. T^{2/3} with switching costs). The database's upper bounds come from the standard Exp3 regret, though, so the standard notion applies.

I couldn't extract the theorem statement from the Auer et al. PDF (the fetch returned binary content). The constant 1/20 and the theorem number come from search snippets of the Bubeck–Cesa-Bianchi survey. A 2016 paper (arXiv 1608.02732) quotes the constant as 1/24. Either way the order is √(KT).

triage.summary:
I found no published result that closes the √log K gap for oblivious adversaries, and none that explicitly calls it open.

The closest result is a 2026 arXiv preprint, Bacchiocchi, Cesari & Colomboni (arXiv:2608.12231). Setting m=1 in their m-set bandit result gives a K-armed high-probability lower bound of order √(KT(log K + log(1/δ))). This matches the Exp3.P / Exp3-IX upper bound O(√(KT log(K/δ))), and the paper says it closes the √log K gap left by Gerchinovitz & Lattimore. However, the lower bound only holds against a deterministic adaptive non-anticipating adversary. It is stated for sufficiently small δ, and the bad event has probability ≥ δ. When I read the paper, it did not discuss oblivious adversaries and did not settle that case. The only open direction it names is extending its method to matroid-base action sets.

So the oblivious gap remains. The upper bound is √(KT log(K/δ)) (Exp3.P, Exp3-IX). The lower bound is √(T(K−1) log(1/(4δ)))/27 (Gerchinovitz & Lattimore, which holds even for fixed loss sequences). I found no algorithm that reaches √(KT log(1/δ)) (or √(KT)+√(KT log(1/δ))) against an oblivious adversary. One useful implication: Exp3.P and Exp3-IX are guaranteed against adaptive adversaries too, so the new lower bound shows any improvement in the oblivious setting would have to rely on obliviousness. My searches did not surface the Lattimore–Szepesvári Chapter 12 notes or any explicit open-problem statement, so I chose "blank" rather than "open_known".

triage.summary: Upper bound O(sqrt(dT log K)): Exp2 with John's exploration; Zimmert & Lattimore 2022 also give O(sqrt(dT log(kT))). Lower bound Omega(sqrt(dT)). I found no paper that proves a matching Omega(sqrt(dT log K)) lower bound for a fixed finite action set under this exact normalization (unit-l2 actions, l2-ball losses, adversarial). I also found no paper that explicitly states this is an open problem. Shamir 2015 (Thm 6) proves Omega((d-1)sqrt(T)) for the hypercube [-1,1]^d. Search results say Dani et al. 2008 show sqrt(dn log|A|) is unimprovable on [-1,1]^d (seen only second-hand). With K = 2^d this equals sqrt(dT log K), but these use l_inf-bounded actions and |<x,l>| <= 1 losses, not l2/l2. Shamir's cylinder bound (Thm 3) also lacks unit-l2 actions. I estimate that rescaling the hypercube to unit l2 with l2-ball losses shrinks the per-arm noise by about sqrt(d), which breaks the argument. Li, Wang & Zhou 2019 prove Omega(sqrt(dT log T log n)) for n <= 2^{d/2}, but the action sets change over time (stochastic/contextual), so it doesn't cover a fixed set. The log K gap therefore looks unresolved for this normalization. Caveats: PDF fetches returned unreadable binary, and I could not read the Lattimore-Szepesvari chapter notes directly.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed: the minimax regret is Θ(√(K·M·T)). Two published results give this, though one step (the Cauchy–Schwarz combination) is my own short derivation, not a quoted theorem.

**Removing the log K from the upper bound.** The database's upper bound runs a separate Exp3 for each context. That gives √(2·K·M·T·log K), because Σ_m √(K·T_m) ≤ √(K·M·T) by Cauchy–Schwarz, where T_m is the number of rounds context m appears. Audibert & Bubeck (COLT 2009) showed that INF / Poly-INF reaches O(√(KT)) pseudo-regret without the log factor, and does not need T to be known. Running one Poly-INF per context and summing with the same Cauchy–Schwarz step gives O(√(K·M·T)) with no log K. The context set and its size M are known to the learner, so this reduction is valid.

**Lower bound.** The database's lower bound is √(KT)/20. It ignores M, so even the dependence on M is not matched. The standard construction splits the horizon into M blocks of T/M rounds, one per context, and applies the multi-armed bandit lower bound √(K·T/M) in each block. This gives Ω(√(K·M·T)). The bound is stated explicitly as Proposition 5.2 of "Bandits with Abstention under Expert Advice" (arXiv 2402.14585, 2024): Ω(√(MKT)) for a contextual bandit with M disjoint context groups. I saw that only in a search-result summary; I did not open the paper to check its exact assumptions.

So the matching rate is Θ(√(KMT)). The remaining log K gap in the database is an artifact of using Exp3 instead of INF / Tsallis-INF. The M dependence was also only loosely bounded in the database. My searches worked normally.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed up to logarithmic factors. Our database's upper bounds are √(KT)-type rates borrowed from plain bandit algorithms. Those rates ignore the graph, which is why there is a polynomial gap in K against the Ω(√(α T)) lower bound.

Alon, Cesa-Bianchi, Dekel & Koren (COLT 2015, arXiv 1502.07617) show that minimax regret is Θ̃(√(α T)) for strongly observable feedback graphs, directed ones included. The adversary may choose a sequence of graphs G_1..G_T, and the paper covers both the informed setting and the uninformed one, where G_t is revealed only after the action is played. According to the search summary, the paper says its algorithm (Exp3.G) carries over to these time-varying settings "with only a few cosmetic modifications". In that case α becomes the average of the per-round independence numbers α_t. That matches the lower bound up to log factors.

Two earlier results also apply in the uninformed setting:
- Exp3-SET (Alon et al. 2013, and the journal version arXiv 1409.8428) is near-optimal in the uninformed setting for symmetric (undirected) graphs.
- For undirected graphs, Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari & Cesa-Bianchi (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2305.15383) sharpen the upper bound to O(√(αT(1+ln(K/α)))). Their abstract says the method extends to time-varying graphs without knowing the independence numbers in advance. They also prove a lower bound of Ω(√(αT ln K / ln α)) for α > 1.

What remains open is only the exact logarithmic factor. Even that is settled for undirected graphs in fixed-graph or informed-type settings. The polynomial dependence on K versus α is resolved.

Caveat: I checked the theorem statements only through search-result summaries, not the full texts. That includes the exact uninformed, adaptive-adversary bound for directed graphs.

triage.summary: No published result found that closes the √(log K) gap for expected regret in adversarial linear bandits with a fixed set of K actions; no paper found states it is open either. Upper bound: O(√(dT log K)) from exponential weights (Exp2 / John's exploration). Best general lower bound seen: Ω(√(dT)), from embedding a d-armed bandit; a 2026 quantum linear bandits paper (arXiv 2608.14319) lists exactly these two bounds for K actions. The √(log K) factor is not needed when K=d (multi-armed bandits, Tsallis-INF gives √(dT)). It is needed when K≈2^d (hypercube lower bound d√T = √(dT log K)), assuming the action set is unrestricted. Partial result: Ito et al. (NeurIPS 2019) prove Ω(√(d k³ T)) for bandit combinatorial optimization with item losses in [0,1]. My own rescaling to action losses in [−1,1] gives Ω(√(dkT)) ≈ Ω(√(dT log K / log(d/k))) for K=C(d,k), so the gap is at most √(log(d/k)) for those action sets. Bacchiocchi–Cesari–Colomboni (arXiv 2608.12231, 2026 preprint) prove a matching Ω(√(dT log(K/δ))) lower bound for m-set bandits against adaptive adversaries. It holds only with probability at least δ (high-probability regret, small δ), and the authors say it closes the √(log K) gap only at fixed confidence, not in expectation. The exact minimax dependence on K for expected regret appears unresolved in what I found. I could not read the Lattimore–Szepesvári book (its PDF came back as compressed binary). One table cites a 'Zhou (2019)' Ω(√(dT log K)) lower bound that I could not confirm. Li et al. (2019) prove a lower bound with a log K factor, but for contextual bandits with changing action sets, so it does not apply.

The authors say this closes the √(log K) gap between confidence-tuned upper and lower bounds; it does not prove a new expected-regret lower bound.

triage.summary: This verdict comes with an important caveat about which adversary model is meant. The gap is a √log K factor: Exp3.P / Exp3-IX give an upper bound of O(√(KT log(K/δ))), and Gerchinovitz & Lattimore (2016) give a lower bound of Ω(√(KT log(1/δ))) that holds even for oblivious loss sequences. Bacchiocchi, Cesari & Colomboni, "An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial m-Set Bandits" (arXiv:2608.12231, Aug 2026), prove a new lower bound. For small enough δ, every randomized policy faces some deterministic adaptive non-anticipating adversary with losses in [0,1] under which, with probability at least δ, regret is Ω(√(KT log(K/δ))). For m=1 this is the K-armed bandit, and the authors say explicitly that this "closes the remaining √log K gap" left by Gerchinovitz–Lattimore when the adversary is adaptive and non-anticipating. They also give a matching O(√(KT log(K/δ))) upper bound. So against adaptive adversaries, with regret measured against the best fixed arm (the setting where Exp3.P's bound holds), the rate √(KT log(K/δ)) is tight up to constants. Caveats: (1) The paper's adversary depends on history through per-block selection counters that reset at block boundaries. It is not a short fixed-window bounded-memory adversary in the policy-regret sense. If this database's 'adversarial_bounded_memory' means a strictly bounded memory m that does not grow with T, or oblivious losses, the new result does not apply. The paper does not analyze oblivious adversaries, and its wording implies the Gerchinovitz–Lattimore gap is still open for fixed loss sequences. No paper I found removes log K for oblivious adversaries. (2) I checked the abstract and HTML body through WebFetch summaries only and did not see the exact theorem constants. The final part of the appendix was not read.

Also, for small δ, a deterministic adaptive non-anticipating adversary forces Ω(√(KT log(K/δ))) regret with probability at least δ. The authors say this closes the √log K gap left by Gerchinovitz–Lattimore for adaptive adversaries. The construction uses per-block selection counters, and oblivious adversaries are not analyzed.

triage.summary:
Short answer: I found no published result that closes the √log K gap for bounded-memory adversaries. The closest result settles it only for general adaptive adversaries.

**The closest result.** Bacchiocchi, Cesari and Colomboni, arXiv:2608.12231 (Aug 2026). Their Theorem 2 (with m=1) gives a high-probability regret lower bound of Ω(√(KT(log K + log(1/δ)))). It holds for small enough δ and large enough T, against "deterministic adaptive non-anticipating" adversaries with losses in [0,1]. The abstract says this shows the log K factor is unavoidable for K-armed bandits against such adversaries and "clos[es] the remaining √log K gap" left by Gerchinovitz and Lattimore. It matches the database's upper bound, Exp3.P's O(√(KT log(K/δ))), and EXP3-KW from Zimmert and Lattimore.

**Why it doesn't transfer to this setting.**
- The paper body says the adversary's round-t losses depend on how many times each arm was chosen earlier in the current block. The counts reset at block boundaries.
- So the adversary remembers a whole block, not a fixed number of past rounds. That is not bounded memory unless the block length is constant, which I could not confirm.
- The proof is only sketched in the parts I read.
- The paper does not claim a matching log K lower bound for oblivious adversaries. For those, the best lower bound I saw is still Gerchinovitz and Lattimore's √(KT log(1/δ)).
- So for bounded-memory (and oblivious) adversaries the gap stays unresolved in what I found, but no source explicitly calls it an open problem. That is why the verdict is "blank" rather than "closed" or "open_known".

**Other sources checked.**
- Gerchinovitz and Lattimore (NeurIPS 2016, arXiv:1605.07416) say there is "little room for improvement" in high-probability bounds. Their stated open problem is about second-order bounds, not this log K gap.
- Neu's Exp3-IX (arXiv:1506.03271) gives 2√(2KT log K) + (√(2KT/log K)+1)·log(2/δ), which still has the log K.
- Zimmert and Lattimore (COLT 2022) get O(√(dT log(kT))) for k actions, still with a log term.

**Tool failures.** PDF fetches of the Zimmert–Lattimore and Gerchinovitz–Lattimore papers came back as unreadable binary. I read a plain-text copy of the latter instead.

The abstract says the log K is unavoidable against such adversaries, closing the √log K gap left by Gerchinovitz–Lattimore. The adversary's losses depend on per-block counts of past arm selections, so it is not evidently bounded-memory. No oblivious-adversary log K lower bound is claimed.

triage.summary: The gap is closed up to constants by results missing from the database. Only abstracts and search snippets were checked, not full PDFs. Upper bound: Tsallis-INF (Zimmert & Seldin, JMLR 2021) gets regret O(sum_i log T/Delta_i + sqrt(C sum_i log T/Delta_i)) in a setting that includes stochastic bandits with adversarial corruption. This is linear in K, has a single log T, matches the Lai-Robbins log T/Delta rate at C=0, and is at most O(sum log T/Delta_i + C) by AM-GM. That removes the extra K and log T factors in the Lykouris et al. 2018 bound. Masoudian & Seldin (COLT 2021) refine the log factor and the C dependence. Lower bound: Ito (NeurIPS 2021) proves a bandit lower bound tight up to a log factor; a search summary gives it as Omega(N/Delta + sqrt(CN/Delta)), N = number of arms, but the exact expression was not seen. With Lai-Robbins this shows the sqrt(C...) shape is near-optimal. Caveats: (1) the KL-based Lai-Robbins bound matches log T/Delta only up to constants when arm means are bounded away from 0 and 1; (2) I believe, but did not confirm in the papers, that Zimmert-Seldin's setting allows adaptive adversaries and bounds regret against corrupted losses; (3) Ito's bandit lower bound leaves a log-factor gap in the C-dependent term only, not in the K, log T or Delta gaps listed for this setting.

triage.summary:
Up to log factors, the gap is closed by a paper missing from your database: He, Zhou, Zhang & Gu, "Nearly Optimal Algorithms for Linear Contextual Bandits with Adversarial Corruptions" (NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2205.06811). Their CW-OFUL algorithm assumes the learner knows the corruption budget C (the sum of corruption magnitudes). In that case it gets regret Õ(d√T + dC). I saw this bound in search snippets of the NeurIPS proceedings paper, where it is written as Õ(d√K + dC) with K standing for the number of rounds. That paper says the d√T term matches the uncorrupted lower bound Ω(d√T), and the dC term matches the Ω(dC) corruption lower bound, which it credits to Bogunovic et al. 2021. A 2026 paper (arXiv:2603.15596) also cites He et al. as achieving Õ(d√T + dC).

This bound is far better than the Õ(C·T^{1/4}d^{3/2} + T^{3/4}√d(C+1)) from Ding et al. in your database. Per variable:
- T: the upper exponent drops from 0.75 to 0.5 plus log factors, which matches the d√(T log T) lower bound of Li, Wang & Zhou 2019 up to logs.
- d: the upper exponent becomes 1, which matches that same d√(T log T) lower bound.
- K: the upper bound has no K dependence. The K^{1/4}√(dT) lower bound from your database's jin2026nearly entry must apply only in a limited range of K (presumably small K relative to d), or it would contradict the d√T upper bound. So it doesn't open a real polynomial gap. I didn't check this entry myself.

Caveats:
- I couldn't read the full PDF of He et al. (the fetched text was unreadable). triage.summary:
The database's upper bound is the wrong theorem for this setting, and the right one closes the T and d gap up to log factors (treating C as a constant). The C-dependence is still open.

**Why the database bound is wrong here.** The listed upper bound, Õ(d^{1/2}(C+1)T^{3/4} + d^{3/2}CT^{1/4}), comes from Remark 1 of Ding, Hsieh & Sharpnack (AISTATS 2022, arXiv 2106.02978). That remark covers their two-layer algorithm for the case where the attack budget C is unknown. Our setting says the learner knows C. For that case, Theorem 1 of the same paper (I read it in the arXiv HTML v3) gives, with high probability, R_c(T) ≤ (2β_T + γ_T(C+C′))γ_{T+1}√T + C for context attacks, where C′ ≥ C is the known upper bound. The paper summarises this as R(T) ≤ Õ(d√T) + Õ(d(C+C′)√T). Taking C′ = C, the regret is Õ(d(C+1)√T).

**Effect on the gap.**
- **T:** the exponent drops from 0.75 to 0.5. This matches the lower bound d√(T log T) from Li et al. 2019 up to logs.
- **d:** the exponent is 1, which matches the d lower bound. The database recorded upper 0.5 against lower 1, which is not a consistent pair. With the right theorem the d-dependence is linear and tight up to logs.
- **K:** the upper bound has no K-dependence, so the K^{1/4}√(dT) lower bound (jin2026) presumably comes with a condition such as K ≤ exp(d). I could not check that paper's conditions; it looks like a parametrisation issue rather than a real gap.

**What is still open: the dependence on C.** The upper bound grows like dC√T (multiplicative in C). The paper proves no lower bound in C. Its Future Work section explicitly lists as open "the optimal balance between C and T in regret lower bounds" for attacked linear contextual bandits, and an algorithm that matches it. The only lower-bound statement it cites is from Garcelon et al. 2020: an algorithm whose regret without corruption is f(T) must suffer linear regret once C = Ω(f(T)).

**Other work checked.** None of the work I found addresses context corruption, and none improves the C-dependence for it:
- Reward-corruption results: He et al. 2022, CW-OFUL, Õ(d√T + dC); Bogunovic et al. 2021; Liu et al. 2024 (arXiv 2410.07533).
- Strategic Linear Contextual Bandits (arXiv 2406.00551) only reports earlier context-corruption bounds of the form Õ(d·C̃·√T).
- A 2026 fairness paper (arXiv 2602.04125) proves a lower bound for a different corrupted-observation model.

**Verdict.** "Closed" applies to the per-variable T and d rates the database tracks, up to logs. If C is treated as a scaling variable, the C-dependence (C√T upper vs. no matching lower bound) is a known open question.

triage.summary: Closed in the worst-case-over-instances sense. Theorem 8 of Bubeck, Perchet and Rigollet (COLT 2013, arXiv:1302.1611), read from a text version of the arXiv PDF fetched through the r.jina.ai proxy, covers two arms, unit-variance Gaussians and a learner that knows only mu*. Instances: nu0 = N(0,1) x N(-1,1) and nu_Delta = N(-Delta,1) x N(0,1) for Delta in (0,1], so mu* = 0 throughout. Statement: for any policy and any n, max(R_n(nu0), sup_Delta Delta*R_n(nu_Delta)) >= (1/2) log(n/139). The paper reads this as 'regret of order log(n)/Delta is unavoidable for some Delta when only mu* is known'. My own step, not stated in the paper: since R_n(nu_Delta) <= n*Delta, the Delta attaining the sup has n*Delta^2 >~ log n, so log n ~ log(1/Delta). Hence no uniform guarantee of order C/Delta, or o(log(1/Delta))/Delta, is possible, and the log(1/Delta)/Delta upper bound (Garivier, Menard and Stoltz 2019, Theorem C.1, taken from the database; I could not read that PDF) is order-optimal in Delta. A per-instance log(1/Delta)/Delta lower bound cannot hold, because an algorithm tuned to one Delta gets order 1/Delta there, so the per-instance 1/(4 Delta) from Theorem 5 (where Delta is also known) remains correct. The K 'poly_gap' is a bookkeeping artefact since K = 2 is fixed. Several fetches failed: the raw arXiv PDFs of 1302.1611 (v1, v2) and 1602.07182 and the PMLR PDF would not extract, and sbubeck.com refused the connection. The r.jina.ai text version of 1302.1611 worked.

triage.summary:
The polynomial gap in K is closed up to log factors. The remaining gap in T is only logarithmic.

The database's upper bound is LinTS-style, of order K·sqrt(T)·polylog. It is loose because it treats d as roughly K and uses an analysis whose dependence on d is d rather than sqrt(d). For K-armed neural bandits in the NTK regime, Kassraie & Krause (AISTATS 2022, arXiv 2107.03144) analyse a Sup-style algorithm, SupNN-UCB, which adapts SupLinUCB (Chu et al. 2011) and SupKernelUCB to this setting. Their Theorem 4.2 gives R(T) = O(sqrt(T)·(sqrt(γ_T σ^-2 log^3 T · log(T log T·|A|/δ)) + σB)), where |A| = K is the number of arms and γ_T is the NTK maximum information gain. I read this statement on the arXiv HTML page. The paper says the bound holds for arbitrary sequences of contexts, and γ_T is defined as a maximum over all input sequences. The theorem also needs a sufficient-exploration assumption (λ₀ I ≼ K_T) and a network width that grows polynomially in |A|.

With d_eff ≈ γ_T, this bound is about sqrt(d_eff·T)·polylog(T)·sqrt(log K). The sqrt(KT) lower bound only applies when the effective dimension is large enough to embed K independent arms (d_eff ≳ K). In that case γ_T ≈ K log T, so the upper bound becomes sqrt(KT)·polylog(K,T), matching Ω(sqrt(KT)) up to logs. When d_eff is fixed and smaller than K, the K-dependence is only sqrt(log K), and the MAB lower bound does not apply. Either way, the per-variable K gap is not a real polynomial gap. Exact log factors in K and T are not settled.

Caveats:
- I did not find a matching sqrt(d_eff·T) lower bound for neural or NTK bandits stated directly. The lower-bound side rests on the standard MAB embedding.
- Salgia, Vakili & Zhao (arXiv 2206.00099) describe a Sup variant with an O(sqrt(Γ_k(T)·T)) bound. I only saw that in a search-result snippet, not on a page I fetched.
- Kim et al. (arXiv 2312.07145, ICLR 2024 version) argue that the standard NeuralUCB/NeuralTS d̃·sqrt(T) analyses can be Ω(T) in the worst case. This affects how the database's other inherited bounds should be read, not the Sup-type result.

Requires a sufficient-exploration assumption and width growing polynomially in |A|.

triage.summary:
For K-armed stochastic bandits with a fixed, known, strongly observable feedback graph, the literature already pins down the instance-dependent rate. It is c*(θ, G)·log T, where c* is the value of a linear program built from the graph and the instance (roughly, a minimum-cost exploration budget over the arms). Neither of your database's bounds reflects this. The upper bounds come from plain bandit algorithms that ignore the graph (UCB1, KL-UCB). The lower bound is just Ω(log T). So the polynomial gaps you see in Δ and K are an artefact of the incomplete database, not an open problem.

- **Lower bound.** Buccapatnam, Eryilmaz and Shroff proved an asymptotic Lai–Robbins-style lower bound that depends on the network structure. Their UCB-type and randomized policies match it up to a factor that does not depend on the network.
- **Matching upper bounds.** Wu, György and Szepesvári (NeurIPS 2015) proved problem-dependent lower bounds that do not need T → ∞. Their algorithms match those bounds up to a universal constant. A slide deck (ICML 2022) says their result is exactly asymptotically optimal in the {σ, ∞} case, which is the graph-feedback case. Marinov, Mohri and Zimmert (NeurIPS 2022) give an algorithm that is quasi-optimal both in finite time and asymptotically. They also show that no algorithm can reach the asymptotic constant c* in finite time on some instances.
- **Still open (refinements, not the main gap).** Marinov et al. leave open which graphs allow the finite-time rate to match the asymptotic rate up to constants. They also leave open graphs that change over time and the case where the learner does not know the graph.

Caveat: these results are stated for Gaussian or sub-Gaussian-type rewards. I did not check whether anyone has proved an exactly matching asymptotic constant for general [0,1] rewards (a KL- or Kinf-based constant). The order c*(G, Δ)·log T is settled up to constant factors.

For a fixed, known feedback graph, gives an algorithm that is quasi-optimal both in finite time and asymptotically relative to the LP-based constant c*. Shows that no algorithm can reach c* in finite time on some instances, and gives a family of graphs where it can be reached.

Proves problem-dependent lower bounds that do not need T → ∞, and gives algorithms matching them up to a universal constant (and the minimax bounds up to log factors). A later slide deck says the result is asymptotically optimal in the {σ, ∞} (graph-feedback) case.

triage.summary:
Verdict: closed, with one caveat below.

**Why it is closed.** The database's best lower bound is a bare Ω(log T) with no dependence on the gaps Δ or on K. That is too weak, and it is the only reason a gap shows up. The setting allows any strongly observable graph sequence. That includes a fixed graph, and it includes the graph with only self-loops, which is the ordinary bandit. So the classical Lai–Robbins bound applies, at least in the worst case over the class: Ω(Σ_i log T/Δ_i) in the Gaussian/Bernoulli kl form. This matches UCB1 / KL-UCB in both Δ and K up to constants.

**Fixed graphs.** Here the asymptotic instance-dependent rate is fully characterised by the optimal value of a graph-dependent linear program (LP):
- Buccapatnam, Eryilmaz & Shroff (arXiv 1704.07943) derive this LP lower bound for uniformly good policies. Their UCB-type and randomized policies match it up to a constant factor.
- Wu, György & Szepesvári (NeurIPS 2015, arXiv 1510.08108) give non-asymptotic problem-dependent lower bounds that recover the asymptotic ones, plus algorithms that match them up to a universal constant.
- Marinov, Mohri & Zimmert (NeurIPS 2022, arXiv 2206.10022) show that "optimal finite-time regret" is not uniquely defined for feedback graphs. For their notion, they give an algorithm that is quasi-optimal both in finite time and asymptotically.

Together, the Δ and K exponents (upper 1 vs. lower 0) are pinned down: the right order is a graph-dependent sum of terms log T/Δ_i, between the independence-number and domination-number scales. The database simply lacks these lower bounds.

**Caveat.** I found no paper that exactly characterises the instance-dependent rate for arbitrary time-varying oblivious graph sequences known in advance. Lykouris, Tardos & Wali (ALT 2020, arXiv 1905.09898) give graph-and-gap-dependent UCB/Thompson-sampling upper bounds. Their abstract does not say whether time-varying graphs are covered, and I did not read the full paper. Mehta (arXiv 2305.04093) sharpens the UCB-N/TS-N analysis for undirected graphs. Read per instance, the exact constant for time-varying sequences may still be open. The polynomial gap in Δ and K as recorded, however, is closed by the known lower bounds.

triage.summary: The log gap is closed by Zimmert, Luo & Wei (ICML 2019, arXiv:1901.08779). Their Theorem 1 holds for any action set X ⊆ {0,1}^d with losses in [-1,1]^d, so it covers i.i.d. Bernoulli rewards. It gives adversarial pseudo-regret O(C_adv·√T), and with γ=1 the paper states C_adv = O(√(md)) with m = max‖x‖₁. I also checked this from the definitions: by Cauchy–Schwarz the sum of √x_i over coordinates outside the best action is at most √(dm), and the other term is O(m). This gives O(√(mdT)) with no √log(d/m) factor. It matches the Ω(√(mdT)) lower bounds of Kveton et al. 2014 (Prop. 2) and Audibert–Bubeck–Lugosi 2014. The 2025 FTPL paper (arXiv:2506.12490) also says O(√(mdT)) is achieved by OSMD and Zimmert et al.'s FTRL, matching the lower bound. Caveat: the theorem formula came from a garbled HTML rendering, and the paper does not spell out 'general sets, no log' verbatim; the O(√(md)) bound on C_adv is the paper's statement plus my own check.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed, up to constant factors, by a known adversarial semi-bandit result. The worst-case minimax regret is Θ(√(dmT)), where d is the number of base arms (ground items) and m is the maximum action size.

**Upper bound.** "Regret in Online Combinatorial Optimization" (Audibert, Bubeck, Lugosi, Math. of OR 2014, arXiv 1204.4710), Theorem 4, gives R_n ≤ 2√(2mdn). This uses OSMD/INF with the potential ψ(x) = (−x)^(−2) against an adversary choosing losses z_t ∈ [0,1]^d. The paper does not discuss stochastic losses. Still, i.i.d. losses are a special case of an oblivious adversary, and since that adversary can be any i.i.d. distribution, the bound covers our stochastic setting. The paper describes this bound as optimal for semi-bandits, and its Table 1 lists a matching √(mdn) lower bound.

**Lower bound.** The stochastic lower bound Ω(√(dmT)) comes from Kveton et al. 2015 (arXiv 1410.0949), the result already in your database.

**Why the database shows a d-gap.** The database's upper bound d√T only matches √(dmT) when m = d. Using 2√(2mdT) instead makes the d-exponent 1/2 in both bounds when m is held fixed, which closes the gap.

**Other upper bound.** In the stochastic-specific literature, CombUCB1 (Kveton et al. 2015) gets O(√(dmT log T)), which matches up to a √log T factor.

This holds adversarially and so also stochastically. For the stochastic setting specifically, Kveton et al. (AISTATS 2015) give O(sqrt(KLn log n)) gap-free regret. Both match the stored lower bound Omega(sqrt(mdT)) (Kveton et al. 2014, Prop. 2), so for T >= d/m the minimax regret is Theta(sqrt(mdT)): tight in T and sqrt(d) in d, with no log factor in the OSMD bound.

triage.summary: The paper your database already uses for the lower bound also closes the gap, up to iterated-logarithm (log log T) factors. That paper is Li, Wang and Zhou, COLT 2019 (arXiv:1904.00242). Its abstract, which I fetched, covers linear contextual bandits with finite action sets. With n ≤ 2^{d/2} actions per round, it proves a minimax lower bound of Ω(√(dT log T log n)). That is about d√(T log T) when log n is of order d, which is where your database's d√(T log T) lower bound comes from. The same paper also gives a Variable-Confidence-Level SupLinUCB algorithm whose regret "matches the lower bound up to iterated logarithmic factors". The abstract does not write the formula out. The SUFE talk abstract states the infinite-action version as O(√(d²T log T))·poly(log log T), and the finite-action bound should be O(√(dT log T log n))·poly(log log T); I inferred the finite-action form from the matching claim. The authors say this saves two √(log T) factors compared with earlier SupLinUCB analyses. Your database's upper bound comes from Agrawal & Goyal's Thompson sampling analysis and carries an extra √(log T) factor (or more), so it is outdated. SupLinUCB works with adversarially chosen, time-varying finite action sets of unit-norm vectors, which matches this setting. The abstract does not say outright that contexts are adversarial; I am relying on how SupLinUCB is set up. Caveat: the gap is closed only up to poly(log log T) factors, not exactly. Also, the lower bound needs K large (log K of order d), consistent with K having exponent 0 in your per-variable entry.

With eps = 0 this is sqrt(dT log K), matching the Omega(sqrt(dT)) lower bound polynomially in d. The 2020 abstract doesn't name the algorithm; a 2025 search snippet attributes the bound to phased elimination. I recall that the same paper shows the eps·sqrt(d)·T term is unavoidable for large K, but I did not confirm this. Only logarithmic gaps remain: log K, plus log T factors in high-probability statements.
